positive_control: Same command form, same tree: `grep -rn 'recover_all|recovery::' --include='*.rs' crates/ | grep -v /target/` returns ONLY crates/busbar-kernel/tests/recovery_and_ticks.rs:{13,40,58,793} and the definition itself. The identical grep for a kernel function that IS production-wired -- `grep -rn 'run_unit(' crates/busbar/src/root/` -- matches crates/busbar/src/root/transports.rs:522 and crates/busbar/src/root/harness.rs:126 (non-test production files), proving the search form, the path and the tree are right.

category: money lost on client disconnect / sweep with no production caller
summary: The whole sweep half of the hold-cell protocol is unbuilt. crates/busbar-kernel/src/tick.rs:267 states `This is the SECOND holder of a key to a hold cell, and there is no third`, and crates/busbar-kernel/src/inflight.rs:305 states `The drop guard MARKS; it never ends a unit. A marked slot whose task is gone is what the sweep turns into TaskLost`. In production NOTHING calls `UnitSlot::mark()`, nothing calls `UnitSlot::touch()`, and nothing calls `tick::sweep` or `tick::sweep_settle`. The production drop guard shown here removes the slot from the table instead of marking it, so even a sweep that existed could no longer find it.
failure_scenario: A client POSTs to the LLM plane. crates/busbar/src/root/units_llm.rs:528-540 opens the arrival hold and inserts the slot; the unit is admitted and dispatched upstream. The client hangs up (or the runtime is shutting down) while `run_unit_async` at units_llm.rs:565 is awaiting the upstream response, so axum drops the handler future. The await point never resumes: `settle_end` at units_llm.rs:585 never runs, the loop never takes the hold out of `slot.cell()`, and `canary.settled()` is never called. `Occupied::drop` then fires and does exactly one thing -- `self.table.remove(self.key)` -- deallocating the `Arc<UnitSlot>` with `Slot::Admitted(Hold)` still inside its `HoldCell` (crates/busbar-contract/src/caps/hold.rs:403-413 has no `impl Drop`). No Posted, no RecordClass::Transaction record, no ledger movement, no alarm: a charge for a call the upstream provider did bill is silently skipped, and it scales with the client-disconnect rate.
positive_control: `grep -rn '\.mark()|is_marked|\.marked' --include='*.rs' crates/ | grep -v /target/ | grep -v busbar-kernel/src/inflight.rs` matches ONLY crates/busbar-kernel/tests/recovery_and_ticks.rs:{189,298,380,457} and crates/busbar-kernel/src/tick.rs:144. The identical grep form against the SAME production files -- `grep -rn 'table.remove|inflight.remove' crates/busbar/src/ | grep -v /tests/` -- matches crates/busbar/src/root/units_llm.rs:991 and crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/admin_mount.rs:199, proving the method reaches production call sites in these exact files. Further control that the codebase KNOWS this hazard: crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/admin_mount.rs:172-176 adds `impl Drop for ExitPath` for precisely this reason ('a client that disconnects mid-walk drops that future, and a statement in a dropped future does not run') -- for the drain release, and not for the hold.

quote: /// This one is the kernel's own and stays here. The journal entry the write-ahead-log unit appends
category: WAL omits money events / doc names a record that is never written
summary: LEAD 2 CONFIRMED with a correction. There is no `RecordClass::Hold`, but that is not the defect -- `RecordClass::Transaction = 1` is documented at crates/busbar-kernel-wal/src/journal.rs:148 as 'A hold, a dispatch, a settlement or an adjustment: money moved', so a hold COULD ride it. The defect is that no production code ever writes one: every production `Entry::new(...)` in the tree is a settlement, an overdraft, a sealed audit record, a checkpoint, a migration marker or an Access record, and every one of them is built at or after SETTLE time. Nothing is appended at the door. This doc line asserts the opposite -- that the WAL unit appends a journal entry at the door -- and it is the premise `HoldRecord` and the whole recovery table are written against.
failure_scenario: Operator configures a data directory, so the journal really is on this node's disk. A unit is admitted, its hold reserves N nano-units, it dispatches upstream, and the node is SIGKILLed (OOM, power loss, `kill -9` during a deploy) before the settle. On reboot `Journal::in_directory` recovers a torn-tail-clean chain whose newest records are the PREVIOUS unit's settlement -- there is no record of the open hold anywhere on the medium, because none was ever written. `HoldRecord { reserved, checkpointed, dispatched, lease_epoch }` cannot be reconstructed from any durable artefact, so even if lead 1 were fixed and `recover_all` were wired in, it would be handed an empty slice and settle nothing. The open hold is unrecoverable by construction on the one deployment shape that keeps a durable journal.
positive_control: `grep -rn 'Entry::new(' --include='*.rs' crates/ | grep -v /target/` returns exactly six production sites: durability.rs:{174,192,213,330,649} and transports.rs:269 -- all post-settle or non-money classes. The same grep DOES match hold-time code elsewhere when it exists: `grep -rn 'record_hold_opened' crates/ | grep -v /target/` matches the ledger API at crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/settle.rs:251 and 30 call sites, ALL of which are test files (crates/busbar/src/root/tests/*, crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/tests/*), proving the grep finds hold-open call sites where they exist and that production has none.

category: money view silently zeroed after restart / replay filters out the records it needs
summary: LEADS 3 AND 4 BOTH CONFIRMED, and they compound. `build_for_node` opens the recovered on-disk journal at durability.rs:765-770 and then, on the very next lines, constructs a brand-new empty `Ledger` and `checkpoints: Vec::new()`. Nothing anywhere replays the journal's `Transaction` or `Checkpoint` records back into it: the only two production `Journal::replay()` calls in the whole tree are durability.rs:232 (`Durability::migration_marker`) and durability.rs:637 (`JournalMigrationRecords::read_marker`), and BOTH immediately `.filter(|r| r.class == RecordClass::Migration)`. The postings are durable and unreadable.
failure_scenario: A node with a configured data directory serves 10,000 requests; `Durability::settle_posted` writes 10,000 `RecordClass::Transaction` postings to `<data_dir>/0000000000000000.wal`, fsynced. The operator restarts the process for a deploy. `build_for_node` recovers the journal head and next_seq off the tail, then hands back a Durability whose `ledger.book()` is empty and whose `checkpoints` is empty. The admin reconciliation view (crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs:474-499 `NodeLedger::rows_of`, served via `identity_snapshot`) now reports zero settled nanos for every bucket, and because the legacy side is a fresh `RecordingRows::new()` as well, the reconciliation identity reports 0 == 0 and PASSES. An operator reconciling the node's books the morning after a deploy is told the identity holds and the node has settled nothing, while 10,000 postings sit verified on its own disk. Repeat per deploy: the node's money view resets to zero on every restart and the check that exists to catch that agrees with it.
positive_control: `grep -rn '\.replay()' --include='*.rs' crates/ | grep -v /target/` returns 24 hits; exactly two are outside a test file or the plugin-loader shim -- durability.rs:232 and durability.rs:637 -- and reading both shows the identical `RecordClass::Migration` filter. The same grep form DOES find non-Migration journal consumers where they exist: crates/busbar/src/root/tests/durability.rs:{385,538,679,745,848} and crates/busbar-kernel-wal/src/tests/journal_chain.rs:{122,409} replay and inspect Transaction records, proving the search reaches replay call sites that read other classes and that production has none.

category: replay path cannot see records past a segment roll
summary: `Journal::replay()` (journal.rs:960) is the only read-back path, and it delegates to `Wal::read_back()`, which scans ONLY the currently-open segment. Segments roll at `SEGMENT_BYTES = 64 MiB` (segment.rs:27), i.e. every 131,072 frames. So every record written before the first roll -- including the one-and-only `RecordClass::Migration` marker, which by construction is written on the first boot after the upgrade and is therefore the OLDEST record on the chain -- becomes invisible to replay for the rest of the node's life.
failure_scenario: A node with a data directory migrates on first boot; the Migration marker is sealed at node_seq 1 in segment 0. It serves ~131k journalled records (a day or two of traffic) and rolls to segment 1. It is then restarted. `JournalMigrationRecords::read_marker` (durability.rs:633-645) calls `replay()`, which scans segment 1 only, finds no Migration record, and returns `Ok(None)` -- which `busbar_kernel_ledger::migration::migrate` (crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/migration.rs:433) reads as 'never migrated'. It therefore re-reads the whole of the previous release's store rows and re-seals an 'opening' checkpoint under `OPENING_CHECKPOINT_SEQ` whose totals are the CURRENT (a year of spend later) figures rather than the opening ones, and appends a second Migration marker. In parallel `Durability::migration_marker()` -- the value the admin ledger view serves through `NodeLedger::migration_marker` (units_admin/mod.rs:571-573) -- answers `None`, telling an operator that a deployment which migrated months ago has never opened its balances. The module's own preamble (durability.rs:225-229) names this exact outcome as the thing the error/absence distinction exists to prevent.
positive_control: The crate's own test helper proves the distinction: crates/busbar-kernel-wal/src/tests/restart_after_a_roll.rs:52-60 defines `fn whole_log(segments: Vec<Box<dyn SegmentBackend>>)` which loops over EVERY segment calling `scan(&segment)`, with the comment 'which is what "the chain" means once the log has more than one segment and no single segment holds all of it'. Production has no equivalent -- `grep -rn 'read_back|highest_index' crates/ | grep -v /target/ | grep -v /tests/` shows `read_back` called only from journal.rs:961 over `self.segment`, and `highest_index` only from `open_tail` (wal.rs:553), which picks the newest segment and never walks back for content.

category: durable write can be lost with its directory entry
summary: A new segment file is created here with no fsync of the holding directory. `sync_holding_dir` exists in this very file (backend.rs:328) and is called from exactly one place, `DirectoryFactory::new` (backend.rs:363), and only when the DATA DIRECTORY itself was newly created. Every subsequent segment created by `Wal::roll` (wal.rs:513-521) gets its data fsynced by `FileSegment::sync` but its directory entry never is.
failure_scenario: A node with a data directory fills segment 0 and rolls; `roll()` opens `<data_dir>/0000000000000001.wal`, writes a batch of settlements into it, and `sync_data()` returns success, so `Journal::append` returns `Ok(JournalAck)` and the settlements are reported durable. The machine loses power before the filesystem commits the parent directory's metadata. On reboot the file `0000000000000001.wal` has no directory entry: `DirectoryFactory::highest_index` (backend.rs:395-405) lists the directory, sees only `0000000000000000.wal`, and `open_tail` resumes in segment 0 -- so the node also re-uses `(node, node_seq)` numbers it already issued for the lost settlements. Every posting acknowledged as durable in segment 1 is gone, which is exactly the outcome the doc comment at backend.rs:352-357 says the parent fsync exists to prevent ('A log that reports a durable write and then loses it to its own holding directory has broken the one promise this crate exists to keep').
positive_control: `grep -rn 'sync_holding_dir' --include='*.rs' crates/ | grep -v /target/` returns backend.rs:328 (definition) and backend.rs:363 (its single caller, inside `DirectoryFactory::new` under `if fresh`). The same grep form shows the pattern IS applied on the other durable-write path in this tree: crates/api/src/durable.rs calls `sync_holding_dir` at lines 125, 151 and 247 -- after the write and after the rename -- proving the search finds post-create directory syncs where they exist and that the WAL's roll path has none.

quote: /// in-place boot restore: apply each matching snapshot's lane-global fields and recreate
category: doc names a path that does not exist
summary: `restore_health_impl` documents itself as 'shared by the state-carrying constructor (config apply) and the in-place boot restore'. There is no in-place boot restore: the function has exactly one caller, `HealthState::new_with_limits_restored` (in_memory/mod.rs:315), which is itself reached only from the config-apply arm at crates/busbar-kernel/src/appbuild.rs:939 (`match prior { Some(p) => ... , None => HealthState::new_with_limits(...) }`, whose own comment says 'boot (None) starts fresh').
failure_scenario: A reader auditing whether the per-lane `max_requests` spend cap survives a process restart reads this line, concludes a boot restore path carries `LaneHealthSnapshot::budget` (vocab.rs:390) across a deploy, and stops looking. It does not -- the reset is deliberate and documented at vocab.rs:785 ('Reliability state is NEVER persisted to disk ... there is no boot-restore path') and enforced by crates/busbar/tests/no_state_persist.rs -- so the only harm is a doc line that contradicts the design decision two files away and invites exactly the wrong conclusion about a cost cap.

category: money under-reported on the operator read
summary: `CostModel::derive_spend_micros` carries the same unpriced-model drop as its cents twin, and it feeds the figure an operator reads as 'spend so far' and the figure they read as 'budget remaining'.
failure_scenario: Same mechanism as cost.rs:755: an unknown model on a present card contributes nothing. The consumer is `crates/busbar-kernel/src/governance/state.rs:1691`, `cost.derive_spend_micros(cell.model_views(), cell.billable_requests, true)`, whose result is immediately turned into headroom at state.rs:1693-1697: `let remaining_micros = bucket.budget_cap.map(|cap| cap.saturating_mul(10_000).saturating_sub(spend_micros).max(0));`. With the same 1,000,000 output tokens under a model the card no longer names, `spend_micros` reads 20,000 (the fee) instead of 19,020,000, so an operator inspecting a bucket that has consumed 1,902 cents of a 1,000-cent cap is shown ~2 cents spent and the FULL cap remaining. The under-report is silent -- there is no arm, no log line and no `unpriced` marker on the row -- so the figure is indistinguishable from a bucket that genuinely consumed nothing. Unlike the admin usage read at crates/busbar-core-admin/src/v1/service.rs:256-300, which reaches the same shape through a DOCUMENTED '#42 PARK' fallback that preserves the published 1.5.5 byte, this path has no such ruling on it: it is the 1.5.5 arithmetic still in place because nobody changed it.
positive_control: `grep -rn --include="*.rs" "derive_spend_micros" . | grep -v /tests/` matches the definition at cost.rs:775 AND the live callers `crates/busbar-kernel/src/governance/state.rs:1691` and `crates/busbar-core-admin/src/v1/service.rs:128,291` -- the same command matching those three is the control that the grep reaches production files, so the absence of any guard arm between :781 and :787 (read in full) is a read fact and not a search miss.

category: unguarded arithmetic in the books-balance verifier
summary: `residual` -- the one function that decides whether the books balance -- does its seven-term i128 sum with bare `+`/`-`, in a crate whose two other book files each carry an explicit 'EVERY BOOK OPERATOR SATURATES' header, so the verifier wraps on exactly the saturated columns those headers were written to produce.
failure_scenario: `crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/settle.rs:20-50` and `crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/totals.rs:22-38` each declare 'ONE GUARD POLICY FOR THIS FILE: EVERY BOOK OPERATOR SATURATES' and both were converted, so `Ledger::post` pins `settled` at `i128::MAX` (settle.rs:221) and `record_release` pins `drawn` at `i128::MIN` (settle.rs:273). `identity.rs` was left out of that conversion: :83-89 sums seven differences with bare `+`/`-` and :90 does `let drawn = now.drawn - since.drawn;`, and `Residual::amount` at :56 is `        self.accounted - self.drawn`. `[profile.release]` in the workspace `Cargo.toml:342-353` sets no `overflow-checks`, so these WRAP in the shipped binary and panic in a debug/test build -- the debug build is why no test catches it. Concrete state, all of it reachable through the saturating writers: `since = Totals::zero()`, `now.settled = i128::MAX`, `now.open_holds = 1`, `now.drawn = i128::MIN`, everything else zero. `accounted` = `i128::MAX + 1` wraps to `i128::MIN`; `drawn` = `i128::MIN`; `Residual::amount()` = `i128::MIN - i128::MIN` = 0, `holds()` = true, and `verify()` (crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/verify.rs:144-151) pushes NO `Finding::Imbalanced`. A maximally broken book -- a fully-drawn settled column, an open hold, and a drawn column pinned at the floor -- verifies CLEAN. The saturating twin of the same expression would pin at `i128::MIN`/`i128::MAX`, which is visibly not a real residual and alarms. The file's own preamble at :36-40 says the residual's MAGNITUDE is what an operator chases ('often recognisably one posting'); a wrapped magnitude is the one output that reading cannot survive.
positive_control: ZERO-CLAIM: identity.rs is absent from the money sweep's own arithmetic census. `grep -rn "kernel-ledger/src/identity" docs/` returns only file-verdicts and unconstructed-sweep rows (LIVE / reachable), never an arithmetic cell. CONTROL for that grep: the same sweep's E-table (`sed -n '118,145p' docs/design/1.6.0-money-sweep.md`) DOES enumerate `.../settle.rs:180,185-188,456` (E4-E6) and `.../totals.rs:199,204` (E7-E8) as 'bare' -- both of which are now converted to `saturating_*` in the tree -- proving the census exists, that it covers this crate, and that identity.rs was simply never in it. CONTROL for 'residual is live': `grep -rn --include="*.rs" "residual(" crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/` matches the definition at identity.rs:82 and the production callers `verify.rs:144` and `identity.rs:169` (`closed_window_is_settled`), so this is reached code, not a dead helper.

category: panic-under-lock / poisoned-mutex cascade
summary: The idle reaper adds an operator-supplied Duration to an Instant WHILE HOLDING the egress pool mutex; on overflow that panic poisons the pool for the process lifetime, and every later request's checkout then panics on `.expect("engine pool lock")`.
failure_scenario: `limits.pool_idle_timeout_secs` is a plain `u64` with no range validation anywhere (declared crates/busbar-kernel/src/config/limits.rs:244; `grep -rn pool_idle_timeout_secs crates/busbar-kernel/src/config/ crates/busbar/src/` finds only serde defaults and copies, no bound check) and is lowered verbatim into `idle_timeout: Duration::from_secs(spec.pool_idle_timeout_secs)` at crates/busbar-kernel/src/egress/engine/mod.rs:339. An operator (config file, or `limits.pool_idle_timeout_secs` through the admin PATCH surface at crates/busbar-core-admin/src/v1/json/handlers.rs:2748) sets it to a value >= 2^63. As soon as one h1 connection parks idle, `reap_loop` takes `inner.pool.lock().expect("engine pool lock")` (pool.rs:779) and evaluates `front.idle_since + timeout` (pool.rs:793; the identical form for h2 at pool.rs:806). `impl Add<Duration> for std::time::Instant` is `self.checked_add(other).expect("overflow when adding duration to instant")`, so it panics WITH THE POOL GUARD HELD. std poisons the mutex. Every one of the nine later `inner.pool.lock().expect("engine pool lock")` sites -- including `checkout` on the hot path (pool.rs:317) and `return_h1_conn` (pool.rs:723) -- then panics on every subsequent request. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS: the workspace leaves `panic = "unwind"` on purpose (Cargo.toml:351-353) and there is NO panic-catching layer anywhere in the tree, so the panic unwinds the hyper connection task -- the client gets a torn-down TCP connection, not a 500, every request multiplexed on that h2 connection dies with it, the process survives, and that client shard's egress is dead until restart. Contrast the rest of the tree, which deliberately poison-recovers for exactly this reason: `plane/handle_engine.rs:401`, `plane/auditlog.rs:443`, `plane/approvals.rs:172`, `plane/quarantine.rs:102`, `egress/mod.rs:368` all use `.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`; only the egress engine (`pool.rs` x9, `client.rs:139`, `engine/mod.rs:991`) and `ingress/byte_duplex.rs` (x6) cascade the poison.
positive_control: Zero-claim 1 (no panic-catching layer exists): `grep -rn 'CatchPanic|catch_panic' --include='*.rs' --include='*.toml' crates/ Cargo.toml` returns 0 matches AND `grep -rn 'tower-http' Cargo.toml crates/busbar/Cargo.toml crates/busbar-kernel/Cargo.toml` returns 0 (tower-http is not even a dependency); the control that the router DOES carry layers is `grep -rn '\.layer(' crates/busbar-kernel/src/router.rs` -> 8 matches (lines 685, 697, 701, 721, 730, 740). Zero-claim 2 (release overflow checks are off, so the debug/release split is real): `grep -n 'overflow-checks|debug-assertions' Cargo.toml` -> 0 matches, with the control `grep -n '^\[profile' Cargo.toml` -> line 342 `[profile.release]` proving the profile section exists and was searched.

category: panic in a plane callback leaks transport state
summary: The neutral duplex pump spawns a plane-supplied `handle` future with NO unwind boundary, so a panic in plane code permanently leaks that frame's `inflight` registry key for the life of the session and makes every later end-of-session drain wait its full 3s bound and report phantom stragglers.
failure_scenario: A peer opens a WS/stdio duplex session and sends one frame whose bytes make the bound plane's `DuplexPlane::handle` panic (an index, an `unwrap` on a parse, an arithmetic overflow in a debug build). `spawn_handler` (byte_duplex.rs:448-468) reserved the key with `shared.inflight.lock().unwrap().insert(key)` (line 449) BEFORE the spawn, and the matching `remove` at line 467 sits AFTER `plane.handle(frame, handle).await` with no `catch_unwind`, so it never runs. Concrete consequences, all inside the session: (a) the panic is swallowed silently -- the `JoinHandle` is dropped, so nothing but the default panic hook's stderr line records it; (b) the caller waiting on that frame's answer gets nothing and hangs to its own deadline; (c) `drain_and_flush`'s `working()` closure (line 486-488) reads `!shared.inflight.lock().unwrap().is_empty()` and is now true forever, so EVERY subsequent close of this session sleeps the full `EOF_DRAIN` = 3s (line 75) and then logs `stragglers = N` (line 504) claiming handlers are still running when none are. The permit itself is released (`let _permit = permit` is dropped on unwind), so capacity is not lost. The locks are NOT poisoned -- the panic is not inside a critical section -- which is why this is a leak rather than the cascade of the pool finding. The codebase's own standard for exactly this hazard is one directory away: `plane/handle_engine.rs:858` wraps the plane's `abandon` callback in `std::panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(..))` with a comment stating that a plane panic escaping there would corrupt engine state; `spawn_handler`'s own doc block (lines 459-464) reasons at length about plane-code hold discipline and never considers the panic case.
positive_control: Zero-claim (this pump has no unwind boundary): `grep -rn 'catch_unwind' crates/busbar-kernel/src/ingress/ crates/busbar-kernel/src/egress/ crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane/` returns exactly ONE match, `plane/handle_engine.rs:858`, and none in `ingress/`; the control that the grep and the path are right is that the same command over `crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/` matches 20+ times (vtable.rs:162,198,235,310,377,416,488; breaker.rs:314,396,442; journal.rs:487; scope.rs:355; egress.rs:1376,1388).

category: money / unchecked arithmetic in an invariant check
summary: `CostBreakdown::new` verifies its one stated money invariant using the raw non-saturating `u128` `Sum`, bypassing the saturating `Add`/`Sum` impls this same module defines twenty lines earlier precisely so a hostile or buggy plugin breakdown cannot wrap the accumulator.
failure_scenario: A plane calls `CostBreakdown::new(total, components)` with two or more top-level `CostComponent`s whose raw nanodollar amounts sum above `u128::MAX` (the type-level doc at cost.rs:56-62 names 'a hostile/buggy plugin breakdown' as the threat this module defends against, so this input is in the module's own stated scope). Line 221-225 sums `c.amount.0` through `impl Sum for u128`, not through `impl Sum for CostAmount` (cost.rs:65-70, which folds with the saturating `Add` at cost.rs:53-63). In the SHIPPED release profile overflow checks are off (`[profile.release]` at Cargo.toml:342 sets `opt-level`/`lto`/`codegen-units`/`strip` and never `overflow-checks`), so the sum WRAPS; if it wraps to exactly `total.0` the `top_level_sum != total.0` test at line 226 passes and an ill-formed breakdown -- the one thing the type promises cannot exist, per the module header at cost.rs:18-22 'a CostBreakdown that violates it cannot be constructed' -- reaches the ledger. In a debug/test build the identical input instead panics with 'attempt to add with overflow' inside the request-handling task, which (no panic-catching layer, see the pool finding's control) tears down the client's connection rather than returning an error. The same pattern repeats in the containment check at cost.rs:235-239 (`children_sum`). The fix is one character of intent: sum through `CostAmount`, or use `checked_add`/`fold` and return `CostError` on overflow, so the invariant check fails closed like every other arm of `new`.
positive_control: Zero-claim (no runtime division/modulo exists anywhere in this slice, so the classic div-by-zero shape is genuinely absent rather than unsearched): `grep -rnE '[a-z_0-9)\]] (/|%) [a-z_0-9(]' crates/busbar-kernel/src/{ingress,handlers,proto,plane,egress} crates/busbar-kernel/src/api.rs --include='*.rs' | grep -v /tests/` yields no arithmetic hit; the control that the regex and paths work is the one real division it DOES find elsewhere in the same tree, `crates/busbar-kernel/src/egress/engine/mod.rs:967` -- `(CONNECTS_PER_AUTHORITY_GLOBAL / super::establishment_shards_or_one()).max(1)` -- whose divisor is provably >= 1 (`set_establishment_shards` stores `n.max(1)` at mod.rs:243-244 and the reader `unwrap_or(1)`s).

category: connection/process leak - cleanup call skipped on all non-success exits
summary: The only call to Transport::close() in the whole egress crate is on the delivered-success path, so every other exit (most importantly any classified upstream error status) drops the dialled Conn without closing it, and Transport::close is the ONLY thing that removes the connection from the transport's own registry and tears down what it owns.
failure_scenario: attempt() binds `first: FirstFrame { conn, frame, frames }` from send()'s success arm (attempt.rs:333), then at line 349 computes `succeeded = matches!(status.class, Some(WireStatusClass::Success) | None)`. When the upstream answers any non-success status - a 429 rate limit, a 401 bad key, a 500/502/503 - line 354 returns classify_failure(&hop, status, permit, now), which is NOT passed `first`, so `first` (owning `conn` and the frame pump) is dropped with no close(). The same shape repeats on five more exits inside send(): write failure (attempt.rs:501), the per-attempt cap firing before the first frame (510), a read error on the first frame (520), a closed stream (522), and the outer budget timeout dropping the whole `work` future (528). Only deliver() reaches `hop.transport.close(conn, ...)` at attempt.rs:741-742. I traced what skipping it costs in the three concrete transports: each close() body is the sole site that does `self.conns.lock().unwrap().remove(&id)` - busbar-transport-grpc/src/transport.rs:395-414 (which also calls state.stop() and state.end_inbound(), the comment noting the task 'holds the socket'), busbar-transport-ws/src/transport.rs:745-771, and busbar-transport-stdio/src/transport.rs:478-507, where close() is the ONLY place `child.start_kill()` is ever called. The Conn handed back is a pure identity wrapper (busbar-transport-stdio/src/conn.rs:17-18: 'It carries nothing but identity: the real state lives in ConnState, looked up by id'), and the real ConnState is owned by the transport's own conns map, so dropping the egress-side Conn frees nothing and the registry's own strong reference keeps the resource alive. There is no Drop impl for ConnState in any of the three transport crates (positive control below), so there is no fallback reclaim. Net effect on a stdio-transport upstream that returns an application error per request: one leaked OS child process plus one permanent conns-map entry per failed request, for the life of the node, until the process table or fd limit is hit; on gRPC/WS the same request leaks a live background task and socket.
positive_control: `grep -rn '\.close(' crates/busbar-kernel-egress/src/*.rs` returns exactly ONE hit (attempt.rs:742), while the same grep style finds the real dial/write/frames call sites (`grep -rn 'transport.dial|transport\.frames|transport\.write'` -> attempt.rs:486, 496, 503), proving the search resolves real call sites and the single-close result is genuine. For the no-Drop-fallback claim: `grep -n 'impl Drop for ConnState' crates/busbar-transport-{grpc,ws,stdio}/src/*.rs` returns zero, while `grep -n 'fn close' ...` on the same files returns the three real close() bodies quoted above.

category: unbounded blocking join defeats the stated timeout backstop
summary: The recovery path for a wedged connect - the very path whose comment promises 'a bounded timeout so a wedged connect cannot pin the caller' - ends in an unbounded join.join() on a per-hop OS thread that cannot yet observe the stop signal, so a pre-head wedge pins the caller for the full duration of that wedge.
failure_scenario: Each governed egress hop spawns its own OS thread at egress.rs:689-691 (`std::thread::Builder::new().name("busbar-egress".into()).spawn(...)`) running run_http_stream. The caller then bounds its wait at egress.rs:723 with `head_rx.recv_timeout(timeout.saturating_add(Duration::from_secs(5)))`. On timeout it does `stop.notify_one()` (726) then `let _ = join.join();` (727). But the ONLY observer of that notify is `() = stop.notified() => break,` at egress.rs:1047, inside the chunk pump loop that is reached only AFTER the connect head has been produced - so a thread wedged before the head never sees it, and join() then blocks the caller for as long as the thread stays wedged. Everything else pre-head IS bounded (`let deadline = tokio::time::Instant::now() + timeout;` at 996 feeding `send_bounded(&client, req, deadline).await` at 997, covering connect/TLS/headers), which leaves exactly one unbounded pre-head step: the DNS resolution at egress.rs:893-900, `crate::net_guard::resolve_and_pin(host_name, port, https, &crate::net_guard::SystemResolver, policy)`, called synchronously inside rt.block_on. That call has no deadline available to it at all (see the companion finding on the Resolver seam). Concretely: an operator-configured upstream whose nameserver is black-holed makes resolve_and_pin block for the OS resolver's own retry schedule (tens of seconds with a default resolv.conf; longer or unbounded with aggressive retry settings or a custom Resolver impl). After timeout+5s the caller's recv_timeout fires, the notify is a no-op, and join() at 727 holds the calling thread for the remainder of that resolver hang. Each concurrent hop to that host wedges one busbar-egress thread plus its caller, so the bound the code advertises is exactly the bound it fails to provide on the one failure it was written for.
positive_control: `grep -n 'stop.notified()' crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/egress.rs` returns exactly one line (1047), while the same grep for the writers `grep -n 'stop.notify'` returns the real notify sites (197, 726) - so the single-observer result is a genuine zero-elsewhere, not a failed search. The close() path at egress.rs:197-203 does the same handle.join() but is safe precisely because the handle only exists post-head, when line 1047 IS live.

category: missing timeout - seam structurally cannot carry a deadline
summary: The Resolver seam that every destination pin runs its one DNS resolution through takes no deadline and returns no future, so the resolution cannot be bounded by GuardPolicy.timeout or by any caller, and the shipped implementation blocks a thread synchronously with no timeout of its own.
failure_scenario: resolve_and_pin (net.rs:847-866) receives `policy: GuardPolicy`, whose `pub timeout: std::time::Duration` (net.rs:407) is documented at net.rs:405-406 as 'How long one hop may take, end to end. Held here rather than at the client so the ceiling travels with the rest of the policy instead of being a fifth argument somebody forgets.' It threads that policy into judge_host_name and pin_answer but never into `resolver.resolve(host)` - and the trait signature has no parameter that could carry it. The only production implementer, busbar-kernel/src/net_guard.rs:78-106, runs `tokio::net::lookup_host(target).await` inside a `std::thread::scope` worker with its own current-thread runtime and `.join()`s it synchronously, with no tokio::time::timeout anywhere. Because the seam is synchronous, a caller cannot rescue it from outside either: wrapping the enclosing async fn in tokio::time::timeout cannot interrupt a call that never yields to the runtime. Concretely, a configured upstream/CIMD/agent hostname whose nameserver black-holes makes every caller of resolve_and_pin block for the OS resolver's full retry schedule with no ceiling the deployment can set - and at plane_host/egress.rs:893-900 that blocked thread is then joined unboundedly by its caller (see the companion finding), converting a DNS stall into a stalled request path with one wedged OS thread per concurrent hop.
positive_control: `grep -rn '\.timeout' crates/` finds real consumers of GuardPolicy.timeout elsewhere - e.g. crates/busbar-oauth2/src/cimd.rs:142 `let deadline = tokio::time::Instant::now() + policy.timeout;` and crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/egress.rs:996 - proving the field is live and consumed in general, and that the grep works; it is specifically the resolve step that never receives it. Quotes at net.rs:407, net.rs:633 and net.rs:847-866 were each re-read directly from the pinned tree.

category: untimed I/O under a lock, amplified into a cascade by the inline sweep
summary: The per-handle mutex is held across an untimed durable-store round-trip, and because the retention sweep runs inline inside unrelated submit() calls and keeps re-selecting the wedged handle, one stuck store write permanently blocks one additional submit() caller every second with no ceiling.
failure_scenario: lock_slot is a poison-recovering std::sync::Mutex acquire (handle_engine.rs:406-408) with no try/timeout variant. It is taken at handle_engine.rs:730 (mutate), 776 (scoped_mutate) and 842 (the sweep's abandon phase), and the guard is held across apply_mutation_to_slot, whose first action is `self.upsert_record(rec)?` (handle_engine.rs:522-523) -> store.upsert_plane_record, a call into an arbitrary dyn PlaneStore plugin. No tokio::time::timeout, Duration or deadline appears anywhere in the plane/ slice. Now the amplification: submit() runs the sweep inline before installing a new, unrelated handle - `if self.claim_sweep(now) { self.sweep(now, bounds, &abandon, &report_fail); }` (handle_engine.rs:681-682) - and claim_sweep hands that work to the first caller of each second. The sweep's abandon phase selects candidates that are non-terminal and whose updated_at is older than abandon_secs, then takes their per-handle lock at line 842. A handle whose store write is stuck never advances updated_at, so once it crosses abandon_secs it remains a candidate forever. Therefore: a store plugin that stalls on one handle's write (network partition, slow disk, plugin bug) wedges that handle's lock indefinitely; every subsequent second, whichever submit() caller wins claim_sweep walks into line 842 and blocks on that same lock forever. The result is a steadily growing pile of permanently blocked caller tasks/threads - roughly one per second for as long as the backend is stuck - with no timeout, no ceiling and no recovery short of a process restart. The design doc's existing mitigation (lifting abandon writes out of the OUTER map lock, implemented at handle_engine.rs:822-829) protects other handles from the outer lock but does nothing about this inner-lock-plus-no-timeout combination.
positive_control: `grep -rn 'tokio::time|Duration::from|timeout' crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane/*.rs` returns ZERO hits; the identical grep run against crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/egress.rs returns six real hits (lines 71, 280, 283, 574, 576, 702), proving the pattern and the method both work and that the plane/ zero is genuine. Quotes at 406-408, 522-523, 681-682 and 842 were each re-read from the pinned tree.

category: unbounded process-global cache, never evicted
summary: The verify-freshness cache behind an unconditionally wired vtable slot is a process-global map that is only ever inserted into and read - it has no remove, retain, sweep or cap - while the two sibling fields of the very same struct do have cleanup paths.
failure_scenario: VerifyCache lives in a process-wide OnceLock (trust.rs:86-89) and its verify_lookup/verify_store pair is wired into the live vtable with no feature gate (vtable.rs:54-55: `verify_lookup: Some(trust::verify_lookup), verify_store: Some(trust::verify_store),`). Across the whole file the `fresh` map is touched in exactly two places: a read at trust.rs:186 (`if c.fresh.get(&ckey).is_some_and(|&exp| now < exp)`) and the single write at trust.rs:251 (`c.fresh.insert(ckey.clone(), expires);`). There is no removal of any kind, and crucially entries are not even reclaimed once they go stale - an expired entry is simply read as a miss and then overwritten only if that same subject is verified again. So a busbar process that verifies many distinct counterparties over its lifetime (dynamically discovered A2A agents, MCP servers, or high volume against many distinct upstreams) accumulates one permanent (u32, Vec<u8>) -> u64 entry per distinct subject ever seen, keyed on subject bytes, growing with the total number of identities ever verified rather than the number currently live. The asymmetry inside the same struct is what makes this an oversight rather than a decision: `leading` and `inflight` are both cleaned up on the verify_store happy path (trust.rs:254-255) and by a DispatchScope-registered reclaim closure for a leader that never stores (trust.rs:205-210); only the field that actually holds the cache entries has no reclaim at all.
positive_control: `grep -n 'fresh' crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/trust.rs` returns only doc lines plus the declaration (76), the read (186) and the insert (251) - no remove/retain/clear. That the search would have found such a call is shown by the same method locating a real amortized sweep in this same slice: crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/creds.rs:101-104 `reg.map.retain(|_, m| now_unix <= m.expires_unix)`, and a real FIFO bound at identity.rs:46/88 (MAX_RETAINED_IDENTITIES). The bounded siblings are also test-covered (tests/creds_tests.rs:133, tests/identity_tests.rs:70) while tests/trust_tests.rs has no bound/eviction test.

category: ABI gap - resource acquirable over FFI with no release verb
summary: cost_reserve is wired into the frozen plane-host C ABI and inserts a lease into a process-global map, but the ABI exposes no close/forget counterpart, so a plane driving the FFI vtable can open leases it has no way to ever release.
failure_scenario: The FFI shim cost_reserve (cost_host.rs:142-176) mints a lease via `let lease = register(hold);` at cost_host.rs:169, inserting into the process-global LEASES map. Unlike its siblings it registers nothing in the DispatchScope arena for automatic reclaim (contrast breaker.rs:326-333 register_settling_admission and govern.rs:68 register_admission) - deliberately, since a lease is meant to outlive one dispatch call. The problem is that the explicit release verb is absent from the ABI: the PlaneHostVtable in crates/busbar-plugin/src/hot/host.rs carries exactly `pub cost_reserve: Option<CostReserveFn>,` (host.rs:722) and `pub cost_settle: Option<CostSettleFn>,` (host.rs:724), with fn-pointer aliases CostReserveFn (host.rs:547) and CostSettleFn (host.rs:562) and no cost_close/cost_forget field or alias anywhere. The working release logic does exist - close_lease at cost_host.rs:118-130, with its double-refund guard - but it is reachable only through the in-process MeteringHost trait (mod.rs:625-626, declared mod.rs:2634), i.e. by statically linked callers such as busbar-voice, not by anything crossing the #[repr(C)] seam. So a plane compiled against the hot ABI that opens one lease per long-running session (the module's own stated use case) can settle against it repeatedly but can never close it: every session it ever opens leaves one permanent CostHold in LEASES for the life of the process. Because the vtable is documented append-only and frozen, this cannot be corrected after ship without an ABI version bump, which is what makes it release-gating rather than merely a leak.
positive_control: `grep -n 'cost_|CostReserve|CostSettle|CostClose' crates/busbar-plugin/src/hot/host.rs` returns only the reserve/settle slots, aliases and stubs - no close. The same grep style finds other real slot families in that identical file (meter_charge at host.rs:587, breaker_admit at 589, breaker_admit_reason at 635), proving the search resolves vtable slots and the cost_close zero is genuine. close_lease's correctness is separately test-covered at tests/cost_host_tests.rs:183-199, so the gap is reachability, not logic.

category: cap does not bound the population that actually grows
summary: max_retained bounds only the terminal handle population; the sweep can never evict an active handle, so a workload that keeps handles active has no ceiling inside this engine at all.
failure_scenario: The eviction rule is implemented at handle_engine.rs:896-907: it walks expiry.by_age and skips every non-terminal entry (`if !*terminal { continue; }` at line 902), so an active handle is structurally unreachable by the cap. The handles map and its expiry index therefore grow with the number of concurrently active handles, bounded by nothing this engine enforces. There is a partial mitigation - the sweep's abandon phase can mark a stale active handle terminal - but it only fires for handles idle longer than bounds.abandon_secs AND only when the plane's abandon callback returns Some(mutation); a handle that keeps being updated, or a plane whose callback returns None, is never reclaimed. So a plane that admits many concurrent long-running handles (the engine imposes no admission control of its own) grows RAM without limit while max_retained never fires, because nothing is terminal to evict. This is acknowledged in-repo - the doc comment at handle_engine.rs:136-142 states it outright and points to docs/design/handle-engine-retention-sweep.md, which explicitly declines to make max_retained a true ceiling and names ADMISSION as the intended place for the bound. It is reported here because the bound lives outside this engine, so whether it exists at all depends on each caller, and the field's name invites the opposite assumption.
positive_control: The eviction machinery does work where it applies, which shows the zero is specific rather than a broken search: rule (1) at handle_engine.rs:801-803 with take_due, and evict_verified at handle_engine.rs:928-950, both remove aged-out TERMINAL handles from handles and expiry together with no orphaned index keys. The active-population zero comes from the explicit `if !*terminal { continue; }` filter re-read at line 902.

category: unbounded in-memory accumulation behind a wired ABI slot
summary: The journal_append/journal_read vtable pair retains every record ever appended for a scope in an in-process Vec with no truncation, compaction or cap, and re-verifies the entire accumulated chain on every read, so both memory and per-read CPU grow monotonically with total volume journaled.
failure_scenario: journal_append (journal.rs:1048) is wired unconditionally into the vtable (vtable.rs:61: `journal_append: Some(super::journal::journal_append),`). Each call appends to ScopeState.rows via `st.rows.push(record);` (journal.rs:1094) in the process-global journals() map (journal.rs:1020-1024), keyed by a bare u32 scope. Nothing in the file ever removes, truncates or caps rows. journal_read additionally calls `crate::audit::verify_chain(&st.rows)` (journal.rs:1131) over the whole accumulated vector on a cold read, so read cost grows with total history too. Once a hosted plane drives this slot, a scope that is appended to steadily grows record bytes plus hashes in RAM for the life of the process, and its reads get progressively more expensive. Reachability caveat, stated plainly: this specific slot is currently dormant - the live in-core appenders (plane/auditlog.rs:746, calllog.rs:693) go through journal_append_scoped* into the separate streams()/DurableStream family, which does have eviction. So there is no failure today; the defect is that the ABI-facing implementation a real plane will bind to has no bound at all, and the module's own doc calls it 'the store stand-in this Phase-2 bridge holds in-process'.
positive_control: `grep -rn 'journal_append\b' crates/` (excluding journal_append_scoped) returns only the definition, the vtable wiring, ABI stubs and tests - no in-core production caller - which is the dormancy claim; the identical grep including the _scoped variants DOES return live core callers (plane/auditlog.rs:704, 746, 917, 1084 and calllog.rs:693, 737), proving the search finds real callers when they exist. The bounded contrast lives in the same file: the streams()/DurableStream family has journal_forget (journal.rs:853-869) and journal_compact (journal.rs:877-903).

category: ABI shape forces the uncapped path
summary: journal_register - the only durable-stream registration reachable over the ABI - always passes usize::MAX, which disables the position-cache LRU, and the descriptor POD has no field that could express a cap, so any third-party plane is structurally stuck with an unevictable position cache.
failure_scenario: journal_register (journal.rs:454-463) hardcodes usize::MAX as the cap, and per the Journal type's own contract that value disables eviction entirely. The bounded entry point journal_register_capped exists (journal.rs:472) and is used by core itself for exactly the unbounded-key-space case - calllog.rs:195 registers the call log that way - but it is not reachable across the seam because JournalStreamDesc carries no cap field. So when a hosted plane registers a durable journal stream keyed by a naturally unbounded scope (session id, conversation id, per-request id), streams()[kind].journal.positions gains one entry per distinct scope ever seen and retains it unless the plane remembers to call journal_forget (journal.rs:853) on every termination path including error, cancel and crash paths. Under sustained traffic with high scope churn that is unbounded per-process growth whose only mitigation is perfect discipline in third-party code. The in-file comment at journal.rs:459-462 documents the rationale (a durable TABLE opts out of eviction; a stream needing an LRU 'registers WITHIN CORE through journal_register_capped, which the ABI descriptor cannot express'), so this is a known and deliberate shape - it is reported because the consequence lands on plane authors who have no way to opt into the bound, and because the ABI is append-only once shipped. Currently dormant for the same reason as the preceding finding.
positive_control: `grep -rn 'journal_register_capped' crates/busbar-kernel/src/` finds the definition (journal.rs:472) and exactly one real caller, calllog.rs:195 - proving the bounded path exists, is used, and that the grep resolves callers; the absence of any cap field is confirmed by reading JournalStreamDesc in crates/busbar-plugin/src/hot/host.rs.

category: expiry only evaluated on a lookup that may never happen
summary: The process-lifetime durable work-handle registry has exactly one removal site, reached only from inside workhandle_resume and only when ttl_secs is non-zero, so handles opened with no expiry, or whose resume never arrives, are never reclaimed.
failure_scenario: workhandle_open inserts into the static DURABLE registry at dispatch.rs:166 (`reg.handles.insert(raw, DurableEntry { ... opened_at_ms: busbar_kernel::store::now_ms(), })`). The only removal in the file is line 211, inside workhandle_resume, guarded by `if entry.ttl_secs != 0` and then by the expiry comparison. There is no periodic sweeper. Two leaks follow. First, any handle opened with ttl_secs == 0 ('never expires') is never removed on any path, resumed or not - a permanent entry per open by construction. Second, a handle with a real TTL whose plane never calls workhandle_resume again - the 202-parked unit is abandoned, the callback that would resume it never arrives, the peer disconnects - also stays forever, because expiry is only ever evaluated as a side effect of a lookup that never happens. A plane that parks many long-running units (the module's own stated use case) with any abandonment rate at all leaks one DurableEntry per abandoned unit for the life of the process. Opting out of the DispatchScope arena is correct here (a durable handle must outlive the request that opened it) but nothing was put in place of what the arena would have reaped. Dormant today for the same reason as the two preceding findings.
positive_control: `grep -n 'reg.handles.insert|reg.handles.remove' crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/dispatch.rs` returns exactly one insert (166) and one remove (211), and no sweep/expire function exists in the file. The contrast within the same slice shows what a paired lifecycle looks like and that the search finds it: egress.rs pairs its insert (egress.rs:804) with an arena closer (egress.rs:806-807) calling close_and_remove (egress.rs:241-242), and pipe.rs:346 does the same via scope.register_pipe.

category: latent unbounded registry - the fix its documented twin already received
summary: The trust-anchor registry registers one entry per config generation with no cap or eviction, which is precisely the hot-reload accumulation bug its documented counterpart identity.rs was given a FIFO bound to fix; it is currently unreachable in production, so this is a latent defect rather than a live one.
failure_scenario: register() (trust_anchor.rs:53-57) mints a fresh ref and does `registry().insert(trust_anchor_ref, roots);` (trust_anchor.rs:55) with no cap, no eviction and no replacement of the prior generation's entry. identity.rs is described in-file as this module's 'mutual-handshake counterpart' sharing the identical boot-time-per-config-generation registration pattern, and it carries the fix plus the failure statement this module lacks: MAX_RETAINED_IDENTITIES = 256 (identity.rs:46) enforced by an eviction loop (identity.rs:88), with its doc at identity.rs:23-27 describing exactly the bug - 'a long-lived process hot-reloading its config accumulated one full private-key set per reload for its entire lifetime - nothing ever evicted the previous generation's entries.' trust_anchor.rs registers per config generation the same way (the a2a trusting_root path) and would accumulate one full certificate set per config reload for the life of the process. Reported at LOW and not higher because it is honestly not exploitable in the shipped build: both modules carry #![cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))] and trust_anchor.rs:26-29 states register() is 'reached only by tests until' the egress call sites are flipped onto the seam. It is worth gating on because the wiring is planned, the sibling already proved the failure mode is real in this codebase, and the fix is a few lines.
positive_control: `grep -n 'MAX_RETAINED_IDENTITIES' crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/identity.rs` returns the bound and its eviction loop (46, 88, plus docs at 23 and 54), while the same grep style against trust_anchor.rs finds no cap constant at all - proving the search locates such bounds when present. Test coverage mirrors it: tests/identity_tests.rs has registering_past_the_cap_evicts_the_oldest_entries_and_bounds_the_registry (line 70) and many_registrations_never_grow_the_registry_past_the_retained_cap (line 101); tests/trust_anchor_tests.rs has no bound or eviction test.

category: ABI-reachable resource mint with no ABI-reachable release verb (same shape as cost_host.rs LEASES, finding above)
summary: identity_admit (unconditionally wired into the plane-host vtable for every plane, vtable.rs:108, "no plane feature gates it") stashes a resolved (AuthPrincipal, PlaneRequestCtx) — including the live enforcement Arc<VirtualKey> — into a process-global REGISTRY keyed by an opaque handle; the only removal function, take() (identity_admit.rs:66-71), is pub(crate) and is not exposed as any vtable slot, so any caller of this ABI-reachable slot other than the one internal caller that happens to pair it today has no verb it could ever call to release what it stashed.
failure_scenario: stash() (identity_admit.rs:53-57) inserts into REGISTRY on every successful admit; take() is the only remove site in the file and is annotated `#[allow(dead_code)]` with the comment "Consumed only by identity_admit_over (the inbound stdio admission path); a build whose planes admit on their own door leaves it uncalled, hence the unconditional dead-code allow" (identity_admit.rs:63-65) — the authors' own words concede a configuration exists where nothing calls take() at all. identity_admit is documented as letting "a plane admit an inbound session WITHOUT naming crate::auth" (identity_admit.rs:7) and is wired with no feature gate for any plane, dlopen or static. Exhaustive search of crates/busbar-plugin/src/hot/host.rs (grep -n "identity_admit\|IdentityAdmitted\|IdentityId") shows exactly one slot family reaching an IdentityId (identity_admit itself) and no identity_take/identity_release counterpart anywhere in the ABI. Today's only in-tree caller, identity_admit_over (mod.rs:305-363), happens to call take() immediately after every stash on the same call stack, so no leak occurs on that specific path. But the moment any other caller invokes this vtable slot directly for its documented purpose — a real out-of-process plane admitting its own inbound session, exactly the use case the module's own header describes — the resulting IdentityId has no ABI verb that could ever consume or release it: the REGISTRY entry (holding a live Arc<VirtualKey> with its group chain and budget buckets) leaks permanently, once per admitted session, for the life of the process.
positive_control: grep -n "identity_admit\|IdentityAdmitted\|IdentityId" crates/busbar-plugin/src/hot/host.rs matches only the one slot's declaration and doc comments, zero release-verb hits; the identical search style for cost_reserve's sibling in the same file (grep -n "cost_reserve\|cost_settle" crates/busbar-plugin/src/hot/host.rs) DOES find a paired release/settle slot (cost_settle, host.rs:724,984,1351), proving the method surfaces a release verb where the ABI actually provides one — so the total absence of any identity-release verb is a genuine ABI gap, not a search miss.

category: missing timeout on a network read — an idle/silent peer pins a task and its per-connection state indefinitely
summary: The WS reader task's only suspension point is an untimed `ws_rx.next().await` with no idle/ping-liveness check anywhere in this file, and no connection-level idle timeout exists anywhere else in ingress/proxy or the wider busbar-kernel crate either, so a peer that completes the WS upgrade and then sends nothing (without closing) parks this task — plus the writer task, the bounded/unbounded channel pair, and the socket — for as long as the underlying TCP connection stays open, with no host-side bound.
failure_scenario: `channel()` (duplex_ws.rs:71-110) spawns a reader task (line 78-96) whose loop condition is `while let Some(msg) = ws_rx.next().await` with no `tokio::time::timeout` wrapper and no periodic ping sent from the host side to probe liveness (the file's own comment at line 91 notes only that "the WS layer answers pings itself" — i.e. it reacts to a peer's ping, it never originates one to detect a peer that has stopped talking). A client that completes the HTTP→WS upgrade and then simply stops sending frames — no malice required, an ordinary NAT/firewall keeping the TCP session open with no traffic, or a client that opened the socket and then hung — leaves this task (and the paired writer task, the `Arc<Shared>` state threaded through `byte_duplex::serve_messages`, and the bounded 64-frame inbound channel) alive indefinitely. Nothing in this file, `ingress/mod.rs`, `proxy/`, or `handlers/` closes an idle WS connection, and a repo-wide search found no idle-connection-timeout mechanism anywhere in `busbar-kernel` (the only "idle" hits in the crate are jemalloc's unrelated memory idle-purge fallback in `crates/busbar/src/main.rs`). Many such connections opened and left silent accumulate tasks and per-connection state with no time-based ceiling; the only backstop is whatever OS-level TCP keepalive or reverse-proxy timeout an operator configures outside this codebase, which this slice neither sets nor documents.
positive_control: `grep -rn "idle\|keepalive\|keep_alive\|ping_interval" crates/busbar-kernel/src/ingress crates/busbar-kernel/src/proxy crates/busbar-kernel/src/handlers` returns zero hits; the broader `grep -rln "idle\|keepalive\|ping_interval" crates/busbar-kernel/src/` and `crates/busbar/src/main.rs` returns only jemalloc-allocator idle-purge code, unrelated to connection liveness — proving the search method finds real hits when the term is used for something, so its complete absence for WS/connection idling specifically is a genuine gap. The same file DOES carefully bound other resources (`MAX_QUEUED_INBOUND_FRAMES = 64` at duplex_ws.rs:38, and the message/frame size cap via `max_inbound_message_bytes()` applied at duplex_ws.rs:128-130), showing the omission of a time-based idle bound is a specific gap in an otherwise resource-conscious file, not a general absence of attention to limits.

quote: //! DORMANT: [`install`] registers ZERO planes, so every gauntlet/session path stays on the substrate
category: money-authority / startup wiring contradiction
summary: This file's own module doc says install() registers zero planes (dormant), but the function doc three lines below (line 51: "W2.b — EVERY plane is FLIPPED onto the unified kernel loop") and the function body itself (lines 63-76) unconditionally register the kernel-loop runner for mcp, a2a, llm-native and voice under their already-default-on feature flags, and this contradicts three OTHER files in the same slice that independently assert the flip has not happened.
failure_scenario: An operator builds busbar 1.6.0 with default features (plane-mcp, plane-a2a, proto-llm, plane-voice, root-mcp, root-a2a, root-llm, root-voice are all default-on per crates/busbar/Cargo.toml:192). At boot, main() calls register_planes() then root::gauntlet_install::install() (main.rs:638). install()'s body (gauntlet_install.rs:64-75) unconditionally calls flip_one_shot_to_kernel(busbar_mcp::PLANE_KEY), flip_one_shot_to_kernel(busbar_a2a::PLANE_KEY), flip_one_shot_to_kernel(busbar_llm::PLANE_DECL.key) and flip_session_to_kernel(busbar_voice::PLANE_KEY) — each of which calls register_gauntlet_runner/register_session_runner in busbar-kernel's plane_host seam, which busbar_kernel::plane_host::run_gauntlet consults on every request (one_shot_runner(key) at plane_host/mod.rs:2356) to decide whether to dispatch through the new unified kernel loop or the legacy inline verify-then-drive fallback. So in EVERY default build, every MCP/A2A/LLM-native/Voice request is already routed through the new kernel-loop money-settlement path (crates/busbar/src/root/gauntlet_kernel.rs's GauntletKernelUnit / busbar_kernel::teller::run_unit[_async]) rather than the legacy path. But three other files in this exact slice say this exact flip has NOT happened and must not happen until an unshipped verification step ("the fleet-box money oracle", DECISIONS #29) goes green: (1) main.rs:635 itself, in the comment immediately above the install() call site: "DORMANT — it registers ZERO planes, so every gauntlet/session path stays on the substrate loop, byte-identical"; (2) crates/busbar/src/root/a2a_kernel_rider.rs:16-17: "DORMANT — DUAL-PATH, MONEY AUTHORITY NOT FLIPPED. The shipped A2A authority stays `busbar_kernel::plane_host::run_gauntlet` at `crates/busbar-a2a/src/a2a/receive.rs:892`" (that rider's own kernel-loop entry point, run_a2a_via_kernel, is correctly gated `#[cfg(test)]` so it cannot affect production — gauntlet_install.rs's flip is NOT so gated); (3) crates/busbar/src/root/units_llm.rs:1931-1933: "IT IS DORMANT. Nothing mounts it, and it is NOT the shipped authority: the shipped `run()` still calls `run_gauntlet`... the flip is thrown only once loop==legacy is proven byte-identical" (that dormant sibling, native_run_via_loop, is also correctly `#[cfg(test)]`-gated at units_llm.rs:1939). If the kernel-loop settlement path has any undiscovered behavioral difference from the legacy per-plane metering — exactly the risk the fleet-box oracle process exists to catch before the flip is thrown — then every MCP, A2A, LLM-native and Voice request in a stock 1.6.0 build is silently exposed to that unproven path today, with no feature flag, changelog entry, or code comment (other than this contradiction) signalling it. Conversely, if gauntlet_install.rs's code is correct and the flip really was deliberately completed, then main.rs, a2a_kernel_rider.rs and units_llm.rs all carry stale documentation that would send an on-call engineer investigating a billing discrepancy to inspect the wrong (already-replaced) code path. Either reading is a release-blocking correctness problem in the composition root's own account of which path settles money.
positive_control: grep -n "flip_one_shot_to_kernel\|flip_session_to_kernel" crates/busbar/src/root/gauntlet_install.rs shows the four unconditional calls inside pub fn install() (lines 65,67,73,75); grep -n "DORMANT" crates/busbar/src/root/*.rs main.rs shows the same string used with the opposite meaning ("registers nothing yet") in main.rs:635, gauntlet_install.rs:11, a2a_kernel_rider.rs:4/16, and units_llm.rs:1931 — proving the search reliably surfaces both the contradicting claim and the contradicted code in the same pass.

quote: //! two are introduced, and it is the whole of what "switching the MCP plane onto the kernel" means.
category: misleading composition-root documentation / dead metering code
summary: units_mcp.rs's module doc presents itself, in the present tense with no dormancy disclosure, as the completed MCP-plane-onto-kernel switch-over, but none of its per-request money/metering functions (arrival, read_ingress, decode, authenticate, admit, route/legs, meter, settle, audit_inputs, evidence, mount) has any caller anywhere in crates/busbar/src outside the module's own test file; the only production call site into this module is the boot-time self-consistency check root::units_mcp::seal(&McpPlane::EMPTY) at main.rs:354.
failure_scenario: A maintainer reads units_mcp.rs, sees no DORMANT marker (unlike units_llm.rs's clearly-labeled `#[cfg(test)]` dormant rider at units_llm.rs:1911-1939, or units_a2a.rs's dormant status which is at least disclosed in the sibling file a2a_kernel_rider.rs), and concludes this file's admit()/meter()/settle() functions are what prices and settles real MCP traffic. They fix a pricing bug here (e.g. in priced/settle logic) believing it changes production billing. Because grep across crates/busbar/src for "units_mcp::arrival", "units_mcp::decode", "units_mcp::authenticate", "units_mcp::admit", "units_mcp::meter", "units_mcp::settle", and "units_mcp::evidence" returns zero non-test matches, the fix ships with the module docs updated and the tests green, but real MCP requests (served through busbar-mcp's own GauntletPlane implementation via busbar_kernel::plane_host::run_gauntlet) are unaffected — the actual money-relevant defect, wherever it lives, remains unfixed and the operator is told it was resolved.
positive_control: grep -rn "units_mcp::seal" crates/busbar/src finds the one real production caller (main.rs:354); grep -rn "units_llm::PATH_INGRESS\|units_llm::BODY_INGRESS" crates/busbar/src finds units_llm.rs's equivalent top-level entry point IS wired into main.rs's register_protocols() (main.rs:219,242) and is reached at runtime via body_arrival/path_arrival calling NODE.answer (units_llm.rs:1715) — proving the grep method finds real wiring where it exists, and its absence for units_mcp::arrival/decode/authenticate/admit/route/meter/settle/evidence is a genuine zero, not a search miss.

category: metering asymmetry / dead field
summary: Decoded.streaming (set to false/true at units_mcp.rs:231/236 depending on whether the plane's ingress was OneShot or Open) is never read by any consumer: units_mcp.rs's own decode() function at line 256 destructures only `decoded.op` (`Ok(Read::Unit(decoded)) => Decision::proceed(token, decoded.op)`), discarding `streaming` and `facts` from the same value, and no other file in the slice reads it either.
failure_scenario: units_llm.rs's sibling plane needs an explicit late-accrual/Drop-based mechanism (LateAccrual/LateBody, units_llm.rs:803-976) specifically because a streaming HTTP response's true token usage is only known after the body drains, past the terminal settlement step — and getting that distinction wrong either bills nothing for a client that hangs up mid-stream or double-reads a cell. units_mcp.rs computes the equivalent streaming-vs-one-shot fact at decode time (Decoded.streaming) but then drops it on the floor before it reaches admit/meter/settle, so if/when this plane's step functions are wired live (see the companion finding on units_mcp.rs's dormancy), a streaming MCP tool call would be admitted, metered and settled with no code path distinguishing it from a one-shot call — the exact distinction the LLM plane treats as load-bearing for correct billing on client disconnect.
positive_control: grep -n "\.streaming\b" crates/busbar/src/root/units_mcp.rs and grep -rn "streaming" crates/busbar/src (excluding the two assignment sites and one test assertion at root/tests/units_mcp.rs:310) return zero consuming reads; grep -n "decoded\.op\b" crates/busbar/src/root/units_mcp.rs:256 shows the sibling field on the exact same struct, produced at the exact same call site, IS read one line later in the same match arm — proving the method detects real field usage when it exists.

category: metering asymmetry / dead field
summary: A2aDraft.streaming ("Whether the answer arrives as a run of events rather than one reply") is read nowhere in units_a2a.rs except the hand-written Debug impl (line 586); every money/metering function that touches the draft (fee_evidence, bytes_located, request_nanos, fee_could_land, the Units-driving A2aUnits methods) ignores it, while the sibling `op` field on the identical struct is read repeatedly for real control flow (self.draft.op at lines 1281, 1345, 1598, 1627).
failure_scenario: A2aDraft documents `response_bytes` as "What the metering step's locator carried — the size of the answer the plane read" (units_a2a.rs:535-536), implying it is a single, already-known figure by the time metering runs. If a streaming A2A answer's true byte count is only knowable once the event stream ends (the same problem units_llm.rs solves with its Drop-based LateAccrual), then request_nanos/fee_evidence/bytes_located pricing off `response_bytes` for a streaming leg would price it as if it were a single synchronous reply, and a client that disconnects partway through a streamed A2A answer has no code path here that would still bill for the bytes already sent — the streaming flag that could have gated that distinction is computed nowhere in this file's construction (A2aDraft itself has no production construction site anywhere in crates/busbar/src; only crates/busbar/src/root/tests/units_a2a.rs builds one) and is never consulted where it is defined.
positive_control: grep -n "draft\.op\b" crates/busbar/src/root/units_a2a.rs returns 4 real-logic matches (lines 1281, 1345, 1598, 1627); grep -n "\.streaming\b" crates/busbar/src/root/units_a2a.rs returns only the field declaration (540) and the Debug formatter (586) — the same identical-struct, identical-file comparison used for the units_mcp.rs finding, confirming the asymmetry is a property of this field and not of the search.

category: scope-table-drift
summary: The live authorization gate for every admin HTTP request (busbar_kernel_scope::admin_required_scope, lib.rs:235-247) is the 1.5.5-only 66-op scope matrix, and was never extended for the 1.6.0 closed verb table in busbar-core-admin, so it computes the wrong (over-restrictive) scope for the one 1.6.0 verb (`verify`) that busbar-core-admin's own scope model deliberately made read-only.
failure_scenario: busbar-core-admin's admin_codec::verbs::resolve() (admin_codec/verbs.rs:37-42) declares `POST /api/v1/admin/verify` as a row of the closed verb table with read_only:true, and busbar-core-admin's own required_scope() (verbs.rs:168-201) returns VerbScope::ReadOnly for KernelVerb::Verify because it is a member of READ_ONLY_NEW_VERBS (verb.rs:719, with the explicit comment 'Asking full of them refuses the operator whose credential was only ever meant to look'). But the ACTUAL authorization decision for every admin HTTP request is made by crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs's approve() step at mod.rs:2237, which calls busbar_kernel_scope::admin_required_scope(&request.method, &request.path) -- NOT busbar-core-admin's required_scope. Tracing admin_required_scope('POST', '/api/v1/admin/verify'): method is not GET/HEAD (skip line 236-238); rel becomes '/verify' after stripping ADMIN_PREFIX (line 242); '/verify' is not in READ_ONLY_POST_PATHS (line 207, which only lists the two 1.5.5 dry-run paths); so the function falls through to `Scope::Full` at line 246. Concretely: an operator mints a ReadOnly-scoped admin credential intending to hand it to a monitoring/verification tool that calls `POST /api/v1/admin/verify` (the exact use case the design and busbar-core-admin's own code call out this verb for), and every such call is refused with a 403 'insufficient scope: requires full' even though the verb is documented, and coded in busbar-core-admin, as read-only. The bug fails closed (denies rather than grants excess access), so it is not a privilege-escalation path, but it is a genuine, reachable drift between the scope table that busbar-core-admin maintains (and cross-checks at compile time and in tests/table_matches_openapi.rs) and the scope table that actually governs dispatch.
positive_control: 1) `grep -rn "admin/verify" crates/ --include="*.rs"` returns exactly one hit in the whole pinned tree -- the row definition itself at crates/busbar-core-admin/src/admin_codec/verbs.rs:39 -- and zero hits anywhere in crates/busbar-kernel-scope or in crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/tests/units_admin.rs, proving no test exercises this path against the live gate. 2) The identical grep/cross-check pattern DOES exist and DOES pass for the other two GET-only 1.6.0 groups: crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/tests/units_admin.rs has `a_ledger_view_is_read_only_in_every_table_that_has_an_opinion` (asserts `busbar_kernel_scope::admin_required_scope("GET", path) == Scope::ReadOnly` for all 5 LEDGER_VERBS paths) and `a_chain_read_is_read_only_in_every_table_that_has_an_opinion` (same check for all 3 AUDIT_VERBS paths) -- both pass because those 8 routes are all GET, which admin_required_scope's blanket GET/HEAD-is-ReadOnly rule (lib.rs:236-238) happens to get right by construction. No equivalent test was ever written for NEW_VERBS's two READ_ONLY_NEW_VERBS members (`verify`, `plane_facts`), and `plane_facts` (GET) also happens to pass by the same GET coincidence, but `verify` (the one POST-bound read-only verb) falls through to `Scope::Full` and is untested. 3) busbar-kernel-scope's own module doc (lib.rs:214) states the function is 'Ported verbatim from 1.5.5's `busbar_kernel::admin::v1::contract::required_scope`' and its own ADMIN_SCOPE_TABLE (lib.rs:270 onward) is documented as exactly 'the 66 operations that matrix was mechanically extracted from at the 1.5.5 tag' -- confirming by the crate's own words that it has no knowledge of the 1.6.0 additions it is nonetheless being used to gate.

category: authorization fail-open / unmetered spend / wrong ledger attribution
summary: An IdP-identified principal that earns no governance key is refused ONLY when it carries roles AND its module has a role_bindings table; every other shape is admitted with `GovCtx { key: None }`, which downstream means no pool ACL, no budget, and spend booked to the anonymous actor.
failure_scenario: Operator config: `auth.chain: [corp-oidc]` with `identity-providers.corp-oidc` and NO `role_bindings:` section (config_validate has a rule for the reverse direction only - a binding naming an inactive module is an error - and none requiring a chain module to have bindings; see the positive control). A plugin chain module verifies an Okta/Entra token and returns `AuthOutcome::Identify(Principal)`. `resolve_data_plane_identity` computes `bindings = app.role_bindings.get("corp-oidc") = None`, `synthesize_principal_key` returns None at its `let table = bindings?;`, and the guard on line 1868 is skipped because `bindings.is_some()` is false. The request is admitted with `GovCtx { key: None }`. `busbar-contract/src/records.rs:1507` defines `is_governed()` as `self.key.is_some()` ("no key, no budget, and nothing to enforce"); `busbar-kernel/src/ingress/mod.rs:72` short-circuits the pool ACL with `let key = gov.key.as_ref()?;`; and `busbar-llm/src/unit/authenticate.rs:73` attributes the unit to `PrincipalId::new(anonymous_actor_id())`. Net effect: every user that IdP authenticates reaches EVERY pool, spends the operator's upstream provider credentials with no budget cap, and every charge lands on the `anonymous` bucket instead of that subject. The SECOND instance is a privilege inversion on the same line: with a role_bindings table configured, a user holding an UNBOUND role is refused `IdentityRefusal::NoGrant` (403), while the same user holding NO roles at all (e.g. no `groups` claim - the shape the in-file `TestIdpModule` at auth/mod.rs:882 produces via `Principal::from_id`, which sets `roles: Vec::new()`) skips the guard and is admitted ungoverned. Fewer roles buys strictly more access.
positive_control: Zero-claim (no test exercises this resolution): `grep -rn "resolve_data_plane_identity" --include="*test*.rs" crates/ | wc -l` -> 0. Positive control, same command shape, a symbol from the same module that IS tested: `grep -rn "extract_client_token" --include="*test*.rs" crates/ | wc -l` -> 41. Zero-claim (no config rule requires a chain module to carry bindings): `grep -n "role_bindings" crates/busbar-kernel/src/config_validate/mod.rs` -> 8 hits, all of which walk `auth.role_bindings` outward (line 923 `for (module, roles) in &auth.role_bindings` / line 926 'names module ... which appears in neither auth.chain nor auth.admin_auth'); none iterates `auth.chain` to require a table.

category: authorization / open-posture interaction with no warning
summary: The authorization server's consent screen mints the `busbar-operator` resource-owner session behind `RouteAuth::Admin` alone, and the explicit open-admin posture (`auth.admin_auth: []`) turns that into an anonymous, full-scope route with no boot warning - the analogous warning exists only for `auth.chain: [keys]`.
failure_scenario: Operator config: `oauth_as: { issuer: https://gw.example.com, signing_key: ... }` plus `auth: { admin_auth: [] }` (the documented open/dev admin posture; `oauth_as` exists for the deployment that has no IdP, so an operator running it without an admin IdP is the expected shape). `run_admin_chain` returns `ChainVerdict::Open` for an empty `admin_chain` (auth/mod.rs:900), the middleware then calls `admin_scope_for(None, None)` which returns `Grants::of(Scope::Full)` (auth/mod.rs:1287), so an ANONYMOUS internet caller passes the `RouteAuth::Admin` bar on both `GET {issuer}/consent` and `POST {issuer}/consent`. That caller drives the whole flow: GET /consent?return=/authorize?... opens a session whose subject is the constant `ADMIN_SUBJECT = "busbar-operator"`, POST /consent stakes the approval, and /authorize then issues an authorization code and an ES256-signed `at+jwt` access token carrying this deployment's audience - i.e. an unauthenticated party mints tokens as the operator. `config_validate` emits `CONFIG_OPEN_ADMIN_MINT` for the structurally identical `auth.chain names keys` + `admin_auth: []` combination (config_validate/mod.rs:1145) but says nothing at all for `oauth_as:` + `admin_auth: []`, so the operator gets no signal.
positive_control: Zero-claim (config_validate's rule body never mentions the AS plane): `grep -c "oauth_as" crates/busbar-kernel/src/config_validate/mod.rs` -> 0. Positive control, identical command against another plane section name in the same file: `grep -c "mcp" crates/busbar-kernel/src/config_validate/mod.rs` -> 1.

category: consent binding / display-does-not-equal-bind
summary: The consent screen renders the redirect host as one of the three facts the operator is approving ("Sends the credential to: <host>"), but the staked approval key is only `client_id\u{1f}scope` - the redirect URI is discarded into `_redirect_host` and is never re-checked when the approval is spent.
failure_scenario: Client X (registered via DCR or materialised from a CIMD document) has two registered redirect URIs, H1 and H2. The operator lands on `{issuer}/consent?return=/authorize?client_id=X&scope=S&redirect_uri=H1`, reads "Sends the credential to: H1", and approves. `consent_submit` stakes `X\u{1f}S`. A SECOND authorize request for the same client and the same scope but `redirect_uri=H2` - which need only reach the operator's browser (a top-level GET navigation, which SameSite=Lax permits and which therefore carries the `busbar_as_session` cookie) - reaches `approval_resolver`, which spends `approval_key(request.client_id.as_str(), request.scope)` (consent.rs:226-229) and returns `ApprovalDecision::Approve`. The authorization code is then sent to H2, a destination the operator was never shown, with the second requester's own PKCE `code_challenge` and `state`. `oauth_as::http::ApprovalRequest` exposes `redirect_uri` precisely so a host can bind it; busbar's resolver never reads it.
