The value is durably stored but the CURRENTLY RUNNING flusher is unaffected (its `interval` was fixed at the last boot) -- so nothing appears to happen, and an operator testing the change by watching behavior for a few minutes sees nothing wrong. On the NEXT process restart (for any reason), `spawn_budget_flusher` re-runs with the new, enormous interval; `tokio::time::sleep(interval)`'s deadline computation (`Instant::now().checked_add(duration).unwrap_or_else(far_future)`, tokio 1.53.1 src/time/sleep.rs:126-128) does NOT panic -- it simply schedules the first flush roughly 30 years out. The write-behind flusher's own doc promises a graceful stop loses nothing and an ungraceful one loses at most one interval's worth; from this restart onward that promise is void -- an OOM kill, SIGKILL, or host failure at any point loses EVERY accrued budget-cell delta and metering row since that restart (or since boot), not one interval's worth, with no warning at PATCH time and none at restart time.
positive_control: `grep -n "usage_flush_interval_ms" crates/busbar-kernel/src/config_validate/mod.rs` returns zero hits -- no floor, no ceiling -- versus its structural sibling `rate_sweep_interval` in the same `AdvancedPatch`, which IS checked (`== 0` rejected in `validate_governance`). `grep -n "Spawned once here" crates/busbar/src/main.rs` confirms the boot-only comment; `grep -n "spawn_budget_flusher" crates/ -r --include="*.rs"` (excluding tests) shows exactly one production call site, matching the same boot-only pattern already independently confirmed for `spawn_probers` above -- two unrelated subsystems sharing the identical 'falsely live' defect shape.

category: unbounded-numeric-config / adjacent-to-admin-patch-defect-class
summary: A fourth instance of the identical overflow class: `export.request-log-webhook.settings.delivery_timeout_secs` is validated only for `< 1` (config_validate/mod.rs:1198, no ceiling) and reaches the same raw, panicking `Instant + Duration` add on every webhook delivery -- adjacent to, not itself on, the admin PATCH surface this hunt targets, because no PATCH/PUT route exists for export-instance settings (only `POST /config/reload`/`config/apply` re-run validation over a config.yaml-supplied value).
failure_scenario: An operator sets `export: [{module: request-log-webhook, settings: {delivery_timeout_secs: 18446744073709551615, ...}}]` in config.yaml and applies it via `POST /api/v1/admin/config/reload` (`grep -rn "export.*settings" crates/busbar-core-admin/src/v1/json/handlers.rs` finds no PATCH/PUT route for export-instance settings, confirming config.yaml + reload is the only path). `config_validate::validate` passes (floor-only check). `webhook.rs:73` lowers it to `Duration::from_secs(...)`, and every webhook delivery (a detached `busbar_kernel::detached::spawn_detached` task, webhook.rs:150) hits line 178's raw addition and panics before `warn_webhook_delivery_failed` can even fire. Blast radius is narrow (one detached delivery task per event) and the trigger requires a config-file edit rather than a single admin-supplied JSON value, which is why this is MEDIUM rather than a repeat of the HIGH findings above -- it is included to show the missing-ceiling gap in `config_validate`'s timeout checks is systemic (four independent sites now) rather than a one-off.
positive_control: Comparing against `request_body_max_bytes`'s floor+ceiling pair (config_validate/mod.rs) shows the codebase ceiling-checks numeric fields when it intends to; every `_secs: u64` timeout field that reaches an ABSOLUTE `tokio::time::Instant::now() + duration` (this site, and the two `health.rs`/`send.rs` sites above) rather than a RELATIVE `tokio::time::timeout`/`sleep` (e.g. `tls_handshake_timeout_secs`, which is safe per tokio's own `checked_add`-based `timeout()`/`sleep()` constructors) is floor-only-validated and therefore exposed to the same overflow.

category: dead-duplicate-implementation / money-adjacent
summary: `Verbs::create_key`/`Verbs::rotate_key` (verbs.rs:303-436) are a complete, independently-idempotent second implementation of virtual-key mint/rotate -- with their own dedicated `IdempotencyCache` fields (`create_key_cache`/`rotate_key_cache`, verbs.rs:214-215) and their own group-planning logic -- that is unconditionally compiled into the release binary and genuinely instantiated in production (`crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs:2329`, `busbar_core_admin::Verbs::new(...)`), yet is entirely unreachable: `Verbs::execute()` explicitly refuses `KernelVerb::PostKeys`/`PostKeysIdRotate` (verbs.rs:461-464), and the ONE production `Governance::mint_key`/`rotate_key` binding (units_admin/mod.rs:933-946, `CoreGovernance`) unconditionally returns `Err(GovernanceError::Validation)`. The live, actually-served `POST /api/v1/admin/keys`/`/keys/{id}/rotate` requests are handled exclusively by the separate, hand-rolled implementation in `crates/busbar-core-admin/src/keys.rs` (its own `IdemState`/`IdemReservation`, `EXISTENCE_GATE`, `check_key_cap`). This is the project's established 'two implementations of one thing' defect class, applied to money-gating credential minting -- currently dormant rather than live, but shipped, instantiated, and carrying real per-process idempotency-cache state that nothing ever reads.
failure_scenario: Today: no live failure -- `CoreGovernance::mint_key`/`rotate_key` always refuse, so `Verbs::create_key`/`rotate_key` can never actually mint anything in the shipped binary; this is a maintenance/audit-surface risk rather than an active exploit. The latent risk: `Verbs::create_key`/`rotate_key` call `self.governance.mint_key(admin, group)`/`rotate_key(admin, id)` directly and enforce NO key-cap (`max_keys_per_principal`) or `EXISTENCE_GATE` concurrency protection of their own -- those live entirely in `keys.rs`'s implementation, not in this crate's `Verbs`. If a future change wires a second transport (an internal RPC surface, or an MCP-exposed admin tool -- `crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/tests/subscribe_tests.rs` already exercises a `.create_key(` call in test code) to a real `Governance::mint_key` implementation instead of `CoreGovernance`'s stub, that transport would mint keys through a completely separate code path with its own idempotency cache and no shared enforcement with `keys.rs`'s cap/concurrency guards -- a double-mint / cap-bypass door opening exactly where the project has already been shown (per the confirmed money-authority-flip and dual-breaker findings) to accidentally wire the wrong one of two parallel implementations live.
positive_control: `grep -n "\.create_key(\|\.rotate_key(" crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs` returns zero hits for the `verbs` instance, while `grep -n "verbs.execute(" crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs` returns one real call site (line 2403) -- proving the grep methodology finds genuine call sites when they exist, and that `Verbs::create_key`/`rotate_key` specifically have none in production. `crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs:933-946`'s `CoreGovernance::mint_key`/`rotate_key` bodies are `Err(busbar_core_admin::GovernanceError::Validation)` verbatim, confirming the seam is a deliberate stub, not an oversight.

category: rate-limit-tier-drift / self-dos
summary: `CONFIG_CLASS_RULES` (rate.rs:53-74) lists only the two 1.5.5-era named-map roots (`/identity-providers`, `/export`) for the tight 10/min CONFIG rate class, but `NamedMapSection::sections()` (crates/busbar-kernel/src/config/named_map.rs:60-67) folds in TWO ADDITIONAL 1.6.0 named-map sections under default features -- `tools:` and `agents:` -- whose mutation routes are mounted by this SAME crate's `named_map::routes()` loop (v1/json/named_map.rs:83) and whose `apply()` handler does the identical full-rebuild-and-swap the rate.rs module doc says earns the tight class ('every mutation under a section's root re-runs the boot pipeline and swaps a whole new App -- the same blast radius as /config/reload'). The ONE production caller, `crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs:56,2340`, imports and passes `CONFIG_CLASS_RULES` verbatim, unextended -- so `PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE /api/v1/admin/tools/{name}` and `/agents/{name}` fall through `MutationClass::for_verb`'s path-prefix match to the roomy 60/min CRUD class instead of the intended 10/min CONFIG class, a self-documented 6x rate-limit-tier gap for a full-App-rebuild operation.
failure_scenario: A credential holding Full admin scope (the operator, or any automation/script using the operator's token, matching this product's trusted-operator model) issues repeated `PATCH /api/v1/admin/tools/{name}` or `/agents/{name}` calls. Because these routes fall through to `MutationClass::Crud`, `admit()`'s rate check (verbs.rs:246-268, confirmed live for every admin HTTP request via the SAME `approve`/'Step 4: the door' pipeline round 2 already traced for scope enforcement in this exact file) permits up to 60/min instead of the 10/min ceiling the codebase's own design applies to every OTHER full-App-rebuild operation (`/config/*`, `/plugins/reload`, `/restart`, `/identity-providers`, `/export`). A misbehaving script or an operator mistake can therefore drive up to 6x more full config-rebuild-and-swap churn through `/tools`/`/agents` than the rate limiter's own design intends before being throttled -- the exact thrash/self-DoS risk the tight CONFIG class exists to bound, reachable specifically because the two 1.6.0 named-map sections were never added to the table their own module doc says they belong in.
positive_control: `grep -n "ConfigClassRule::" crates/busbar-core-admin/src/rate.rs` lists all 9 entries; none names `/tools` or `/agents`. `grep -n "CONFIG_CLASS_RULES" crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs` shows it imported at line 56 and passed unmodified at lines 2092/2340 -- no extension step anywhere in that file. `NamedMapSection::sections()`'s own doc states 'Under the default/test/openapi feature set the fold is [identity-providers, export, tools, agents]', confirming both missing sections are present under the default build, not an obscure feature combination.

category: streaming assembly / field dropped in one direction
summary: A streaming Anthropic content_block_start for a tool_use block missing id or name makes the whole event silently vanish (the `?` bails the match to None, and read_response_events turns None into an empty Vec at reader.rs:648-650), while the byte-identical malformed block on the buffered response path is explicitly rejected with an IrError (anthropic/mod.rs:933-950: "reject the malformed block rather than inventing an id").
failure_scenario: A self-hosted 'Anthropic-compatible' backend (a real traffic class this same reader explicitly tolerates elsewhere, e.g. its own missing-usage leniency at reader.rs:723-728) streams a tool_use content_block_start missing `name`. The BlockStart is silently dropped, but the content_block_delta events for the same index are not gated on 'was this index opened' and proceed normally through proto_stream.rs to the egress writer. Egress=openai_chat: writer.rs's InputJsonDelta arm (:606-624) emits a tool_calls delta chunk carrying only an index, no id/name -- OpenAiStreamFraming::remap_tool_call_index (openai_chat/mod.rs:1150-1192) assigns this as the tool call's FIRST-seen chunk, so the client accumulates a tool call it can never name or correlate a tool_result against. Egress=gemini: writer.rs's InputJsonDelta arm (:913-924) does `guard.iter_mut().find(|(idx,_,_)| idx==index)` -- no entry exists, so the delta is silently dropped every time and the tool call vanishes entirely, with normal usage/billing continuing regardless.
positive_control: grep -n tool_use_missing_id_rejects crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/anthropic/tests/input_hardening_tests.rs matches a real test (line 83) proving the buffered-path strict-reject is deliberate and tested; grep -n content_block_start crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/anthropic/tests/*.rs matches 21 occurrences, none of which exercise a tool_use content_block_start missing id/name (the only tested malformation is the block-index clamp), confirming the asymmetry is real and untested rather than a search miss.

category: usage/token extraction (money) -- extends the confirmed pattern to a new call site
summary: recover_truncated_usage -- the last-chance usage-salvage path for a response too large to fit the reassembly buffer, wired directly into production billing (crates/busbar-llm/src/engine/response_body.rs:~806-820) -- reads its primary input/output counts via the same read_count_u64(..).unwrap_or(0) pattern already confirmed on the main usage path, in ALL SIX dialects' own recover_truncated_usage implementations (anthropic/reader.rs:12-13; gemini/reader.rs:32-39 for promptTokenCount/candidatesTokenCount; cohere/reader.rs:29-34 for tokens.input_tokens/output_tokens; openai_chat/reader.rs and openai_responses/reader.rs, both `u64_field(...).unwrap_or(0)` on prompt_tokens/completion_tokens and input_tokens/output_tokens respectively; bedrock via the same trait method). This call site was not among round 2's listed occurrences.
failure_scenario: response_body.rs has a deliberate anti-fail-open-to-free floor for exactly this scenario: `recover_truncated_usage(&buf).or_else(|| Some(estimate_usage_from_truncated_tail(tail_len)))` -- but that `.or_else` floor ONLY fires when recover_truncated_usage returns None entirely. If the tail-scan DOES find a usage object but one count inside it is present-and-unparseable (e.g. a self-hosted-compatible backend stringifying `"input_tokens": "1500"`, the exact shape read_count_u64 is proven to refuse), recover_truncated_usage still returns `Some(TokenUsage{input:0,...})` -- a fake-successful zeroed value indistinguishable from a real small usage -- so the `.or_else` floor never engages. A response that by definition overflowed the reassembly cap (i.e. is large and real) bills at or near zero, exactly the outcome wire_shim.rs's own doc comment says the floor's 'only job' is to prevent ('keep a truncated-beyond-recovery response from billing ZERO').
positive_control: grep -n 'billed_count(' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/*/handler.rs shows the strict, refusal-based reader IS used in production elsewhere (openai_chat/handler.rs:520,522,1309,1445,1447) -- proving the correct primitive exists and works -- but grep -n 'recover_truncated_usage' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/*/reader.rs shows all six implementations use `read_count_u64`/`u64_field` with `.unwrap_or(0)` on the primary token fields, none uses billed_count.

category: usage/token extraction (money) -- ledger write path, previously unopened file
summary: tier_usage() -- the function every dialect's usage funnels through before the ledger/metering write -- collapses a cache-token field that is None purely because an upstream read_count_u64 call refused an unparseable-but-present value into the exact same sparse-map omission as a field that legitimately reported nothing, silently recording zero cache activity for a turn that had real, separately-priced cache reads/writes.
failure_scenario: Every dialect reader populates cache_read_input_tokens/cache_creation_input_tokens (both Option<u64>) via bare `.and_then(read_count_u64)` with no billed_count/refusal anywhere on this field family (confirmed in anthropic/reader.rs:14-15 and mirrored in the other five dialects); ir/types.rs's to_token_usage() (line 1129-1130: `cache_read: self.cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation: self.cache_creation_input_tokens`) passes the Option through completely unchanged, with no re-defaulting. A malformed cache-count value (string, negative, or >=2^53) reads as None -- indistinguishable from 'provider never reported a cache field'. tier_usage() (wire_shim.rs:96-108) then applies `.unwrap_or(0)` to both cache fields, and because the map is built sparse ('Zero tiers are omitted so the map stays sparse', wire_shim.rs:94), a None tier is left out of the ledger entirely -- UNIT_CACHE_READ/UNIT_CACHE_WRITE are two of the four reserved units that can become money at all. A customer whose completion read thousands of cached input tokens is billed $0 for that line item on any request where the upstream happens to spell that one field oddly, silently, with no warning anywhere on the path.
positive_control: tier_usage's production call chain is confirmed live via crates/busbar-llm/src/engine/usage.rs -> ledger_and_meter -> host.meter_ledger (a real money-ledger write, not test/metrics-only). billed_count (the strict refusal reader) is proven to exist and work via the same grep as the prior finding, confirming the codebase already knows how to do this correctly but never applies it anywhere to the cache-tier fields reaching wire_shim.rs.

category: usage/token extraction (money) -- lenient reader used where the crate's own strict one exists, on an embeddings billing tap
summary: The Titan-embeddings response reader collapses 'absent' and 'present-but-unreadable' inputTextTokenCount into the same None (via read_count_u64, not the crate's own usage_count::billed_count), and EmbeddingsResp::billing() (ir/embeddings.rs:189-191: `self.usage.clone().map(Billing::Tokens)`) turns that None into NO billing entry at all -- not even a zero-token row. The comment at this exact line mislabels read_count_u64 as "BILLED COUNT: through the one seam", when the crate's actual strict/refusing primitive is the differently-named `billed_count`, which is wired into production elsewhere (openai_chat/handler.rs:520,522,1309,1445,1447) but never here.
failure_scenario: A Titan-compatible backend/proxy returns `{"embedding": [...], "inputTextTokenCount": "512"}` (a string-typed count -- the exact class of value the crate's own test `negatives_and_non_numbers_are_refused` proves read_count_u64 refuses, returning None). `usage` becomes None, `EmbeddingsResp::billing()` returns None, and a real, paid embeddings call produces zero ledger rows -- silently, with no warning, no floor, and no flat fee to fall back on (embeddings billing IS the token usage here, not a separate flat charge).
positive_control: grep -n "billed_count" crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/bedrock/handler.rs returns nothing, confirming this read site never uses the strict primitive; the identical grep against openai_chat/handler.rs returns 5 hits, proving the search method finds the strict primitive where it IS used.

category: streaming tool-call accumulator / adversarial index
summary: Bedrock's contentBlockStart{toolUse} arm unconditionally (re-)opens and emits a BlockStart for the index with no check that it is already open, unlike its sibling arms in the same match block (reasoningContent, empty-start text) which explicitly guard with `!state.thinking_block_open` / `!state.text_block_open`. The same match block clamps the wire index via `clamp_content_block_index` against `MAX_CONTENT_BLOCK_INDEX = 1023` (bedrock/mod.rs:1268-1279), so two distinct out-of-range indices (e.g. 2000 and 3000) also collide at 1023 -- a second, independent trigger for the identical missing-guard gap.
failure_scenario: A malformed/buggy Bedrock-compatible backend sends two contentBlockStart{toolUse} frames for the same contentBlockIndex (directly, or via the 1023 clamp) with no contentBlockStop between them -- one for call_1/tool_a, one for call_2/tool_b. Busbar emits two BlockStart{index:N, ToolUse{...}} events for the same index with no BlockStop between; every subsequent contentBlockDelta{toolUse.input} for that index is guarded only by `state.open_tools.contains(&idx)` (index-blind to WHICH tool is open), so both calls' argument fragments land in one accumulator slot. On an Anthropic egress (which tracks blocks purely by index) a real client SDK concatenates both tool calls' JSON fragments into one buffer keyed to one tool id, corrupting or losing one of the two calls -- the same failure class already confirmed for Anthropic-ingress/Gemini-egress, reproduced here via a completely different, previously-unaudited ingress reader.
positive_control: grep -n '!state.text_block_open\|!state.thinking_block_open' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/bedrock/reader.rs matches lines 869, 883, 896, 927, 985 -- proving the guard pattern exists and is found by this method when present, so its absence on the tool-use arm is a genuine asymmetry, not a search miss. bedrock_eventstream_tests.rs only asserts distinct, monotonically increasing indices across blocks and never exercises a duplicate/overlapping contentBlockStart.

category: default values silently substituting for absent required fields
summary: A streaming Bedrock toolUse block with an absent/blank toolUseId silently becomes id "" and is still emitted as a normal BlockStart (and the buffered response reader at reader.rs:1296-1298 makes the identical silent-default choice), while the exact same field on the REQUEST-parsing path (reader.rs:327-343) is explicitly rejected: 'An absent/blank/wrong-typed id yields an empty IR id that silently breaks that pairing -- reject rather than invent an id.'
failure_scenario: A response emits two parallel tool_use blocks in one turn, both missing toolUseId (a third-party 'Bedrock-compatible' backend bug -- this file elsewhere goes out of its way to tolerate such backends). Both collapse to IR id "". Re-emitted to any egress writer that writes id verbatim (e.g. anthropic/writer.rs), the client receives two content_block_start events with the identical empty id; a client correlating a later tool_result.tool_use_id back to a specific call can no longer distinguish which result belongs to which call -- precisely the correlation-breakage the request-side reject exists to prevent, left unguarded here on the response side.
positive_control: The identical field, same file, has a working strict-reject implementation 500 lines away (reader.rs:333-343, 'reject rather than invent an id'), confirming this is an inconsistently-applied capability, not a missing one.

category: streaming tool-call accumulator / adversarial and non-adversarial index reuse
summary: state.open_tools/state.tool_ir_index are, by explicit design, never shrunk for a Cohere stream's lifetime (mod.rs comment: 'Neither ... is ever shrunk for the stream's lifetime'), so cohere_assign_tool_ir_index treats ANY lookup hit for a wire frame_idx -- whether that tool is still open, or was closed frames ago -- as a duplicate start and silently discards the new call's id/name; a later delta for the reused index then resolves to the FIRST (already-closed) tool's IR index. A second, independent trigger is clamp_frame_index (mod.rs:352-357) forcing any two distinct out-of-range wire indices above MAX_TOOL_FRAME_INDEX to the same clamped value.
failure_scenario: A Cohere-v2-compatible backend emits tool-call-start{index:0} -> tool-call-end{index:0} for call A, then reuses index:0 for a genuinely distinct call B (tool-call-start{index:0, id:"call_b", name:"different_fn"}) -- a plausible non-adversarial pattern for a backend that numbers tool calls per turn. Call B's BlockStart is silently swallowed (id and name lost entirely, no warning), and its argument deltas are emitted as BlockDelta against call A's already-stopped IR index -- either dropped by a strict downstream consumer or misfolded into A's already-finalized arguments. The model's second tool call never executes, or its arguments are attributed to the wrong call, with no error surfaced anywhere.
positive_control: cohere/tests/tests.rs:4118 (test_duplicate_tool_call_start_is_noop) locks in exactly this 'lookup hit => no-op' behavior for a still-OPEN duplicate, proving the mechanism is real and intentional for that case; test_stream_two_sequential_tool_calls_get_distinct_indices (tests.rs:2970) only covers non-reused sequential indices -- no test exercises index reuse AFTER a close for a DIFFERENT tool, confirming the reuse-after-close path is real and untested.

category: streaming assembly / field dropped only in streaming mode
summary: Cohere's streaming read_response_events has no ET_CITATION_START/ET_CITATION_END match arm at all -- both fall into this catch-all and produce zero IR events -- even though the IR fully supports streamed citations, the crate's own constants ET_CITATION_START/ET_CITATION_END exist (cohere/mod.rs:312-321), and this crate's OWN Cohere writer emits native citation-start/citation-end frames from IrDelta::CitationsDelta (cohere/writer.rs:690-712, 900). The buffered Cohere reader correctly reads message.citations (reader.rs:1186-1194). The writer's own doc comment for ET_CITATION_START says this exact bug class was already found and fixed once, on the writer side: 'the writer used to suppress every streamed citation on the belief that Cohere v2 had no citation frame, which made a grounded answer arrive with sources when not streaming and without them when streaming.' That fix was never mirrored onto the reader.
failure_scenario: A client makes a grounded (RAG/documents) Cohere v2 request with stream:true. A real Cohere backend streams citation-start/citation-end frames alongside the answer text. Every one is silently discarded by the catch-all arm -- the client's streamed answer arrives with zero source citations, while the identical non-streamed call to the same endpoint returns citations correctly.
positive_control: cohere/tests/tests.rs:2158-2167 (test_stream_unknown_event_is_noop) explicitly feeds {"type":"citation-start","index":0} into the reader and asserts the result is empty, using a well-known, well-documented event type as its example of an 'unknown' one -- confirming this is the reader's actual, current, tested behavior, not an inference from a grep. Gemini's reader, by contrast, correctly ingests its analogous streaming-citation shape (candidates[].citationMetadata.citationSources) at gemini/reader.rs:1188-1235, proving the pipeline can carry streamed citations end-to-end and this is Cohere-reader-specific.

category: error mapping / upstream error read as a success shape
summary: The buffered read_response only checks that the `message` KEY is present, never that its VALUE is an object. Cohere's own documented error-response shape is `{"message": "<string>"}` -- a top-level string, not the success shape's `message: {role, content, ...}` object. Since `obj.get("message")` succeeds for a string value too, `message_val` becomes a JSON string, and every subsequent `.get(...)` call on it (tool_plan, content, citations) silently returns None on a non-object Value -- producing a fully-formed, syntactically successful, but completely empty `Ok(IrResponse{content: vec![], ...})` for what is actually an API error.
failure_scenario: extract_error(status, body) normally intercepts non-2xx responses before read_response is ever called -- but a Cohere-compatible self-hosted backend or proxy (a real traffic class this crate explicitly tolerates elsewhere) that returns a 200 status with an error-shaped body (a known 'soft error' pattern some gateways use) bypasses that HTTP-status gate entirely and reaches read_response directly. The caller receives a normal, billable Ok(IrResponse) with empty content and no error signal, for a request that actually failed -- indistinguishable from a legitimately empty completion, with no code path anywhere that would flag the mismatch.
positive_control: grep -n 'is_object\|as_object' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/cohere/reader.rs around this call site shows no type check on message_val before the .get() calls proceed; the immediately preceding request-side parse of the SAME shape (`obj.as_object().ok_or(...)`) at reader.rs:1153 DOES type-check the outer body, showing the codebase knows how to guard against a wrong JSON type and simply didn't apply it one level down to `message`.

category: error mapping -- buffered path missing a fix the streaming reader already has
summary: Cohere's BUFFERED read_response maps a `finish_reason: "ERROR"` body straight into `stop_reason: Some(IrStopReason::Error)` inside a normal `Ok(IrResponse{...})` (built at line 1345) with no error-classification step. The STREAMING reader (reader.rs:905-940) already has an explicit, heavily-commented fix for the identical case: pushing a dedicated `IrStreamEvent::Error` alongside the MessageDelta, because (per that comment) 'the only thing it produced was IrStopReason::Error on the terminal MessageDelta ... no cross-protocol writer has a native error token for that reason, so every one of them renders it as a SUCCESS terminator ... terminal_error() stays None, the breaker records no fault, and the failed stream is billed as a completed one.' The buffered path never received the equivalent fix.
failure_scenario: A Cohere backend returns a 200 response for a generation that failed mid-flight due to a generic infrastructure error (Cohere's documented `finish_reason: ERROR`), with a well-formed `message` object (unlike the prior finding) but partial/no real content. read_response returns Ok(IrResponse{stop_reason: Some(Error), ...}) -- a Result::Ok, the only channel available for this function to signal failure to its caller. Any egress writer maps IrStopReason::Error to its own generic-success stop token (there is no native 'error' finish reason on any dialect's writer, per the streaming fix's own comment), so the client sees a normal completion, and the request is billed as a successful generation.
positive_control: grep -n 'IrStreamEvent::Error' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/cohere/reader.rs matches only the streaming arm (~line 930); the buffered read_response function has no equivalent push and returns Result<IrResponse, IrError> exclusively via the terminal Ok(...) at line 1345, confirming there is no Err(...) path for this finish_reason value.

quote:
let oai_idx = tc
                    .get("index")
                    .and_then(|i| i.as_u64())
                    .map_or(0, |v| v.min(MAX_TOOL_INDEX) as usize);
category: streaming tool-call accumulator corrupted by adversarial index
summary: serde_json::Value::as_u64() returns None for a negative number, a non-integer float, or an absent index key; all three collapse via map_or(0, ...) to oai_idx = 0 -- the SAME slot a legitimate, distinct tool_calls[{"index":0}] entry already uses -- letting a malformed/adversarial chunk's argument fragment silently concatenate into an unrelated, real tool call's accumulated JSON.
failure_scenario: Stream opens tool_calls[{"index":0,"id":"call_1","function":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"loc"}}] (BlockStart, tool_ir_index[0]=0). A later chunk (malformed backend, proxy, or MITM) carries tool_calls[{"index":-1,"id":"call_evil","function":{"name":"evil_tool","arguments":"\":\"nyc\"}"}}]. Because as_u64() returns None for -1, oai_idx defaults to 0; already_open is true so evil_tool's name/id are discarded, but its arguments fragment is still routed via tool_ir_index.get(&0) (reader.rs:893-897) and appended into get_weather's argument buffer -- producing {"loc":"nyc"} silently assembled from two distinct, differently-named tool calls. This is JSON-fragment cross-contamination into whichever tool's arguments actually execute, a data-integrity defect, not mere loss.
positive_control: The reader correctly bounds legitimate duplicate/unopened indices elsewhere in the SAME function (already_open check at line ~860; the tool_ir_index.get-or-continue guard at ~893-897 correctly drops args for an index never opened) -- proving the collision-handling model works for real, distinct values; the gap is that map_or(0, ...) manufactures a FAKE value 0 for garbage input instead of routing it to a non-colliding key or dropping it, and the surrounding comment only reasons about the upper-bound (u64::MAX) hazard, never the negative/absent case.

category: streaming assembly / index namespace collision between block kinds
summary: Reasoning (Thinking) and function-call (ToolUse) items share ONE open_tools key namespace keyed on raw output_index (only text gets a disjoint TEXT_INDEX_KEY_OFFSET). The reasoning-delta arm's guard suppresses a duplicate BlockStart when idx is already open, but the BlockDelta push below it is unconditional -- so a ThinkingDelta can land on an index whose BlockStart declared ToolUse. The mirror EVT_FUNCTION_CALL_ARGS_DELTA arm (reader.rs:961-984) is equally type-blind: it only checks `state.open_tools.contains(&idx)`, so an arguments-delta can land on an index opened as Thinking.
failure_scenario: Upstream opens a reasoning item at output_index:0, then (a re-numbering/splicing backend bug) emits response.function_call_arguments.delta also at output_index:0 before any output_item.added for a function_call there. The reasoning block silently receives InputJsonDelta fragments; on an Anthropic egress this produces a content_block_start{type:"tool_use"} at index N followed by content_block_delta{type:"thinking_delta"} at the same N -- invalid per Anthropic's own schema, which a strict client rejects or misrenders.
positive_control: EVT_OUTPUT_TEXT_DELTA in the SAME function correctly guards its delta push, not just its open (reader.rs:~933-939: 'must NOT push a TextDelta into a tool block') -- proving the codebase's own design explicitly anticipates and defends against exactly this class of cross-injection for text, but the reasoning/tool pair sharing raw open_tools was left without the equivalent type check.

category: streaming assembly / field dropped only in streaming mode
summary: The Responses streaming read_response_events never handles annotations/citations: there is no `response.output_text.annotation.added` event constant anywhere in openai_responses/mod.rs's EVT_* set, and the terminal response.completed handler only scans each output content part for type=="refusal" (this line), never for the sibling `annotations` array on an output_text part it already has in hand. The buffered read_response path on the SAME struct DOES read them (reader.rs:238-251, item.get("annotations").map(openai_annotations::read_url_annotations)), and the writer fully supports emitting them mid-stream (openai_responses/writer.rs:979-985, IrDelta::CitationsDelta => self.append_citations(...)).
failure_scenario: A client streams a Responses request using the built-in web_search tool; the model's answer carries output_text.annotations (URL citations), arriving either via a mid-stream event (there is no handler for it at all) or in the final response.completed body (the refusal-only scan at this line skips every non-refusal content part). Any cross-protocol egress, or a same-protocol Responses answer rebuilt through the IR, receives the cited text with zero citation metadata -- sourced claims are silently stripped of their sources on the streaming path while the identical non-streaming request preserves them.
positive_control: gemini/reader.rs:1188-1235 is this exact bug class already found and fixed for a sibling dialect -- its own comment states 'Without this arm a streamed Gemini citation was silently dropped' and it now emits IrDelta::CitationsDelta mid-stream -- proving the team has fixed this precise failure mode elsewhere and it survives, unfixed, in openai_responses' streaming reader. grep -n 'annotation' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/openai_responses/mod.rs matches only doc comments about the buffered/writer paths, none about a streaming event constant.

category: error mapping -- upstream generation failure rendered as a success terminator, money-adjacent
summary: When a Gemini streaming candidate's finishReason is MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL (the model emitted an unparseable tool call -- per gemini/mod.rs:1268's own doc comment, 'generation FAILED, there is NO valid call to run'), map_gemini_finish_reason (gemini/mod.rs:1256-1270) maps it to IrStopReason::Error, but this finishReason arm only folds that into a normal MessageDelta+MessageStop -- it never pushes a dedicated IrStreamEvent::Error. proto_stream.rs's own terminal_error() doc comment is explicit: 'Set when a reader emits an IrStreamEvent::Error' and 'a non-None value records a breaker transient and suppresses token billing' -- so this path leaves terminal_error() as None, the breaker unfaulted, and the failed generation billed as a completed one. Cohere's reader has the identical bug class (its own generic ERROR case) already found and explicitly fixed with exactly this push, 'mirroring the gemini/bedrock inline-error arms' -- but Gemini's OWN candidate-level MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL path is not one of those fixed arms.
failure_scenario: A Gemini-compatible backend streams a response where the model's tool-call generation is malformed (finishReason: MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL). The reader emits MessageDelta{stop_reason: Some(Error)} + MessageStop with no IrStreamEvent::Error. crates/busbar-llm/src/engine/response_body.rs's billing gate (`billing_failed = terminal_error().is_some() || translate_aborted`) sees terminal_error()==None, so billing_failed is false and the request is charged in full for a generation that produced no usable output, while the breaker never records the fault (so a genuinely broken/misconfigured backend keeps receiving full traffic).
positive_control: Gemini's OWN inline error-envelope arm (reader.rs:844-860, top-level `{"error":{...}}` chunk) and prompt-blocked-envelope arm both correctly push IrStreamEvent::Error, proving the reader knows the correct pattern; grep -n 'IrStreamEvent::Error' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/gemini/reader.rs shows it is pushed in those two arms but not in the candidate-level finishReason arm (~1275-1323) that handles MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL.

category: streaming assembly -- content silently dropped with no signal
summary: Inside the Bedrock event-stream drain loop, a validly length/CRC-framed event whose JSON payload fails to parse is silently skipped via a bare `continue` -- no error frame, no abort, no metric, no signal of any kind -- in the same function whose surrounding code explicitly documents that adjacent corruption classes (a malformed prelude, a buffer overflow with no terminator) 'must surface an error, never a silent truncation' and drives `self.abort()` specifically to guarantee that.
failure_scenario: A self-hosted 'Bedrock-compatible' backend (a real traffic class this crate explicitly tolerates) emits one event-stream frame whose payload is not valid JSON (a backend encoding bug, not necessarily an attack) amid an otherwise normal stream. Every other frame type funnels through this same loop, including the terminal `metadata` frame that carries token usage for the whole response; if that specific frame's payload fails to parse, its content (or usage) is dropped with nothing downstream able to tell the difference between 'this stream had no more content/usage to report' and 'a frame silently vanished'.
positive_control: The same function's handling of MalformedPrelude and MAX_BUF overflow (proto_stream.rs:775-787, 'Without this the stream would silently truncate') explicitly calls self.abort() to guarantee a terminal error frame is emitted -- proving the file's own design standard is 'never a silent truncation' -- while the non-JSON-payload branch a few lines above has no such call and no comment justifying the asymmetry.

quote: a hidden constructor CI's symbol scan confines to the kernel's own source. See the crate-level
category: doc-vs-code conformance: security-invariant claimed CI-enforced, gate is currently RED
summary: busbar-contract documents that only the kernel crate can obtain a `KernelSeal` -- "There are exactly two proof types and one root minter, and no others survive" (token.rs:19) and "Only the kernel mints tokens | one audited symbol ... | CI" (caps/mod.rs:51) -- confined by a CI symbol scan, but the actual enforcing gate is RED against this exact tree right now, and so are its sibling rows for the crate's other sealed mints.
failure_scenario: Running `cargo run -p xtask --quiet -- gate seal-witness` from the pinned worktree exits 1: row `seal-witness:single-minter` FAILs with 135 real call sites of `KernelSeal::acquire_for_kernel(` outside `crates/busbar-kernel/src/`, spanning busbar-llm, busbar-kernel-ledger, busbar-kernel-budget, busbar-kernel-audit, busbar-kernel-identity, busbar-transport-tls, busbar-contract's own tests, busbar-core-admin, plugin-loader and busbar's root tests. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:574` runs this exact command and labels the step "Seal-witness gate (BLOCKING -- the money facts-line has one root minter, kernel-only)" with no posture/excuse escape valve. Independently, `cargo run -p xtask --quiet -- gate construction --posture` (the exact command CI's construction-gate job runs) also exits 1, naming `token-sealed:kernel-seal` (135 sites), `token-sealed` itself (264 sites of `Pass::mint(`/`Grant::<...>::mint(` outside the kernel crate), `token-sealed:admit-token-mint` (48 sites of the arrival-hold mint) and `token-sealed:secret-once-mint` (5 sites) all as NEW, unexcused reds -- none of the four rows appear in `xtask/src/gates/mod.rs`'s `CONSTRUCTION_STANDING_REDS` allow-list. Because the row is already failing on 135+ pre-existing sites, it cannot distinguish a new, genuinely unauthorized production call site (e.g. inside a plugin crate) from the existing noise -- the security property busbar-contract's own doc asserts in the present tense is not actually true of the tree under audit, and the gate meant to make it true cannot currently signal a fresh violation. Every downstream crate that treats busbar-contract's "kernel-only, CI-enforced" claim as a real boundary is trusting a guarantee that does not presently hold.
positive_control: `cargo run -p xtask --quiet -- gate seal-witness` (run from /Users/matthew/.cache/busbar-codeaudit/round2) exits 1 and prints `FAIL seal-witness:single-minter ... 135 site(s) of KernelSeal::acquire_for_kernel( outside crates/busbar-kernel/src/: ...`; the paired row in the same run, `seal-witness:no-surviving-proof-name`, PASSES with 0 hits, proving the scan mechanism can and does distinguish a clean row from a failing one. `cargo run -p xtask --quiet -- gate construction` independently reproduces the same population plus three siblings (264 / 135 / 48 / 5 sites respectively, each with a full file:line list), and `cargo run -p xtask --quiet -- gate construction --posture` exits 1 reporting all four as unexcused new reds -- all four commands were executed directly against the pinned audit worktree, not inferred.

quote: the encoded bytes do not contain it exactly once at that location, the unit fails and the mint
category: doc-vs-code conformance: unimplemented security invariant + false confinement claim
summary: `SecretOnce` documents both an active "encode step" that fails and reverses the mint if the nonce does not appear exactly once in the encoded output, and a "Verbs unit only" (`egress.rs:149`) confinement on `mint()` -- neither holds: no production code anywhere in the workspace calls the accessors (`.matches()`, `.nonce()`, `.target()`) needed to perform the exactly-once check, and the construction gate's `token-sealed:secret-once-mint` row is independently RED with 5 real non-`busbar-core-admin` call sites.
failure_scenario: `busbar-core-admin/src/verbs.rs:285` is the one production site that mints a `caps::egress::SecretOnce` (for `POST /api/v1/admin/keys`). A grep for every accessor capable of reading the nonce/target back out across the whole workspace shows they are called only from the type's own unit tests (`crates/busbar-contract/src/caps/tests/{mod.rs,what_the_record_reads.rs}`, `crates/busbar-core-admin/src/tests/verbs_tests.rs`, `crates/busbar-contract/tests/secret_carriers_print_nothing.rs`) -- never from the admin_codec/verbs response-rendering path (`grep -n "SecretOnce\|\.matches(\|\.target()" crates/busbar-core-admin/src/admin_codec/*.rs` returns only doc-comment mentions). But `approve` only INSERTS `At(digest)` for each OBSERVED skill; the stale `summarize -> At(h_old)` entry survives, so `drift.removed` is STILL non-empty, `state()` is STILL `Quarantined`, and the agent still serves nothing. The in-code comment at busbar-a2a/src/a2a/verbs.rs:617-618 asserts the opposite in so many words: 'The approval just adopted this exact observation, so it derives no drift and the state is `Approved` either way.' The only API that clears the axis is `Approval::reject_capability` (trust/mod.rs:421), which has ZERO production callers anywhere in the workspace -- and no A2A/MCP admin verb exposes it. Net: an operator-facing approve reports 200/APPLIED and the agent is permanently undelegable, recoverable only by deleting and re-adding the registration in config.

Position 2 (`plan-us`) -- a provably interchangeable, healthy twin -- is never considered and never even appears in `passed_over`. The caller renders `selected.pin_mismatch` (route.rs:216-218) and the submission is refused, so registering a third pool member takes the pool's existing failover offline the moment the primary trips. Contrast the module's own header at failover/mod.rs:47-49, which describes the rule as refusing the CANDIDATE ('a candidate that presents `None` ... is REFUSED ... rather than quietly served'), not the walk; the MCP site has the same shape (busbar-mcp/src/mcp/reroute.rs:60, :294).

Control for the reachability half: `grep -rn "fn interchange_key" crates/` -> 3 production impls (busbar-llm/src/engine/select.rs:445 returns `Some(pool)` so the model plane is immune; busbar-a2a/src/a2a/route.rs:50 and busbar-mcp/src/mcp/reroute.rs:60 both return `self.pin.as_deref()`, i.e. `None` while pending).

category: telemetry reports a figure the system does not hold
summary: `busbar_lane_state` mixes a PER-POOL cooldown with a LANE-GLOBAL `usable`, so when a lane is shared by two pools and one pool's breaker cell is fully Open the gauge for that pool reports 1 (`half-open`) instead of 2 (`tripped`) -- while `busbar_lane_available` on the very same label pair, rendered two lines later from the real per-pool `classify`, reports 0.
failure_scenario: Lane index 3 (model `gpt-4o`) is a member of pools `fast` and `bulk` -- a configuration the same function's own memoization comment assumes exists ('a lane shared across K pools would otherwise recompute the identical ... fold K times', metrics.rs:501-505). `fast`'s (pool, lane) cell trips Open with 30s of cooldown; `bulk`'s cell stays Closed. On scrape: `pool_cooldown = cooldown_remaining_in("fast", 3, now) = 30` (metrics.rs:526), but `snap.usable` is `lane_usable_any_cell` -- 'readiness is purely whether ANY per-pool cell would admit' (store/in_memory/mod.rs:717-731) -- and `bulk`'s cell admits, so `snap.usable == true`. Line 527's first arm is therefore false and the walk falls to `else if pool_cooldown > 0 { 1.0 }` (:529-530). `/metrics` renders `busbar_lane_state{pool="fast",lane="gpt-4o"} 1`, whose published HELP text is '1=half-open' (metrics.rs:1292) and whose const doc says '1 = half-open (cooling but probe admitted)' (:989) -- neither is true: pool `fast` admits nothing and no probe was won. Two lines down, `emit_lane_gauges` renders `busbar_lane_available{pool="fast",lane="gpt-4o"} 0` from `app.store.classify("fast", 3, now)` (:551-552), which IS per-pool. An operator whose page fires on `busbar_lane_state == 2` ('tripped') never sees this pool trip, and the two gauges on identical labels contradict each other on the same scrape. Single-pool lanes are unaffected, which is why the arm reads correct in isolation.
positive_control: Not a zero-claim. The lane-global vs per-pool split is quoted from the store itself: `sed -n '717,731p' crates/busbar-kernel/src/store/in_memory/mod.rs` shows `lane_usable_any_cell` folding `per_lane.iter().any(...)` across every pool cell, and `crates/busbar-kernel/src/store/vocab.rs:347-359` documents `availability`/`breaker_state` as 'Lane-GLOBAL ... best-case across the routed cells, matching `usable`'.

category: audit chain integrity
summary: `Journal::forget` drops a scope's cached chain position WITHOUT latching `overflowed`, but both resume paths short-circuit to a fresh seq-1 chain when `overflowed` is false -- so on an ABI-registered stream (cap = usize::MAX, where `overflowed` can never latch) a forget-then-append FORKS the durable hash chain at seq 1 even with a sink attached, which is the exact opposite of what `forget`'s own doc promises.
failure_scenario: `journal_register` over the plugin ABI hardcodes `cap = usize::MAX` (plane_host/journal.rs:459-464), so `commit_position`'s `while positions.len() > cap` (journal.rs:240) never fires and `overflowed` is false for the whole process lifetime. `journal_forget` is wired live on the host vtable (plane_host/vtable.rs:89 -> plane_host/journal.rs:853-871 -> `h.journal.forget(&scope)` at :870). A plane calls it on a scope it believes terminal (forget's doc at journal.rs:360-365 names exactly that use: 'a task reaches a terminal state and is evicted from the working set'). A late event for that scope then calls `journal_append_scoped`: `positions.get(scope)` misses, `resume_scoped` runs, and its FIRST statement is `if !self.overflowed.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { return Ok(Chain::new()); }` (journal.rs:481-483) -- it returns a seq-1, empty-prev_hash chain BEFORE it ever consults `self.sink()` on the next line. The append mints seq 1 with an empty `prev_hash` and `append_plane_record` writes a SECOND seq-1 row into a store that already holds seq 1..N for that scope. Forever after, `restore_scoped` at boot runs `Chain::from_persisted` -> `verify_chain` (genesis-anchored) and returns `SequenceBreak { expected: 2, found: 1 }`, which the journal reports as TAMPER EVIDENCE on `Restored::chain_breaks` -- a permanent false positive on busbar's own write, in the one subsystem whose product claim is tamper-evidence. `forget`'s doc explicitly asserts the safe outcome instead: 'reopening it would resume from the store tail (with a sink) or FORK at seq 1 (without one)' -- the parenthetical is false for every ABI-registered stream. `resume_missing` carries the identical short-circuit at journal.rs:263-265.
positive_control: Zero-claim is 'no in-tree plane calls journal_forget today (so this is a wired trap, not a live regression)'. Control -- the same command finds the sibling ABI entry points that DO have in-tree reachable callers: `grep -rn "journal_forget" crates/ | grep -v "busbar-plugin/"` -> only crates/busbar-kernel/src/plane_host/vtable.rs:89 (the live vtable wiring) and the definition at plane_host/journal.rs:853, while the same grep shape for `compact_via_seam` -> crates/busbar-kernel/src/calllog.rs:838 and for `journal_register_capped` -> crates/busbar-kernel/src/calllog.rs:195. The method finds callers where callers exist.

category: validate/boot divergence
summary: The identity-provider exemption is gated on `cfg!(test)` while its sibling 22 lines above is gated on `cfg!(any(test, feature = "test-support"))`, and the stand-in modules it exempts are registered under the WIDER gate -- so in a `test-support` build `--validate`/boot refuse an `identity-providers:` definition that `AuthPlugins::build` would have accepted.

That claim is false against the code: both arms in auth/mod.rs carry `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-support"))]` (auth/mod.rs:226 for the admin chain, :296 for the data chain, :879/:882 for `TestGroupsModule` itself) -- which is exactly why the auth-chain predicate at preflight.rs:98 passes `cfg!(any(test, feature = "test-support"))`. The two predicates disagree about the same vocabulary at the same call site, and the direction is the mirror image of the very bug preflight.rs:684-692 was written to close.

Both halves are direct reads: `sed -n '98p;120p' crates/busbar-kernel/src/preflight.rs` shows the two different gates, and `grep -n "test-groups-module\|test-scope-module" -B 2 crates/busbar-kernel/src/auth/mod.rs` shows `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-support"))]` immediately above lines 227, 297 and 880.

quote: // `stream_options` present but not an object: leave the body untouched (the upstream will 400
category: money/served-not-billed
summary: A client can send a syntactically-valid-but-wrong-typed `stream_options` field (e.g. `"stream_options": "x"`) on a streaming OpenAI-family chat request; busbar's own forced include_usage injection explicitly detects this and gives up rather than fixing it, on the documented assumption that the upstream will reject the request -- an assumption the code does not verify and that does not hold for every OpenAI-compatible egress an operator can configure a lane against. When it doesn't hold, the request is served normally and busbar's own, separately-confirmed 'no usage frame means zero tokens billed' rule silently zeroes the entire per-token charge for real, delivered output.
failure_scenario: A pool's lane speaks an OpenAI-compatible egress dialect (`stream_usage_requires_opt_in: true`, e.g. `busbar-llm-codec/src/openai_chat/mod.rs:130`) pointed at a self-hosted or third-party OpenAI-API-compatible server (vLLM, a local gateway, or any of the many 'OpenAI-compatible' providers busbar's own free-form `base_url` config is built to support). A caller sends `{"model":"m","stream":true,"stream_options":"x",...}`. `read_stream_intent` (engine/pipeline.rs:974-995) computes `client_has_stream_options = wants_stream && v.probe().get("stream_options").is_some()` -- true, because the key is merely PRESENT, its type is never checked -- and `client_include_usage = false` (the `.and_then(|b| b.as_bool())` on a string value yields `None` -> `unwrap_or(false)`). `inject_stream_usage` (assemble.rs:217-232) therefore enters its injection branch and, because `client_has_stream_options` is true, calls `inject_openai_stream_include_usage` (assemble.rs:240-261), which does `so.as_object_mut()` on the `stream_options` value, finds it is a `Value::String`, and executes the quoted line: it returns the ORIGINAL payload completely unmodified (assemble.rs:254, `return payload;`). The malformed field is forwarded upstream verbatim. If that specific upstream is lenient about an unrecognized/wrong-typed optional field (common in many OpenAI-compatible server implementations, which is precisely the class of provider busbar is built to let an operator point a lane at), it streams a normal 2xx answer with no trailing usage chunk. `crate::engine::tests::stream_no_usage_bills_zero_tests.rs`'s own `stream_without_usage_frame_bills_zero_on_every_dialect` test independently confirms the consequence: a stream with no usage frame bills the token ledger `0` and records a metering row with every tier at `0`, while the client received a complete, real answer. No estimation fallback exists anywhere in busbar-llm/busbar-llm-codec (`grep` for `estimate_tokens`/`token_estimate`/`estimated: true` in non-test source returns nothing) to catch the gap. Only the flat per-request fee (if the operator has one) still posts; the per-token charge -- the dominant cost component for almost every real deployment -- is silently zero for a request that consumed real, paid-for upstream compute.
positive_control: The developers' own comment at assemble.rs:206-210 states the threat model explicitly ('an OpenAI Chat Completions upstream only emits that usage ... when the request carried stream_options.include_usage: true. A client that did not opt in would otherwise leave the upstream silent on tokens and busbar would bill ZERO') and assemble.rs:237-238 names the exact fallback this finding concerns ('the worst case is the pre-existing zero-usage billing gap') -- proving the code path and its consequence are real, not speculative. The idempotent DOM-injector path (`inject_openai_stream_include_usage_pristine`, assemble.rs:296-332) independently defers to the SAME `inject_openai_stream_include_usage` function on the identical non-object check (assemble.rs:303-305), so this is not a one-path quirk: both entry points into the injector share the one gap. `stream_no_usage_bills_zero_tests.rs`'s `stream_without_usage_frame_bills_zero_on_every_dialect` (line 43) is the positive control proving the zero-billing consequence is real, tested, intended behavior for a missing usage frame, not a hypothetical.

category: money/ledger-key-divergence
summary: The new kernel-loop step chain's Admit step builds the request's `UsageSink` (the pool-scoped token-ledger accounting key) from the caller's raw destination string at Step 4, before candidate resolution (Step 5) has decided whether that destination is a configured pool or a bare/by-model lane -- while the legacy `NativePlane::drive` it is meant to replace byte-for-byte defers building the identical `UsageSink` until AFTER candidate resolution, so a bare-model request's token spend is filed under a DIFFERENT pool-accounting key ("gpt-4" vs the canonical empty-string default cell) depending on which of the two live drivers happens to serve it.
failure_scenario: An operator reaches model "gpt-4" only as a bare/ad-hoc model (no `pools:` entry -- resolved via `by_model()`), a shape `unit/route.rs:150-151` documents explicitly: "a bare model lane routes on the default (empty) cell, exactly as it always has." Driver 1 (legacy): `native_ingress.rs:440-452` resolves candidates FIRST (`pool_name == ""` for the by-model branch) and only THEN builds `usage_sink(host, req.gov, pool_name, ...)` at line 518 -- the sink's `pool` field is `""`. Driver 2 (new step chain): `admit()` (this file, line 152-191) builds the SAME `UsageSink` via the SAME `native_ingress::usage_sink()` function at line 175, but at line 173 sets `pool = downgraded.unwrap_or(ctx.destination)` -- `ctx.destination` is the raw caller-requested string "gpt-4", never normalized, because `AdmitCtx.destination` is read at Step 4, structurally before Route (Step 5) has run (this file's own module doc: "candidate resolution ... stay AFTER this call, in the Route step"). `UsageSink.pool` feeds directly into `host.meter_ledger(..., &sink.pool, ...)` (engine/usage.rs) on every delivered response, so the exact same model's token spend is filed under `""` via one driver and `"gpt-4"` via the other. Any pool-scoped budget cap or per-pool spend breakdown an operator relies on for the shared default/ad-hoc cell would silently stop (or start) counting that model's traffic the moment production requests happen to be served by whichever driver is currently live for a given request -- and which driver is live is itself the subject of contradictory documentation elsewhere in the tree (three files call the kernel-loop flip dormant, one unconditionally activates it), so this is a real, reachable divergence today, not a hypothetical migration gap. No test anywhere exercises the Admit step against a bare/by-model destination in either implementation.
positive_control: The POOL-based branch of the identical split proves the method still works when the two agree: `native_ingress.rs:441-442` and `unit/route.rs:156-157` both resolve to the SAME pool-name string for a configured pool, confirming the two implementations are faithfully parallel everywhere except the by-model branch. `grep -n 'AdmitCtx {' crates/busbar-llm/src/unit/tests/*.rs` shows every test construction (unit/tests/admit.rs:165,314; unit/tests/chain.rs:863,1497) uses `destination: "p"` or `&model` where `model` resolves to the named pool `POOL` (`"p"`) for every fixture except the already-refused `UnknownModel` case -- i.e. no test in this crate exercises Admit against a bare-model destination, confirming the zero-test-coverage half of this claim.

category: money/two-books-disagree
summary: MCP-sampling-triggered LLM completions are structurally wired to the legacy `run_gauntlet` money path only and can never reach the new kernel-loop/durable-ledger book that direct HTTP LLM traffic already posts to by default, so the two books permanently disagree by an entire, real, revenue-bearing traffic class -- independent of whatever the DECISION #29 oracle-flip status is for ordinary HTTP requests.
failure_scenario: An MCP client calls a tool that triggers server-side LLM sampling. `busbar-mcp/src/mcp/sampling.rs:415` calls `EngineHost::synthesize_completion(...)`, unconditionally wired (`crates/busbar/src/main.rs:250-252`, gated only on the default-on `proto-llm` feature) to `busbar_llm::native_ingress::synthesize_completion` (native_ingress.rs:878-942). That function always calls `operation_resolved` -> `run()` (native_ingress.rs:611-642, 564-603), which ends at the quoted line: the OLD substrate loop that performs only the legacy synchronous ledger/metering-series accrual. It has no path to the new loop that drives `unit::admit/route/meter/audit` and settles onto the composition root's durable ledger book -- that loop is entered ONLY through the HTTP arrival tables' own registration, never for the completion-synthesis re-entry point. Meanwhile the feature that swaps ordinary HTTP LLM traffic onto the new loop is default-on and shipped in the release build. So in the shipped default binary, every direct HTTP chat-completion request is already dual-posted (matching the already-confirmed dual-accrual finding), while every MCP-sampling-originated completion posts to the OLD ledger only -- the new book is permanently missing an entire traffic class by construction, not merely 'not yet migrated'. Any consumer that treats the new durable-ledger book as the authoritative spend/invoice source would silently under-report or under-invoice all MCP-sampling spend forever, with no code path available to close the gap short of wiring `synthesize_completion` onto the new loop too.
positive_control: `grep -n 'synthesize_completion' crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/sampling.rs` matches at line 415, a live call site, not a test; `grep -n 'install_completion_ingress' crates/busbar/src/main.rs` matches at line 250, gated only on the default-on `proto-llm` feature -- together proving the MCP-sampling re-entry is live and unconditionally bound to this crate's `native_ingress::synthesize_completion`. Contrast with the one function that DOES drive a resolved-op arrival through the new loop end-to-end: it is `#[cfg(test)]`-gated, i.e. compiled out of every production build, confirming there is no live alternate path from the completion-synthesis re-entry to the new book.

category: audit-method/oracle-blind-spots
summary: The step-chain-vs-legacy-plane money-parity oracle -- the mechanism this crate built specifically to prove the two drivers agree -- has two blind spots that between them make it structurally unable to catch either dual-driver money bug above: it never reads or compares which pool-accounting bucket a charge landed in (only key-wide totals and per-model rows), and it never reads the new async ledger/durable book at all, only the legacy `GovState`/`metering_for` surfaces.
failure_scenario: `observe()` (unit/tests/chain.rs:421-517), the one function every parity assertion in this file is built from, sources its money fields entirely from the quoted `derived_bucket_usage` call (key-wide totals keyed by the fixed period string "total", not by pool) and `gov.metering_for(...)` rows compared only by `(model, provider)` -- confirmed by `grep -n 'fields.push(("'` enumerating every tracked field (status, headers, ledger_requests, ledger_tokens, ledger_spend_cents, metering_rows, admissible, breaker, cooldown) with no `pool`/`bucket` dimension anywhere in the list. Because a caller's TOTAL spend and token count are identical whichever pool-accounting bucket they are filed under, `the_chain_leaves_the_money_where_the_legacy_plane_leaves_it` and `the_chain_matches_the_legacy_drive_on_every_fixture` (lines 1023, 1258) would report a clean PASS even for the exact bare-model pool-key divergence described above -- that dimension is invisible to this oracle. Separately, and independent of the pool dimension: `grep -rn 'reported_after_terminal|LateAccrual|settle_late'` across every file under `crates/busbar-llm/src/unit/tests/` and `crates/busbar-llm/src/engine/{tests,engine_tests}/` returns zero matches -- the function that feeds the NEW async ledger book (`Walk::reported_after_terminal`, walk.rs:474) is referenced only in walk.rs's own doc comments and its live caller in the composition root (outside this crate), never exercised or asserted against by any test in this crate. So the crate's own 'the chain leaves the money where the legacy plane leaves it' proof is, by construction, a proof about the OLD ledger only: it establishes nothing about whether the new book agrees with either driver, which is exactly the open question this round was asked to help resolve. The old ledger is the only one this crate's own tests treat as ground truth today.
positive_control: `grep -n 'fields.push(("' crates/busbar-llm/src/unit/tests/chain.rs` enumerates every field the oracle tracks -- a positive list proving the oracle DOES carefully track several dimensions (this is not 'no oracle exists'), with pool/bucket attribution specifically absent; a further `grep -n 'pool'` on the same file matches only the fixture constant `POOL` and candidate-resolution lookups, never an `Observed` field. For the second half: `grep -n 'reported_after_terminal'` DOES match live, non-test call sites in `unit/walk.rs` itself (proving the function exists and is reachable) while the identical grep restricted to `*/tests/*.rs` and `*_tests.rs` paths in this crate returns nothing -- the same search that finds the live code finds zero test coverage of it, which is the required positive control for the zero-claim.

quote: // refund is offloaded/async and is covered by the flat-fee refund tests.)
category: documentation/audit-risk
summary: Two comments in the same test file describe the identical flat-fee refund mechanism (`refund_request`, fired by `finish`/`finish_admitted` on a charged-but-non-2xx end) in directly contradictory terms: one says it is now purely synchronous in-memory accounting with no store offload, the other -- describing the exact same charged=true/non-2xx case -- calls it 'offloaded/async'.
failure_scenario: Lines 228-229 of this file state, of `test_finish_refunds_flat_fee_on_non_2xx_keeps_on_2xx`: "No-runtime `#[test]`: `refund_request` now decrements the AUTHORITATIVE in-memory cell (no store offload), so it is observable synchronously," and that test then drives `finish(...)` synchronously with no `.await` and asserts the refund landed immediately. Later in the SAME file, `finish_admitted_does_not_refund_an_uncharged_admit` (around line 3377-3399) says of the charged=true case it deliberately does not exercise: the quoted line, "the positive charged=true refund is offloaded/async." Since this round was specifically asked to determine whether the live refund mechanism matches the tested-but-dead `Walk::refund()` computation, a reader who trusts the stale 'offloaded/async' comment could wrongly conclude the refund is eventually-consistent and add unnecessary reconciliation logic around it, or dismiss a real future ordering regression as 'expected async behavior' when the actual code path is synchronous.

category: money/cache-accounting-mismatch
summary: The OpenAI Chat Completions dialect table asserts (comment at line 91) that this dialect 'reports no separate written-to-cache quantity,' but the crate's own sibling codec genuinely reads and separately prices a cache-write quantity for this exact dialect (`usage.prompt_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens`), so this table's cache accounting silently diverges from both the provider's real wire format and busbar's own other reader of it.
failure_scenario: `crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/openai_chat/mod.rs:206` (`fn read_cache_write_tokens`) reads and documents `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens` off a real OpenAI Chat Completions response, wired into `openai_chat/reader.rs` (buffered and streaming both) and verified against a captured golden fixture. If `busbar-plane-llm`'s `dialect.rs` table (or a future consumer of it) is ever used to extract usage instead of the codec reader it currently has no live production path to, an OpenAI response that actually wrote to the prompt cache would have its cache-write tokens silently folded into plain input or dropped rather than priced at the cache-write tier -- underbilling a real, provider-reported quantity. Currently inert: this plane's `Plane`/`PlaneMeta` implementation has no live HTTP call site (confirmed independently this round -- production traffic runs entirely through busbar-llm's own `unit/` step files and engine, a structurally different type from this crate's `LlmPlane`), so no dollars are at risk today, but the wrong fact is committed to the file architecturally positioned to become the live one if this crate is ever activated.
positive_control: The `bedrock` and `responses` entries in the SAME file DO carry a real, codec-verified `cache_write_pointer` (line 118: `"/usage/cacheWriteInputTokens"`; line 130: `"/usage/input_tokens_details/cache_write_tokens"`), proving the table is capable of stating this field correctly and that the `openai` entry's `None` is a specific, isolated miss rather than a general 'this crate never tracks cache-write' limitation.

quote: caller twice and can never send a second email. That is why `Repeatable::Yes` here is a
category: documentation/money-invariant-risk
summary: The comment explaining why an `AfterDispatch` failover retry is safe reads as if a repeat dispatch 'charges the caller twice,' the opposite of the invariant the surrounding code and every sibling comment on this exact property actually state -- a dropped negation inverts the sentence documenting precisely the money property (no double-charge on retry) this audit round was asked to check.
