But a future maintainer reading this exact line while touching failover/retry billing -- exactly the surface this round's brief calls high-risk -- would read a false statement of the invariant at the one place in the crate that documents why repeat dispatch is considered safe, which is the class of stale/inverted money-invariant comment that misleads a reviewer or a future edit rather than a live defect.
positive_control: The sibling comment two lines above and the model plane's actual behavior (`Repeatable::Yes` unconditionally, contrasted with other planes' `Repeatable::No` unless configured, per the same comment block) both describe a plane deliberately repeat-SAFE because a completion is idempotent to request twice -- confirming the intended sentence is the negation of what is written, not an accurate description of a real double-charge the code then tolerates.

category: spec-MUST-unenforced / inconsistent-validation
summary: The SEP-2663 async task-completion path never calls busbar_plane_mcp::outputschema::check, so a tool that is BOTH task-capable and has a published output_schema gets zero structured-output validation when it finishes as a task, even though the identical tool calling synchronously (method.rs:2047-2078) IS validated.
failure_scenario: An operator declares a tool with `task_support: optional` (or `required`) AND `output_schema: {...}` in the same tools_allow entry -- config.rs places no restriction preventing this combination (grep for `task_support` in config.rs shows only an ask_caller/task_support cross-check at line 1533, nothing about output_schema). A caller invokes it; busbar answers CreateTaskResult and the async runner (tasks.rs `dispatch`/`run`) drives the identical `inputreq::drive` loop as the synchronous path. When the upstream's leg completes with Round::Done(value) whose structuredContent violates (or entirely omits) the published schema, tasks.rs's completion arm runs ONLY `sanitize::normalise_json` and stores the result verbatim via `task.complete()` (tasks.rs:382-392, no schema check inside it either). The lying/malformed structured result is later served byte-for-byte to `tasks/get`/`tasks/result`, the task is marked `completed` with no audit flag, and the model/caller receives structured data busbar itself published a schema for and never checked -- the exact hostile-upstream scenario the synchronous path's check exists to catch, silently bypassed for every task-shaped tool.
positive_control: grep -n "output_schema\|outputschema\|structuredContent" crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/tasks.rs returns ZERO matches; the identical grep against crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/method.rs returns hits at lines 2047-2054 showing the check IS present and wired there (`if let Some(schema) = &selected.output_schema { if let Some(structured) = value.get("structuredContent") { if let Err(why) = super::outputschema::check(structured, schema) ...`), proving the validator exists, is reachable, and is simply never called from the task file.

category: spec-MUST-partially-unenforced
summary: Even on the synchronous tools/call path, the outputSchema conformance check only runs when the upstream's result carries a `structuredContent` key at all; an upstream that has an operator-published output_schema and simply omits structuredContent entirely (rather than sending a type-violating value) skips the whole check and is served to the caller as an ordinary success.
failure_scenario: Operator publishes `output_schema: {required: ["status","findings"], ...}` for a tool (busbar's own catalogue.rs render() comment at line ~1355 says the PRESENCE of outputSchema on the wire is what turns conforming structured results into a MUST for busbar). A buggy or hostile upstream answers `tools/call` with only `content: [...]` text and no `structuredContent` member at all. `value.get("structuredContent")` is `None`, so method.rs:2047-2080's entire `if let Some(schema) = ... if let Some(structured) = ...` block is skipped; the call is audited OUTCOME_APPLIED and returned to the caller as a normal success with no violation ever recorded, even though the spec's MUST ("If an output schema is provided, servers MUST provide structured results that conform to it") was violated by the simplest possible means -- not sending the field at all.
positive_control: grep -rn "structured_output_violation" crates/busbar-mcp/src shows the concept is named only in a comment (catalogue.rs:1356) pointing at this exact block; there is no second check anywhere in method.rs or tasks.rs for a MISSING structuredContent when output_schema is Some -- confirmed by grepping method.rs for every `output_schema`/`structuredContent` occurrence (only the two lines at 2047-2048 exist).

category: absent-control / spec-field-unmodeled
summary: busbar's MCP Tool representation models only name, description and input_schema (lines 70-79); the MCP Tool schema's `icons` field is not parsed on the client-parsing side, not representable in the operator's tools_allow config grammar, and not published on the server-rendering side -- there is no icon-scheme validation anywhere in the plane because there is no icon handling anywhere in the plane.
failure_scenario: Per the round-3 conformance hunt (CLI.HOSTILE.BAD-ICON-SCHEME), a hostile upstream advertises a tool with `icons: [{src: "javascript:alert(1)", mimeType: "image/png"}]`. Today this is harmless in practice only because busbar drops every upstream field outside {name, description, inputSchema} when it re-hashes/re-publishes a tool (connect.rs's parse_tool_list at lines 121-154 reads only name/description/inputSchema; catalogue.rs's render() at ~1330-1360 emits only name/description/inputSchema/outputSchema/_meta) -- so no javascript: URI a hostile upstream supplies can ever reach a caller through busbar's own catalogue today. But that safety is an accident of the current field allowlist, not a deliberate scheme gate: there is zero validation code ready to catch a `javascript:`/`data:`/`file:` icon scheme if a future change adds `icons` pass-through (the natural next step, given description/inputSchema/outputSchema all already have dedicated operator-controlled equivalents) -- unlike those three fields, an icons feature would have no digest-pinning, no sanitize::normalise_opt call, and no scheme allowlist to reuse, because none was ever written.
positive_control: grep -rni "icon" --include="*.rs" crates/busbar-mcp crates/busbar-plane-mcp returns zero matches, in the same tree where the sibling fields this finding contrasts against (description, input_schema, output_schema) each have multiple real matches (e.g. `pub(crate) description: String` at client/catalogue.rs:77, `output_schema: Option<serde_json::Value>` at config.rs:226 and catalogue.rs:126) -- proving the grep methodology finds real fields when they exist and the icon absence is genuine, not a naming mismatch.

category: self-documented-unresolved-defect
summary: The plane's compile-time contract Claim hardcodes the MCP mount path to the literal `/mcp` default, while the actual runtime mount path is operator-configured and derived from `mcp.canonical_uri` (mod.rs:926-1094, validated to accept any absolute-URI path, not just `/mcp`) -- the file's own header calls this out by name as an open, unfixed finding.
failure_scenario: An operator configures `mcp.canonical_uri: https://gateway.example.com/api/tools-mcp` (a fully valid, boot-accepted configuration -- mod.rs's own validate_canonical_uri only rejects an empty path or a bare `/`, not a non-default one). The plane's actual HTTP route is correctly registered at the derived path (mod.rs:642-672 use `mount_path()`, the real derived value), so live requests to the real endpoint are served correctly. But the plane's declared `Claim` used by busbar-kernel's boot-time cross-plane collision check (registry.rs's `claims_overlap`, invoked from `register()`) still names the fictional default `/mcp`, not this deployment's real `/api/tools-mcp` -- so the one mechanism that exists to catch two planes claiming the same path at boot is validating a path this deployment does not actually serve at, and could both (a) falsely clear a genuine collision between the MCP plane's real path and another plane's claim that happens to sit at the literal string `/mcp` (never checked against what MCP actually uses), and (b) fail to warn an operator who assumes the disjointness check covers their configured path.
positive_control: The defect is self-documented in the file's own module header (claims.rs:8-21): "Those two facts cannot both be honoured... a deployment that configures a different path is a deployment this plane's claims do not cover... It is a finding, it is not fixed here." Cross-checked against mod.rs:926 ("The MOUNT PATH is derived from this [canonical_uri] rather than configured separately") and registry.rs:327 (`claims_overlap(&left.claim, &right.claim)` called from `register()`), confirming the claim is consumed for boot-time overlap detection and is not resynced to the operator's actual configured path.

category: config-accepted-but-dead / transport-parity-gap
summary: On the stdio client transport, EVERY server-initiated authority ask (sampling/createMessage, elicitation/create, roots/list) that the operator has granted is unconditionally answered `Unsatisfiable` -- including `sampling`, which DOES have a full, working satisfier on the HTTP/MRTR leg (`crate::mcp::sampling::satisfy_upstream_ask`, wired at method.rs:1953 and tasks.rs:924) -- and config.rs's boot-time validation never warns that a `transport: stdio` registration's `grants.sampling: true` + `sampling:` policy block can never fire.
failure_scenario: An operator registers an upstream with `transport: stdio`, `command: /usr/local/bin/my-mcp-server`, `grants.sampling: true`, and a complete `sampling: {model, max_tokens, max_requests_per_minute}` policy block. config.rs's boot validation (lines ~1481-1500) checks only that `grants.sampling` is true whenever a `sampling:` block is present -- it has no transport-awareness at all, so this configuration is accepted cleanly with no warning. At runtime, the locally-spawned child asks `sampling/createMessage` over stdio; `client/peer.rs::decide_ask` (line 308-317) checks only `grants.allows(ask.key())`, finds it true, and returns `AskOutcome::Unsatisfiable` unconditionally for every kind on this leg (the comment at line 341-345 says so explicitly: "busbar holds the `{kind}` grant ... but has no satisfier for that ask on the stdio leg in this release") -- so an operator who followed the documentation, set the grant, and wrote a full sampling policy gets a config that looks completely wired, passes boot, and can never do anything: every sampling ask from that stdio child is refused with `-32001` forever, and the only way to discover this is to read the runtime error text after the fact.
positive_control: grep -n "satisfy_upstream_ask" crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/sampling.rs crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/method.rs crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/tasks.rs shows the sampling satisfier IS called from the HTTP/MRTR leg (method.rs:1953-1955, tasks.rs:924-926); the identical grep against crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/client/peer.rs and crates/busbar-mcp/src/mcp/client/stdio.rs returns nothing, and `decide_ask`'s own match arms (lines 308-317) have no branch that ever calls a satisfier -- `Unsatisfiable` is the only outcome for a granted ask on this file's whole reachable path.

category: config-accepted-but-dead
summary: `grants.elicitation: true` passes boot-time config validation as an ordinary grant (config.rs has no elicitation-specific boot check the way it has for roots/sampling), but no code path anywhere in the plane can ever satisfy an elicitation ask from an upstream: both call sites that would satisfy a granted non-sampling ask (method.rs:1953-1958, tasks.rs:924-929) route it through `roots::satisfy_upstream_ask`, which immediately refuses anything whose kind is not literally `"roots"` -- so `grants.elicitation: true` is accepted as configuration but is unconditionally a no-op at runtime, on every transport.
failure_scenario: An operator, reading that `grants.sampling`/`grants.roots`/`grants.elicitation` are the three symmetric authority grants (config.rs's own doc comments describe them as a set of three), sets `grants.elicitation: true` on a registration believing it lets that upstream ask busbar's caller for confirmation via a human-in-the-loop elicitation. Boot succeeds with no warning (there is no `elicitation:` policy block to cross-validate against, unlike roots/sampling, so nothing at boot time can catch the mismatch). At runtime, any `elicitation/create` ask from that upstream is refused with "busbar holds the `elicitation` grant ... has no satisfier for that ask in this release" (roots.rs:121-125) -- a refusal the operator only discovers the first time the upstream actually tries to use the capability they believe they granted.
positive_control: roots.rs's own doc comment (lines 101-105) states the design choice directly: "`elicitation` (and any kind this build has never heard of) falls through to the standing refusal below ... there is no human to interrupt, and that decision is recorded in `qa/WAIVERS.md` rather than here" -- confirming this is a known, documented, intentional product limitation rather than an oversight, which is why this is rated LOW rather than MEDIUM/HIGH: the risk is operator-facing config confusion (a grant that silently does nothing), not a security bypass, and the team has already recorded the decision elsewhere.

category: money/tamper-evidence unwired

CONTROLS PROVING THE METHOD: the same command shape finds real cross-crate users of the same crates -- `busbar_kernel_ledger::` matches 32 times in crates/busbar/src/root/kernel.rs, `totals_as_of` matches in production at crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs:1449, and `AuditInputs` matches in production at crates/busbar/src/root/units_mcp.rs:62 and units_voice.rs:1898.

category: money/journal unwired

category: money/test-cannot-fail
summary: The 64-case `saturating_the_books_moves_no_ordinary_settlement` sweep asserts the overdraft column against `posted.overdraft()`, which is zero in all 64 cases; 28 of those cases have used > reserved, exactly the input that breaks the ledger identity, and the sweep never asks the identity.
failure_scenario: The sweep at settle_tests.rs:362-413 runs `reserved x used` over 8 amounts each. `hold("p", reserved)` is a fresh `Hold::open` that never spends, so `posted.overdraft()` is 0 for every case and `assert_eq!(figures.overdraft_carried_out, i128::from(posted.overdraft()))` is `0 == 0`, 64 times. In the 28 cases where used > reserved (e.g. reserved=0/used=1, reserved=999/used=1_000_000) `Ledger::post` writes open_holds -= reserved, settled += used, remainders += 0, overdraft_carried_out += 0 -- so `residual(zero, figures).amount() == used - reserved != 0`: money settled that nothing drew. The sweep's own doc (:355-360) claims 'the reference is computed here from the definition ... so this is a check of the arithmetic and not of itself', yet `want_settled` and `want_released` are both read back off `posted.settled()`/`posted.reserved()` -- the same values `post` consumed. Meanwhile identity_tests.rs:61 hand-repairs the coupling (`h.record_overdraft(spent - reserved)`) before asserting the identity, so the only test that checks the identity under over-spend is checking a book the test itself made consistent.
positive_control: Not a zero-claim. The 28 over-spend pairs are enumerable from settle_tests.rs:364-373's `amounts` array; `record_overdraft` has zero production callers (`grep -rn --include='*.rs' 'record_overdraft' crates/` -> only identity_tests.rs:61,166, caps tests, budget tests/cells.rs:763, and the definition at hold.rs:258,273), control: `hold.spend(` matches production at crates/busbar-kernel/src/teller.rs:1323 and crates/busbar-kernel-budget/src/lib.rs:271 under the identical command.

category: money/two-paths-disagree
summary: The one production exit path spends the hold by the kernel accrual meter's total and then settles the posting at the settlement table's amount -- two different numbers -- so `Posted.overdraft` and `Posted.settled` are derived from different figures and the ledger identity does not close.
failure_scenario: A COMPLETED unit whose destination reported no usage: `settle_amount` returns `(0, ...)` (teller.rs:386-391), while `hold.spend(run.meter.total(), 0)` at :1323 records overdraft O>0 because the meter ran past the reservation with no headroom. `Posted::settle(hold, 0, ...)` then carries reserved=R, settled=0, overdraft=O; `Ledger::post` writes open_holds -= R, settled += 0, remainders += R, overdraft_carried_out += O, and `identity::residual` reads -O: the books are out by the whole overdraft on a unit that billed nothing. The mirror case is worse: a located figure above the kernel meter's own count (settle_amount:385 returns `located`) settles `located > reserved` while `hold.overdraft()` stayed 0, so `Posted::settle` sets the OVERDRAFT FLAG from `settled > reserved` (hold.rs:677) but never the overdraft FIGURE -- value is settled that nothing drew and the overdraft column reads zero.
positive_control: Not a zero-claim. Both lines are in the same function body: teller.rs:1323 spends `run.meter.total()`, teller.rs:1346 settles `u128::from(amount)` where `amount` comes from `settle_amount(&outcome, &evidence)` at :1311; `settle_amount`'s table (teller.rs:372-405) has six arms that return something other than the meter total, including `(0, PostingFlags::VOIDED)` and `(left.min(right), METER_DISPUTED)`.

category: money/two-paths-disagree
summary: The recompute prices a line at the ARCHIVE's sealed tier and treats the line's own tier as the thing that can be forged; the production statement path prices at the LINE's own tier and documents the opposite rule. The only path that would catch a forged tier is the unwired one.
failure_scenario: recompute_tests.rs:226-242 (`a_tier_the_line_invented_is_found`) states the rule: 'A recompute that had priced at the line's own tier would have agreed with a line that invented a discount for itself.' But `totals_as_of` -- the read path the admin usage endpoint actually calls (crates/busbar/src/root/units_admin/mod.rs:1449) -- prices at `line.tier_bp` (totals.rs:381), and totals.rs:363-366 asserts the contrary rule: 'The tier is the line's own'. `adjusting_entries` (settle.rs:436-437) also prices at `line.tier_bp`. So a booked line whose `tier_bp` reads 5_000 instead of 10_000 bills at half price on every statement the node serves, and the arbiter that would report `Divergence::Tier` has zero production callers. A second, non-adversarial form of the same divergence: `SealedHistory::tier_bp` defaults to BASIS_POINTS for any key absent from the `tiers` map (recompute.rs:124), and `SealedHistory::new` (recompute.rs:105) builds that map EMPTY -- so on any archive built that way the recompute would reprice every discounted line at full price and write that figure back into `posting.cached`.

The certifying test `it_equals_the_posting_lookup_on_the_same_quantities` (cost/tests/view_tests.rs:343-358) uses STANDARD_TIER_BP and whole counts, i.e. exactly the inputs where a disagreement is impossible.

category: money/under-enumerated park
summary: The owner-signed PARK that lets the admin usage read fall back to the legacy projection enumerates three of MoneyError's four variants; the wildcard arm also swallows NoCardInForce, so a hole in the dated rate-card history prices at the caller's pinned card instead of refusing.
failure_scenario: service.rs:245-252 names the fallback's cases as 'an unnamed lane ..., an unnamed class, or an accumulator that left the representable range' -- LaneUnpriced, ClassUnpriced, Overflow. `MoneyError` has a fourth variant, `NoCardInForce` (cost/view.rs:235), which cost/history.rs:266-269 describes as 'a hole, which is a refusal and never a zero. A zero would price a gap in the record as a free request.' A metering row whose `arrived_ms` falls in a gap between dated entries reaches `Err(_)` here and is priced by `derive_spend_micros` against the `card` parameter, which is whatever card the caller pinned rather than the (non-existent) card in force at that instant -- a figure the module's own design says nobody may invent, served without the PARK's doc ever naming the case.
positive_control: Not a zero-claim. `MoneyError`'s four variants are enumerated at crates/busbar-kernel-ledger/src/cost/view.rs:232-261; the PARK doc at service.rs:245-247 names three.

quote: /// active handles is bounded by ADMISSION or by nothing — see
category: unbounded map / no cap on the active (non-terminal) population
summary: DurableHandleEngine::submit inserts every new handle into the working-set HashMap unconditionally; SweepBounds::max_retained (handle_engine.rs:889-914, sweep rule 2) caps only the TERMINAL population, so a population of handles that stay ACTIVE forever is never evicted and never capped by this engine at all.
failure_scenario: A caller with access to this engine (confirmed: crates/busbar-a2a/src/taskstore.rs:635 calls engine.submit() with no admission/capacity check before it) repeatedly submits new handles and keeps each one 'active' by touching it more often than SweepBounds::abandon_secs, so it never becomes terminal. Sweep rule 0 never abandons an actively-touched handle and rule 2 only ever walks and evicts the TERMINAL population (handle_engine.rs:886-914 returns early once under max_retained and otherwise only selects victims where `!*terminal` is skipped) -- it has nothing to evict when nothing is terminal. The handles map (each entry an opaque Arc<dyn Any> row plus provenance-chain state) grows without bound for the life of the process, exhausting host memory. The field's own doc comment (handle_engine.rs:136-143) and docs/design/handle-engine-retention-sweep.md explicitly acknowledge this is a deliberate design tradeoff whose only intended backstop is caller-side admission control -- which the one in-tree caller checked does not implement.
positive_control: The same file DOES enforce a real, working bound elsewhere for the population it targets: sweep rule 2 (handle_engine.rs:889-914) walks the ExpiryIndex oldest-first and evicts once the TERMINAL population is at/over max_retained, and evict_verified/evict_if_terminal/compact (lines 951-973, 1099-1110, 1114-1133) are all correctly gated, paired removal paths (re-verified independently: grep of every `handles.remove(` call site in the file shows all three are gated on `meta.terminal`) -- proving the method finds and credits a real enforced cap in this file when one exists. No equivalent cap exists anywhere in the file for the ACTIVE population.

category: unbounded map / missing sweep, even on the success path
summary: The process-lifetime durable work-handle registry (DurableRegistry.handles, backing the wired `workhandle_open`/`workhandle_resume` ABI slots) grows on every workhandle_open and has no background sweeper; a handle that is never resumed is never reaped, and even a handle that IS successfully resumed is left in the map forever because the live/success path never calls `.remove()`.
failure_scenario: workhandle_open (dispatch.rs:143-176) does `reg.handles.insert(raw, DurableEntry { .. })` on every call with no cap. workhandle_resume (dispatch.rs:188-220) only removes an entry on one narrow path: a *second* resume call after the handle's ttl has already elapsed (line 211, `reg.handles.remove(&handle.0)`). The live/success path (line 217-218) reads the entry and returns `StatusClass::Ok` without ever removing it. So (1) a handle whose callback never arrives (upstream never resumes it) is never reclaimed by anything -- there is no background sweep, only this reactive per-key check triggered by a resume call that in this scenario never happens -- and (2) a handle that IS successfully resumed leaks permanently, since the happy path never calls `.remove()`. Over the life of a long-running gateway processing many units of durable work, DURABLE.handles grows monotonically; only a process restart reclaims it. There is also no ABI slot to explicitly close/forget a handle -- the vtable exposes only workhandle_open/workhandle_resume.
positive_control: The same directory applies the fix pattern correctly for structurally identical process-global registries: plane_host/creds.rs's mint() self-sweeps expired entries via an amortized doubling watermark on every insert, and plane_host/identity.rs's register() enforces `const MAX_RETAINED_IDENTITIES: usize = 256` with FIFO eviction (identity.rs:46, 83-95; verified directly: `while reg.order.len() > MAX_RETAINED_IDENTITIES { ... reg.map.remove(&oldest); }`). dispatch.rs's own module doc even names the general failure class by prior experience ('Reclaiming it at future-drop was the v4 arena bug', dispatch.rs:119) -- the codebase has previously been bitten by mishandling this exact table's lifecycle -- yet no sweep or close path was added for the never-resumed/happy-path case. No caller of workhandle_open/workhandle_resume exists outside tests and the vtable wiring itself (grep across the full checkout), so this is a live, wired ABI capability with no current in-tree production caller, not dead scaffolding -- the same posture as several already-confirmed findings in this audit.

quote: /// The hard session wall-clock ceiling (`streams.session_max_secs:`) the pump enforces.
category: money / duration ceiling never enforced
summary: The operator-configured `streams.session_max_secs` (documented as a "hard session wall-clock ceiling", default 3600s) is parsed, defaulted, and threaded through `VoiceRuntime`, but no code anywhere in the runtime ever reads it to compare against elapsed session time or hard-close a session — the field this doc comment says "the pump enforces" is never consulted by the pump.
failure_scenario: `StreamsCfg::session_max_secs` is declared at crates/busbar-voice/src/config.rs:33-36 ("Hard session wall-clock ceiling default — 3600s (60 minutes)") and copied onto `VoiceRuntime.session_max_secs` at crates/busbar-voice/src/runtime/mod.rs:68,96,110,231 (storage/plumbing only — `with_streams`, `VoiceRuntime::new`, `build_runtime_hosted`). The one thing named as its consumer, "the pump", is `serve_with_sweep` (crates/busbar-voice/src/runtime/session.rs:455-475): its periodic tick only checks `core.carrier().is_closed()` and calls `core.sweep_expired(now_ms())`, and `sweep_expired` (session.rs:171-176) forwards to `GovernedCalls::expired` — the TOOL-CALL-DEADLINE sweep, a completely different concern. A grep for `session_max_secs` across the whole repository (`grep -rn session_max_secs --include=*.rs .`) turns up exactly six sites and every one of them is a declaration, a default, a struct field, or a copy from one struct to another (config.rs, runtime/mod.rs, tests/config_tests.rs) — none is a comparison against a session-open timestamp or `now`. Concretely: an operator sets (or relies on the documented default of) `streams.session_max_secs: 3600` believing busbar hard-closes any voice session — WebRTC sideband, telephony, or Gemini-Live — after one hour, bounding worst-case per-session spend. In production nothing enforces this: a session whose client and upstream keep the socket open (a stuck client, a call that is never hung up, a barge-in loop that keeps regenerating turns) runs indefinitely and keeps accruing real D2-lease settles for as long as the presenting key's budget allows, with the documented 60-minute safety ceiling being a complete no-op. This is exactly the class the brief calls out: the clock and the session lifecycle are money inputs, and here the one lifecycle ceiling stated in nanodollar-adjacent language ("hard", "ceiling", "the pump enforces") is declared but never constructed.
positive_control: The sibling field on the SAME struct, `VoiceRuntime.denied_destinations` (runtime/mod.rs:61), is read and acted on: `grep -n "destination_denied\|denied_destinations" crates/busbar-voice/src/topology/mod.rs crates/busbar-voice/src/mount.rs crates/busbar-voice/src/runtime/mod.rs` shows it stored (runtime/mod.rs:61,94,124,229) AND consumed as a real gate condition at topology/mod.rs:315 (`deny: rt.destination_denied(&destination)`) and mount.rs:1455 — proving the identical grep-for-consumption method finds real enforcement sites on this struct when they exist. `session_max_secs` has none under the same search.

category: correctness / money — served-but-unbillable, billed-without-service
summary: busbar-voice's live, mounted, governed, provider-dialing telephony WS endpoint (`/v1/realtime/telephony/{call_id}`) feeds raw client-socket bytes straight into `OpenAiRealtimeCodec::read_up`, which only recognizes OpenAI Realtime's own `type`-tagged JSON vocabulary — so a real Twilio Media Streams caller's `{"event":"start"/"media"/"stop", ...}` frames all fall through this catch-all arm as unrecognized and are silently discarded. The purpose-built Twilio envelope decoder that would translate them (`busbar_voice_codec::topology::twilio::TwilioEnvelope`) exists, is fully implemented and tested, and has zero production call sites anywhere in the tree.
failure_scenario: Wiring trace: mount.rs's `voice_ws_arrivals()` (crates/busbar-voice/src/mount.rs:585-617) mounts `TELEPHONY_PATH = "/v1/realtime/telephony/{call_id}"` as a live `RouteAuth::Key`-gated WS accept under the default-on `plane-voice` feature, dispatching to `ws_accept(a, Ingress::Telephony, OpenAiRealtimeCodec)`. `ws_accept` (mount.rs:1481-1519) admits, gates, dials the composed provider, and hands the RAW upgraded client stream straight into `TelephonyProxy::run(provider_in, provider_out, stream, sink)` (crates/busbar-voice/src/topology/telephony.rs:193-261) with no decode step in between. `run()` feeds the client half through `serve_messages(client_in, futures::sink::drain(), uplink_plane)` (telephony.rs:245), where `uplink_plane: UplinkForwarder<C>`'s `handle` calls `self.core.on_client_frame(WireEvent(Bytes::from(frame)))` (crates/busbar-voice/src/runtime/session.rs:577) using the SAME generic codec `C` the caller chose — `OpenAiRealtimeCodec` for this ingress. `on_client_frame` (session.rs:361-367) calls `self.codec.read_up(frame, &mut g.decode)`, whose OpenAiRealtimeCodec impl (crates/busbar-voice-codec/src/ir/codec/mod.rs:587-668) parses the frame's `type` field and matches it against `wire::SESSION_UPDATE`/`INPUT_AUDIO_APPEND`/etc. — OpenAI's own vocabulary. Twilio's Media Streams frames use an `event` field (`connected`/`start`/`media`/`mark`/`dtmf`/`stop`, per `busbar_voice_codec::topology::twilio::TwilioEvent`'s own doc), have no `type` field at all, and therefore hit line 667's `_ => Vec::new()` on every single frame. `grep -rn "TwilioEnvelope" .` across the whole tree returns matches ONLY inside `crates/busbar-voice-codec/src/topology/twilio.rs` itself and its own test file (`topology/tests/twilio_tests.rs`) plus design docs describing it as a future/DESIGN-stage adapter (`docs/design/playbook/t2-twilio.md`'s own header: "Status: DESIGN (not build)") — zero production callers exist for `TwilioEnvelope`, `assert_g711_ulaw`, `AdmissionGuard`, or `render_twiml_for_call`. Concretely: an operator enables voice (default-on), composes a realtime provider, and points a real Twilio phone number's Media Streams `<Connect><Stream>` at this endpoint. Every frame Twilio sends — including `start` (the negotiated media format) and every `media` chunk carrying the caller's actual speech — decodes to zero IR events. The caller's audio never reaches the upstream model. Meanwhile the session is fully admitted, governed, audited, provider-dialed (a real outbound WSS connection is opened and held), and has a live D2 lease open for as long as the call lasts. If the session's locked config auto-issues a response (a common IVR pattern — an initial greeting, or `create_response: true` on VAD, though VAD itself will never fire since it never sees real audio either) the model can still generate and stream OUTPUT audio and a real `response.done` usage report, which busbar bills normally via `TurnMeter::record_turn`/`lease.settle()` — so a customer can be billed for a "call" in which the model can never hear them: served (a governed, billed, provider-connected session) without the substance of the feature being served, or served-and-billed for one-way output on a call that is functionally broken.
positive_control: The generic (non-Twilio) `g711_config()` helper this same telephony leg calls to lock the audio FORMAT does have real callers under the identical search: `grep -rn "g711_config(" crates/busbar-voice/src` matches its definition (topology/telephony.rs:35) plus two live call sites (mount.rs:729, mount.rs:1427). `grep -rln "TwilioEnvelope" crates/busbar-voice-codec/src` under the same method matches only the type's own definition file and its own test file — zero elsewhere — confirming the zero-callers claim is a real absence, not a missed search.

quote: //! would have tripped the boot's claim-overlap check. The reframe (#18: the plane is streaming, voice
category: architecture / money — inoperative safety gate on the dual voice/streaming pipeline
summary: This module's own doc comment asserts the boot's cross-plane claim-overlap check (`seal_claims`) is what makes it safe for `StreamingPlane` to claim the same `/v1/realtime` audience busbar-voice claims, on the premise that the old `"voice"` registration was replaced. In fact `busbar-voice`'s `PLANE_DECL` is still live and default-on (round-2-confirmed), and the overlap check the comment leans on structurally CANNOT see its claims at all: `plane_claims()` (crates/busbar/src/root/registry.rs:241-261) is built only from `PlaneMeta::CLAIMS` associated constants (`LlmPlane`, `McpPlane`, `A2aPlane`, `StreamingPlane`, `AdminPlane`) — a different type system from `busbar_voice::PLANE_DECL`'s `claims: fn(&dyn Any) -> Vec<(String, &'static str)>` field (the older `busbar_kernel::plane::registry::PlaneDecl` shape busbar-mcp/a2a/voice all predate `PlaneMeta` with). `busbar_voice` is never imported into registry.rs at all.
failure_scenario: Both planes are compiled and registered under the SAME default-on `plane-voice` feature (`busbar_voice::PLANE_DECL` pushed at crates/busbar/src/main.rs:300; `StreamingPlane` pushed at crates/busbar/src/root/registry.rs:463) — this is the round-2-confirmed 'two voice planes ship, both registered' fact. `busbar-voice`'s own audience claim on the literal string `/v1/realtime` (`MOUNT_PATH`, mount.rs:322, returned by `voice_claims()` at mount.rs:522-534: `(MOUNT_PATH.to_string(), crate::OPENAI_REALTIME)`) is documented as covering 'every `/v1/realtime/*` path a token is presented on' (mount.rs:518-520) — the SAME literal base `StreamingPlane` claims via `Selector::PathSuffix("/v1/realtime")` (crates/busbar-plane-streaming/src/claims.rs:150, matched by `path.ends_with(suffix)` at claims.rs:219). But `plane_claims()` — the ONE function `seal_claims`'s boot refusal is computed from (registry.rs:4-79's own doc: "`seal_claims` is the cross-plane overlap rule ... a root that skipped the check to get a node running would be choosing which plane owns a request by accident") — never enumerates `busbar_voice::PLANE_DECL`'s claims at all: it is built by chaining `claims_of::<LlmPlane>()`/`McpPlane`/`A2aPlane`/`StreamingPlane`/`AdminPlane` (registry.rs:253-259), and `busbar_voice`/`PLANE_DECL` do not appear anywhere in registry.rs (confirmed by a zero-match grep). So the ONE mechanism this module's own comment cites as the reason two plane registrations claiming the same audience is safe ('registering "streaming" alongside a "voice" plane would have tripped the boot's claim-overlap check') never actually runs against `busbar-voice`'s claims — it only ever compared `StreamingPlane` against `LlmPlane`/`McpPlane`/`A2aPlane`/`AdminPlane`. A node ships today with both planes' realtime-voice claims live and NO boot-time signal that they overlap, contradicting the comment's own stated invariant ('every declaration change that turns a resolved pair into a tie ... has to say so here') for this exact pair. Concretely for money: an operator who trusts that invariant — 'if my voice config and my streaming config collided, boot would refuse' — has no such protection for this pair; the two pipelines (`busbar-voice`'s D2 nanodollar lease vs. `busbar-plane-streaming`'s meter-class rate card, round-2-confirmed) can silently diverge on which audience/config governs a given realtime client with nothing at boot to surface it, and a future change that DOES make the two literally collide on a mounted route (e.g. a route added at bare `/v1/realtime`) would ship with zero warning from the one gate designed to catch exactly that.
positive_control: `grep -n "StreamingPlane\|claims_of" crates/busbar/src/root/registry.rs` shows `StreamingPlane` correctly imported (line 94) and folded into `plane_claims()` via `claims_of::<StreamingPlane>()` (line 258) and pushed into the plane registry (line 463) — proving the overlap-check plumbing exists and the grep method finds it when present. `grep -n "busbar_voice\|PLANE_DECL" crates/busbar/src/root/registry.rs` (the identical file, identical method) returns zero matches — `busbar_voice::PLANE_DECL` is invisible to this file and therefore to `seal_claims` entirely.

quote: // DRIFT GUARD: every documented GET path is both listed in the doc AND actually mounted.
category: missing-test-coverage / instrument-cannot-produce-a-no
summary: The only test claiming to guard router/OpenAPI-doc parity for the admin surface (`test_admin_v1_openapi_paths_all_resolve`) iterates just the 14-entry `V1_GET_PATHS` constant, not the actual document -- leaving 46 of 60 documented paths and 67 of 81 documented operations (every non-GET verb, every named-map section GET/{name}/settings route, every a2a/mcp plane trust verb) with zero proof they resolve, and checks nothing in the reverse direction at all.
failure_scenario: The committed openapi.json documents 60 paths / 81 operations (verified directly against the file); V1_GET_PATHS (handlers.rs:3611-3654) has exactly 14 entries, all GET. A separate comment at tests/tests.rs:12996-12997 -- "every path in it is proven mounted (`test_admin_v1_openapi_paths_all_resolve`), so keying off it closes the loop: router → doc → this audit" -- asserts a guarantee the cited test does not hold: it only proves 14 of 81 operations, and only in the doc→router direction (via an HTTP GET expecting non-404), never router→doc. No other test in the crate iterates the full `doc["paths"]` object against the live router in either direction (grepped every `openapi` mention across tests/tests.rs, v1/json/tests/tests.rs, admin_codec/tests/verbs.rs). The crate also has no route-introspection utility (grepped for list_routes/route_list/mounted_routes/enumerate_routes: zero hits), so a reverse check is not just untested but currently unbuildable without one. Concretely: if a future change adds a mutating admin route (e.g. a new PUT/DELETE verb) and forgets to add its OpenAPI entry, or renames/removes a route the doc still documents, no test in this crate fails -- the release ships a discovery contract (consumed by busbar-ui's own openapi-prep.py, per v1/json/tests/tests.rs:170) that silently disagrees with the live server in either direction. (In the pinned tree today, I independently reconstructed the full router-mounted (method,path) set from mod.rs's literal `.route()` calls, named_map.rs's `NamedMapSection::sections()` fold, and busbar-a2a/busbar-mcp's `admin_routes()` specs, and diffed it programmatically against openapi.json's 81 operations: 0 mismatches. So there is no LIVE drift right now -- the finding is that nothing in CI would catch it if there were.
positive_control: python3 diff of the openapi.json `paths` object (60 paths / 81 get+post+put+patch+delete entries, counted programmatically) against a manually-reconstructed router set built from mod.rs + named_map.rs + busbar-a2a/mod.rs's admin_routes()+openapi_fragment() + busbar-mcp/mod.rs's mcp_admin_routes()+mcp_openapi_fragment(): both sets have exactly 81 ops and the set-difference in both directions is empty -- proving the reconstruction method is accurate (it would have surfaced a real mismatch had one existed). Separately, `grep -c '(' <<< V1_GET_PATHS-entries` = 14 confirmed by direct read of handlers.rs:3611-3654, versus 81 total documented operations from the same openapi.json parse.

category: test-does-not-exercise-defect / wrong-detection-pattern
summary: The two source-scanning regression guards that this file's own doc comments say exist specifically to stop the confirmed 'unreadable count billed as zero' defect from recurring (`no_dialect_reads_a_count_with_the_bare_defaulting_idiom`, `no_dialect_reads_a_billed_count_field_with_a_bare_as_u64`) both search for the string `as_u64`/`as_i64` -- but the confirmed-live defect (r2-codec.json: anthropic/reader.rs:732, 'for all six dialects') is spelled `read_count_u64(...).unwrap_or(0)` / `u64_field(field).unwrap_or(0)`, and the substring `as_u64` does not occur anywhere inside the identifier `read_count_u64`. Both tests pass today with 40 live occurrences of the exact banned idiom, in production code, across all six dialects.
failure_scenario: usage_count_tests.rs:170-262's own doc comment states the intent in so many words: 'NO DIALECT MAY REINTRODUCE THE BARE READ... the leaf-op handlers were fixed once, the fix was lost, and sixteen live billed reads came back... precisely because nothing was watching it.' Yet flattening every non-test, non-usage_count.rs source line in the crate (the identical technique the test itself uses) and searching for `read_count_u64) . unwrap_or(` or `u64_field("<field>") . unwrap_or(` finds 40 matches, 100% production dialect-reader code (0 test fixtures, 0 comments), spanning ALL SIX dialects: anthropic/reader.rs (10 hits, incl. lines 12-13, 421-429, 559-573, 731-745 -- the primary AND truncated-recovery usage paths for input/output tokens), bedrock/reader.rs (6), gemini/reader.rs (2) + gemini/mod.rs (6), cohere/reader.rs (6), openai_chat/reader.rs (6), openai_responses/reader.rs (6). Confirmed empirically: `cargo test -p busbar-llm-codec --lib usage_count::tests::` in the pinned tree reports 14 passed, 0 failed -- including both lint tests -- while every one of those 40 call sites bills 0 for a present-but-malformed billed field instead of refusing via the crate's own `billed_count()`. A dialect author who 'fixes' a future defect the same way these two tests intend (route through `read_count_u64` to accept float-spelled integers) but keeps a trailing `.unwrap_or(0)` reintroduces the exact original bug and both guards stay green.
positive_control: `grep -c as_u64 <<< read_count_u64` = 0 (the banned string is not a substring of the primitive's own name, so the scan is structurally blind to any call that goes through it). Flattened-line regex scan for `read_count_u64)\s*\.\s*unwrap_or\(` and `u64_field\("[a-zA-Z_]+"\)\s*\.\s*unwrap_or\(` over crates/busbar-llm-codec/src (excluding /tests/ and usage_count.rs, same exclusion rule the crate's own lint uses) returns 40 hits across all 6 dialect reader.rs/mod.rs files -- proving the method finds real, live matches when the correct pattern is used, in contrast to the two existing tests' zero-offender result against the identical files.

category: test-encodes-the-defect-as-correct
summary: `rerank_resp_billing_flat_regardless_of_search_units` does not merely fail to catch the confirmed rerank-billing defect (r2-codec.json: `RerankResp::billing()` always returns `Billing::Flat` and discards `search_units`) -- it REQUIRES it: the test constructs a response with `search_units: Some(3)` specifically to assert that `.billing()` ignores it. Fixing the confirmed defect (making billing vary with search_units) would fail this test, which would have to be deleted or rewritten as part of any fix.
failure_scenario: A rerank call to Cohere or Bedrock that consumes N search units is billed identically to one that consumes 1 -- `RerankResp::billing()` (ir/rerank.rs:97-100) is `Some(Billing::Flat)` unconditionally, verified still live in the pinned tree. The only test in the crate connecting `search_units` to a billing outcome, `rerank_resp_billing_flat_regardless_of_search_units` (this file, lines 17-25), asserts this is the REQUIRED behavior ('Even when Cohere reports billed search units, the projection stays Flat... the count is echoed, not priced here'). cohere/tests/rerank_tests.rs separately verifies `search_units` is read correctly off the wire (including the float-spelled case) but never chains that value into a `.billing()` assertion -- so across the whole crate, the one place read-value and billing-outcome are tested together locks in the wrong answer. `cargo test -p busbar-llm-codec --lib ir::rerank::tests::rerank_resp_billing_flat_regardless_of_search_units` passes (1 passed, 0 failed) in the pinned tree.
positive_control: `cargo test -p busbar-llm-codec --lib ir::rerank::tests::rerank_resp_billing_flat_regardless_of_search_units` -> 'test result: ok. 1 passed', confirming the test both exists, targets exactly this behavior, and currently passes by requiring the defect. `grep -rn billing crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/cohere/tests/rerank_tests.rs` returns zero hits, confirming the dialect-level rerank tests never assert on `.billing()` at all -- so this ir-level test is the crate's only connection between the two, and it asserts the wrong one.

category: test-encodes-the-defect-as-correct
summary: Cohere's BUFFERED `read_response` path for `finish_reason: "ERROR"` (the confirmed 'failed generation billed as completed' defect, r3-codec.json) is covered by two tests -- `read_write_response_error_finish_reason_round_trips` (this line) and `test_generic_error_does_not_fold_into_safety_and_round_trips` (line 1185) -- both of which require `read_response` to return `Ok(...)` and treat the ERROR body as a normal, billable completion whose stop_reason merely happens to be `Error`, then explicitly assert the writer round-trips it back out as a successful-shaped response. Neither test checks for any billing-suppression signal, because the buffered path has none to check.
failure_scenario: r3-codec.json already established the mechanism and even the fix pattern: Cohere's STREAMING reader was fixed to push a dedicated `IrStreamEvent::Error` alongside the terminal MessageDelta specifically so `terminal_error()` is set and the breaker/billing layer knows the generation failed (see the correctly-designed `test_stream_generic_error_finish_pushes_ir_error_event`, cohere/tests/tests.rs:5283-5340, which explicitly checks `evs.iter().find_map(|e| matches!(e, IrStreamEvent::Error(_)))`). The BUFFERED reader (reader.rs:1240-1247) never received the equivalent fix -- it just sets `stop_reason: Some(IrStopReason::Error)` inside an otherwise-normal `Ok(IrResponse{...})`. The two buffered-path tests cited here do not merely fail to notice this: `read_write_response_error_finish_reason_round_trips`'s own doc comment (lines 4725-4727) frames the current shape as the intended contract -- 'a `write_response` re-emits the native `ERROR` token -- so a Cohere infra stop survives the seam' -- i.e. the test requires the exact round-trip-as-success behavior that lets a failed non-streaming Cohere generation be billed as a completed one. Fixing the buffered path (e.g. making `read_response` return `Err` for a terminal ERROR, mirroring the streaming fix) would break both of these tests.
positive_control: `grep -n IrStreamEvent::Error crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/cohere/tests/tests.rs` finds 8 hits, including the correctly-designed streaming test at line 5283-5340 that explicitly checks for the Error-event push -- proving the crate's authors know how to write this exact assertion, and that grep-for-the-signal is a working method here. None of those 8 hits are inside `read_write_response_error_finish_reason_round_trips` (lines 4731-4746) or `test_generic_error_does_not_fold_into_safety_and_round_trips` (lines 1172-1200ish), confirming the buffered-path tests never look for it.

category: test-checks-wrong-field
summary: `finish_reason_malformed_function_call_stream_is_error` -- the test whose own doc comment says it guards the exact streaming call site where Gemini's MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL (a failed generation, per gemini/mod.rs's own doc comment) is supposed to suppress billing -- only inspects the `stop_reason` field on the `MessageDelta` event. It never checks whether an `IrStreamEvent::Error` was also pushed, which is the actual signal `proto_stream.rs`'s `terminal_error()` (and therefore billing suppression) keys off. The confirmed defect (r3-codec.json) is precisely that no `IrStreamEvent::Error` is pushed for this case -- so this test cannot fail on it.
failure_scenario: gemini/mod.rs's finishReason handling for MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL only emits a normal `MessageDelta` (with `stop_reason: Error`) followed by `MessageStop` -- confirmed still true in the pinned tree, matching r3-codec.json's finding verbatim. `finish_reason_malformed_function_call_stream_is_error` (gemini/tests/tests.rs:4842-4859) drives this exact path and its `find_map` (line 4852) only ever matches `IrStreamEvent::MessageDelta`, extracting `stop_reason`; the surrounding `events` vector is never scanned for an `IrStreamEvent::Error` variant, so a fix that started pushing one (correct) and a regression that never does (the current, confirmed-defective state) are indistinguishable to this assertion -- both leave `stop_reason == Some(Some(IrStopReason::Error))` on the MessageDelta. Elsewhere in the SAME file the test suite demonstrates it knows exactly how to check for the Error-event signal (e.g. lines 3934-3982, checking `[IrStreamEvent::Error(err)] => {...}` and panicking with 'expected exactly one IrStreamEvent::Error' if absent) -- that pattern is simply never applied to this test.
positive_control: `grep -n IrStreamEvent::Error crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/gemini/tests/tests.rs` finds 7 hits elsewhere in the file (lines 2263, 2292, 3950, 3958, 3971, 3982, and the doc comment at 3934), proving both that the crate's own test idiom for asserting this event's presence exists and that grep-for-the-signal correctly surfaces it when used. None of those 7 hits fall inside `finish_reason_malformed_function_call_stream_is_error` (lines 4842-4859).

category: missing-test-coverage
summary: `tier_usage()` -- the function r3-codec.json already flagged (wire_shim.rs:103) for collapsing a cache field that is `None` because an upstream `read_count_u64` refused an unparseable value into the same sparse-map omission as a field that legitimately reported nothing -- has no dedicated test file or `#[cfg(test)]` module of its own, and is exercised by exactly two tests anywhere in the crate, neither of which ever constructs the distinguishing case (a cache field absent due to refusal vs. absent because the provider never reported it).
failure_scenario: wire_shim.rs declares no `mod tests` (grepped the whole 111-line file: zero matches) and there is no `wire_shim_tests.rs` among the crate's 80 test files. The only two call sites of `tier_usage()` in any test are ir/tests/tests.rs:360 and bedrock/tests/tests.rs:6079/6079-6094 (`bedrock_input_tier_excludes_cache_at_billing_boundary`); both always pass fully-valid, always-Some or always-None cache fields (e.g. `cacheReadInputTokens: 1000, cacheWriteInputTokens: 200`, or both cache fields None throughout), never a case where a cache field is `None` specifically because the wire value was present-but-unreadable. Since `tier_usage()`'s `u.cache_read.unwrap_or(0)` / `u.cache_creation.unwrap_or(0)` (the confirmed defect) treats both causes of `None` identically, neither existing test could have caught the defect, nor would either fail if a future fix (distinguishing the two `None` causes, e.g. by refusing the whole request instead of silently zeroing the tier) were reverted.
positive_control: `grep -n 'mod tests' crates/busbar-llm-codec/src/wire_shim.rs` -> 0 hits (confirms no test module declared in the file itself, in contrast to every dialect mod.rs/reader.rs/handler.rs and usage_count.rs, which all declare one). `grep -rn tier_usage crates/busbar-llm-codec/src --include='*.rs'` finds exactly 4 hits total: the definition plus 2 test call sites (ir/tests/tests.rs:360, bedrock/tests/tests.rs:6079) plus one production caller -- proving the search finds real matches and that the function's only test exposure is these two sites, both read and confirmed to use only fully-readable cache values.

category: required check that can never report / trigger resolved against the wrong branch
summary: Twenty-one of predev's twenty-eight workflows do not exist on the default branch `main`, and GitHub resolves `schedule`, `workflow_run`, `workflow_dispatch`, `release` and `branch_protection_rule` against the default branch only - so none of them can fire by those triggers today.
failure_scenario: `git ls-tree -r --name-only origin/main -- .github/workflows/` returns exactly 10 files (ci, docker, monthly-refresh, plugin-ci, prepare-release, qa-gate, release, security, tag-on-main, verify-deploy); `origin/HEAD -> origin/main` confirms main is the default branch; origin/dev and origin/qa carry the same 10. Predev carries 28 + qa-gate.dispatcher.json. Concrete consequence per workflow: (a) qa-security.yml, qa-codeql.yml, qa-conformance-mcp.yml, qa-conformance-a2a.yml, qa-conformance-voice.yml fire ONLY on `workflow_run: [CI]` (+ schedule/dispatch) - none can ever run, so cargo-deny/cargo-audit, CodeQL, and the MCP/A2A/Voice conformance batteries render no verdict at all, and the four contexts required-status-checks.md:53-56 tells an operator to mark required on `qa` never report (that file's own line 70: 'a required status check that never reports does not pass - GitHub leaves the merge pending on it forever'); (b) turnstile-dispatch.yml is dispatch-only and is the ONLY route from `predev` (which by its own line 22 'carries NO automatic CI') to the turnstile - a candidate cannot be announced at all; (c) manual-keep-proof.yml is dispatch-only and is 'the ONLY judge of an agent hand-back' (its line 895) - no hand-back can be judged; (d) gate-mutants.yml, manual-bolt-pass.yml, oracle-proof.yml are dispatch-only - unreachable; (e) fleet-autoscaler.yml's `release gate` status and its daily 41 6 * * * rot cover never run, so a shipped release that regresses is never detected; (f) sched-cost-watch.yml (DECISIONS #78's $100 hard cap), sched-scorecard.yml, sched-oracle-store-cells.yml, sched-ci-images-mirror.yml never fire on their crons; (g) sched-monthly-refresh.yml is shadowed by main's older monthly-refresh.yml, which is what the 0 9 1 * * cron actually runs; (h) release-stage.yml and qa-fuzz.yml keep their `push: [qa]` trigger (push uses the pushed branch's files) but lose workflow_dispatch; (i) main's tag-on-main.yml, deleted on predev, still runs on every push to main.
positive_control: The same `git ls-tree` command against origin/predev returns all 28 workflow files, and against origin/main returns 10 - so the command and the paths are right. `grep -rn predev .github/` matches 16 lines (required-status-checks.md:42, turnstile-dispatch.yml:22,29,34, gate-mutants.yml:82,91,92,...), proving the grep method finds strings that are present.

quote: # Checks (each independently PASS/FAIL, ANY failure -> exit 1):
category: prose asserts a guarantee the code does not hold / one failure hides thirteen checks
summary: The fourteen release checks (a)-(n) are sequential steps of ONE job and not one of them carries `if: always()`, so the first failing check skips every check after it - the opposite of the 'each independently PASS/FAIL' guarantee on line 13.
failure_scenario: Check (a) fails on a release run. Steps (b), (b2), (c), (c2), (d), (e), (f), (g), (h), (i), (j), (k), (l), (m), (n) all skip because a step `if:` defaults to `success()`. The operator fixes (a), re-runs the ~45-minute job, and discovers (b) is also broken - serially, one defect per round trip, on the gate that stands between a staged image and `latest`. The file itself records this having happened, at verify-deploy.yml:937: '# check after it in the job was skipped - a whole verifier taken out by a file being one' - and then fixed only the one manifest fallback, never the skip semantics.
positive_control: `grep -n 'if: always()\|!cancelled()' verify-deploy.yml` returns ZERO lines; `grep -c 'if: always()' ci.yml` returns 11 under the identical command, proving the pattern and the grep both work. Every step-level `if:` in verify-deploy.yml (lines 805, 841, 867, 1065, 1169, 1211, 1238, 1358, 1486, 1522, 1622, 1882) is `inputs.stage != 'staging'` or `== 'staging'`.

category: an instrument that cannot produce a NO / fail-open on the live condition
summary: Six of the fourteen release checks become green no-ops under the edge-block condition the file says is currently live: checks (h), (i), (k) and (n) `exit 0`/`return 0` on HTTP 403/429, and the (g), (j) and (l.1) halves downgrade to `::warning::`/VISIBLE SKIP without touching `fail`.
failure_scenario: getbusbar.com's Cloudflare bot rules refuse GitHub/Latchkey runners (the file asserts this is the state today at line 1284 and 1377-1384). Then: (h) `exit 0` at 1395 under the `403|429)` arm opened at 1390; (i) `exit 0` at 1498 guarded by `if [ -f /tmp/site-blocked ]` at 1496; (k) `return 0` at 1640 inside check_api, whose callers use `|| fail=1` and so cannot tell it from a real 200; (n) `exit 0` at 1898 which terminates the step before the GitHub-star half at 1918-1943 ever runs; (pointers) P6 `::warning::` at 576; (g) at 1284/1305; (l.1) at 1751. Result: `curl -fsSL https://getbusbar.com/install.sh | sh` can 404 on every platform, the live counters can be frozen, and the `verify` job reports GREEN. release.yml:1147 consumes this workflow as `consumer verification (PUBLIC, last step)` and release-stage.yml:1469 consumes it as `consumer verification (STAGED, this is the gate)`, so both gates inherit the vacuous pass. Additional: `/tmp/site-blocked` is only removed inside (h) (line 1369), and these jobs run on the self-hosted `latchkey-small` label where /tmp persists between runs, so a stale marker from an earlier run makes (i) pass forever without reading a byte.
positive_control: The same file DOES fail closed elsewhere under the identical grep: verify-deploy.yml:1075 `[ -f "$bin" ] || { echo "::error::(c2) ..."; exit 1; }` and 1670 `[ "$fail" = 0 ]` - so `exit 0` versus `exit 1` on the 403/429 arms is a real asymmetry, not a search artefact.

quote: echo "::error::REFUSING TO STAGE FROM A RED COMMIT. ${SHA:0:7} is red on: ${names}. There is no override, no waiver and no exception list, and that is deliberate: 'unrelated to my change' and 'known, tracked, not blocking' are how a red release shipped. If one of these checks should not block a release, change or delete the CHECK - do not bypass it here. Nothing has been built, no tag exists, no release is listed and nothing was fanned out."
category: the thing that decides is not the thing that is checked
summary: Gate 0's red sweep reads `/tmp/runs.json`, which line 386-391 has already filtered down to `REQUIRED_WORKFLOWS: "CI"` alone - so the sweep whose error text says 'no exception list' can only ever name the CI workflow, and every other workflow red on the same commit is structurally invisible to it.
failure_scenario: A push to `qa` leaves CI green but `qa-gate` (the ~2h promotion soak), `Fuzz`, `CodeQL`, `Security` or any conformance verdict red on the same SHA. `release-stage.yml:389` keeps only runs whose `.name` is in `$want` ("CI"), line 420 computes `red` from that filtered set, line 452 `[ "$fail" = 0 ] || exit 1` passes, and line 453 prints `::notice::${SHA:0:7} is green across every check. Proceeding to stage.` - a false statement about the commit. The full pipeline then stages a release image, draft and asset set from a commit whose promotion soak was red. The env comment at 350-356 acknowledges the inclusion filter, but neither the line-424 error text nor the line-453 notice does, and those two strings are what an operator reads.
positive_control: The sibling gate in release.yml filters by EXCLUSION instead (release.yml:341 `NOT_COMMIT_CHECKS: "Release,Verify deploy"` and 379 `map(select(.id != (env.GITHUB_RUN_ID | tonumber) and (.name | IN($not[]) | not)))`), so its line-434 sweep really does see every run on the sha - proving the exclusion shape exists in this tree and that release-stage's inclusion shape is a deliberate difference, not a misreading.

quote: # and actionlint says so before it is pushed.
category: a gate whose command is quoted in a comment but never run
summary: actionlint is configured here and is invoked by NO workflow; its only caller is scripts/land.sh, behind `if command -v actionlint`, so the runner-label check this file claims 'says so before it is pushed' never runs in CI at all.
failure_scenario: Someone writes `runs-on: latchkey-xlage` (or any label no Latchkey runner carries) in ci.yml. Nothing in `.github/workflows/` lints it. The job is queued and never picked up - a self-hosted label with no runner does not fail, it waits. If that job is one of ci-umbrella's 28 `needs:`, ci-umbrella never starts and the `ci umbrella` required context never reports, which by required-status-checks.md:70-71 leaves the merge pending forever. The 106 `runs-on:` lines in this slice are protected by a lint the pipeline does not execute. Compounding: `busbar-xl` is declared at line 18 but appears in no `runs-on:` line anywhere (only in eight comments), and line 7 names `keep-proof.yml`, a file that does not exist (it is `manual-keep-proof.yml`).
positive_control: `grep -rn actionlint .github/ scripts/ xtask/src` returns only actionlint.yaml's own comments plus scripts/land.sh:697-698. The identical command for a lint that IS wired - `grep -rn release-script-lint .github/workflows/*.yml` - returns ci.yml:337 and ci.yml:339 as `run:` steps, proving the method finds real invocations.

quote: | `cargo-deny (advisories · licenses · sources · bans) + cargo-audit` | `qa-security.yml` | Single-job workflow; its own status is the aggregator. |
category: required check that can never report
summary: The required context name carries a ` + cargo-audit` suffix that exists only in predev's qa-security.yml; the job that actually reports on main/dev/qa today is named `cargo-deny (advisories · licenses · sources · bans)`, so the required context never appears.
failure_scenario: An operator follows this file and ticks `cargo-deny (advisories · licenses · sources · bans) + cargo-audit` as required on `qa`. `git show origin/main:.github/workflows/security.yml` line 30 is `    name: cargo-deny (advisories · licenses · sources · bans)` - no ` + cargo-audit` - and that is the only Security job that exists on main/dev/qa. GitHub matches required contexts by exact check-run name, so the ticked context is never posted by anything and every merge into `qa` stays pending forever - the exact hazard this file's own line 70-71 warns about. The predev job that would post the longer name (qa-security.yml:25) cannot run at all, because qa-security.yml is absent from the default branch (see the workflow-presence finding).
positive_control: The other three names in the same table DO match their jobs verbatim: `MCP conformance verdict` == qa-conformance-mcp.yml's verdict `name:`, `A2A conformance verdict` == qa-conformance-a2a.yml's, `CodeQL (rust)` == qa-codeql.yml:65 - so the comparison method is sound and the cargo-deny row is the odd one out.

quote: this file exists to prevent. **Adding a new blocking workflow means adding its terminal status here
category: an aggregator ledger that omits two whole workflows
summary: The cross-workflow required-status ledger never names `Voice conformance verdict` or `cargo-fuzz (bounded, qa boundary)` - neither in the required tables nor in the 'Intentionally NOT branch-protection-required' section - so a 9-job Voice conformance battery and the fuzz gate can go red on a qa promotion and block nothing.
failure_scenario: qa-conformance-voice.yml's nine legs (spec battery per dialect, transcript replay, cross-parity, provider-dial, composition, boot-validate, governance probe) all go red on a promotion commit. Its `verdict` job posts `Voice conformance verdict` = failure. Nothing requires that context: it is absent from this file's qa table (lines 51-56), absent from the main table (line 18-20), and absent from the deliberate-exclusions list (lines 91-113). qa-fuzz.yml's `cargo-fuzz (bounded, qa boundary)` is likewise absent from all three. `qa` -> `main` proceeds. The file's own rule at line 11-12 makes this an omission by its own standard, and the voice workflow's line 37 - '# AND `verdict` IS NOT OPTIONAL. Ten green ticks mean nothing if one is green because it never ran.' - asserts a property nothing enforces.
positive_control: `grep -n 'Voice\|voice\|fuzz\|Fuzz' .github/required-status-checks.md` returns nothing. The identical grep for `'MCP conformance verdict\|A2A conformance verdict'` returns lines 54 and 55, proving the file, the path and the grep are correct.

quote: for target in $(cargo +nightly fuzz list); do
category: an instrument that cannot produce a NO / empty denominator
summary: The whole Fuzz gate is a `for` loop over an unasserted command substitution: if `cargo +nightly fuzz list` prints nothing or exits non-zero, the body never runs, the step exits 0, and the workflow reports green having fuzzed nothing.
failure_scenario: The tree declares exactly ONE fuzz target (fuzz/fuzz_targets/codec_embeddings_read_request.rs, `[[bin]]` at fuzz/Cargo.toml:27). Delete or rename it - or rename the fuzz directory, or have nightly resolution fail - and `cargo +nightly fuzz list` yields an empty list or a non-zero exit; `set -euo pipefail` at line 47 does NOT fire for a failing command substitution used as a `for` word-list, so the loop iterates zero times and the step succeeds. `Fuzz` reports green on the qa promotion having executed zero fuzz iterations. There is no `[ -n "$targets" ]` guard and no count floor anywhere in the 66-line file.
positive_control: Measured, not assumed: `bash -euo pipefail -c 'for x in $(sh -c "echo err >&2; exit 3"); do echo iter; done; echo REACHED AFTER LOOP'` prints 'REACHED AFTER LOOP' and exits 0. The same tree DOES guard this shape elsewhere - ci.yml:3428 `[ -s "$led" ] || { echo "::error::no candidate ledger..."; exit 1; }` and ci.yml:3316 `[ "$pass" -gt 0 ] || { echo "::error::the committed golden carries no PASS rows - the replay below would be vacuously green"; exit 1; }` - so the missing assertion here is an omission, not a house style.

category: an aggregator that scores a collapsed matrix result / vacuous pass on a shrunken fan-out
summary: The qa-gate umbrella scores `needs.slow.result`, which is identical whether one matrix leg ran and passed or all ten did, and nothing in the workflow asserts the leg set or count against qa/segments.toml.
failure_scenario: The `slow` matrix comes from `matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.fast.outputs.matrix) }}` (qa-gate.yml:289), produced by scripts/qa-gate-run.sh's cmd_matrix, which refuses only a fully empty list. A manifest edit - a `status` flipped off `active`, a `tier` typo, a dropped row - shrinks the real-money tier from ten legs to one. `needs.slow.result` is `success`, the umbrella prints GREEN, and the ~2h promotion gate reports having proved the whole segmentation when it proved a tenth of it. The file's own header at lines 20-24 records this exact incident happening on qa c736177 ('the auto-fired gate ran ONE job while the whole segmentation umbrella sat unused ... the run went green, it had just done less than anyone thought'); the rewrite moved the gate logic onto the commit but did not add the count assertion. Per-leg check-run contexts cannot cover the gap either: qa-gate.yml:272 is `    name: ${{ matrix.segment.id }}`, so every individual segment's context name is manifest-derived and no branch-protection rule can pin one.
positive_control: release-stage.yml DOES floor its equivalent matrices: line 908 `if len(inc) < 6:`, line 957 `if len(images) != 2:`, line 1321 `if len(declared) < 6:` - so a count floor on a fromJSON matrix is an established pattern in this slice and its absence in qa-gate.yml is a real difference.

category: two implementations of one concept / the arm signal is settable from outside the commit
summary: `battery-subject` publishes `armed=true` when a repository VARIABLE is non-empty, even with no busbar binary present - directly contradicting the adjacent design note eleven lines earlier that says no repository variable arms this any more.
failure_scenario: `vars.MCP_SUBJECT_SERVER_CMD` is set to any non-empty string in repo settings (lines 427-428 pipe it into SERVER_CMD/CLIENT_CMD). The build of `target/debug/busbar` fails or is skipped; line 431's right-hand disjunct is still true, so the leg declares `armed=true`. The verdict job reads only `needs.battery-subject.outputs.armed`, so `MCP conformance verdict` goes green having judged no busbar at all - the one distinction the arm flag exists to make. The file's own design note at 270-272 states 'NO SECRET AND NO REPOSITORY VARIABLE ARMS THIS ANY MORE. The arm is a FILE this job just built, so the leg cannot silently disarm because somebody deleted a variable', and the verdict's remediation text at line 585 tells the operator the opposite: 'Set the repository variable that arms it.' Three statements, two of them wrong.
positive_control: The sibling A2A workflow arms from a built artifact only and its `arm` step writes armed=false rather than reading a variable (qa-conformance-a2a.yml:674-689, guarded at :707) - so the file-based arm the MCP comment describes does exist in this tree, and the MCP leg is the divergent one.

quote: echo "::warning::docker.io/getbusbar/busbar:${V}-armv8.0 does not resolve; skipping the compat-name assertions (pre-dual-arm64 version recovery only)."
category: unknown degraded to a pass
summary: An unreadable compat digest is indistinguishable from an absent one, and both skip all four armv8.0 partial-promote assertions with a warning while `fail` stays 0 - the step then exits green.
failure_scenario: `v8_v` comes from `reg_digest auth.docker.io registry-1.docker.io getbusbar/busbar "${V}-armv8.0" || true` (docker.yml:312), so a rate limit, a 5xx or an auth blip yields the empty string exactly as a missing tag does. Line 320 then takes the warning branch, the digest-inequality check (325-328) and the three-name agreement loop (333-340) never execute, line 342 `[ "$fail" = 0 ] || exit 1` passes, and line 345 suppresses even the PASS line. `X.Y.Z` publishes green while `X.Y.Z-armv8.0` on GHCR and the floating `armv8.0` pointer silently never move; every RPi4-class user pulling `getbusbar/busbar:armv8.0` keeps getting the previous release, indefinitely, with nothing red. The justification at line 322 - 'Any version that staged one had it created above or the job already died' - is refuted by the step's own premise at 253-255: '`imagetools create` exiting 0 says the API call was accepted; it does not say the registry now serves that name'.
positive_control: The same step DOES fail closed on the main four names: line 303-305 `if [ "$got" != "$hub_v" ] || [ -z "$got" ]; then ... fail=1`, i.e. an empty digest there IS red. The compat branch is the only place emptiness is forgiven.

quote: echo "Docker Hub tag ${V} is free (HTTP ${code} on HEAD manifest)."
category: unknown degraded to a pass / prose asserts the opposite
summary: The Docker Hub tag-immutability pre-flight treats every non-200 - including the `000` its own `|| echo 000` manufactures on a network failure, and 429/5xx - as 'the tag is free', and a failed token fetch skips the pre-flight entirely with a warning.
failure_scenario: Docker Hub rate-limits the anonymous HEAD (429) or the request times out. Line 225's `|| echo 000` sets `code=000`; line 226 only refuses on exactly `200`; line 230 prints the positive claim that the tag is free. The stage then spends ~40 minutes of two-arch PGO build, SBOM, OpenAPI and asset upload on a version whose image name is already taken and, because Docker Hub tags are immutable, can never be published - which is the precise waste this pre-flight exists to avoid. The token-fetch path is worse: line 220 ends `|| true`, so a failure falls to line 247's `::warning::could not obtain an anonymous Docker Hub pull token; skipping the tag-immutability pre-flight` and `release=1` is written anyway. Both contradict this file's own doctrine at 306-309: 'UNKNOWN IS RED. If the status lookup errors, times out, is rate-limited, or simply cannot find a CI run for this commit, this job REFUSES. It never degrades to a pass.'
positive_control: The rc-tag arm twenty lines below has the identical defect (line 239 `|| echo 000`, line 240 `if [ "$rccode" = "200" ]`, line 244 prints 'is free'), while `branch-green` in the same file does fail closed on an unreadable API (line 379-381 `if ! runs="$(api ...)"; then ... exit 1`), proving the fail-closed shape is available here and simply not used.

category: a floor set below what its own arithmetic requires
summary: The expected-asset floor is 5 while `expected` is built from the platform targets AND the two metadata assets, which the adjacent comment itself says should total 7 - so the SBOM and the OpenAPI document can silently go unchecked.
failure_scenario: `expected` is filled by two loops at verify-deploy.yml:969 (`for t in spec["targets"]:`) and 973 (`for a in spec["metadata_assets"]:`). If `metadata_assets` is missing or renamed in .github/release-targets.json, the Python raises KeyError AFTER printing the five platform archive names (CPython flushes stdout on exit even on an uncaught exception). The comment at 977-979 states that a `mapfile` whose process substitution died 'does not trip `set -e`', so the shell continues with exactly 5 elements. The floor of 5 passes. Check (c) then verifies the five platform tarballs and NEVER checks the CycloneDX SBOM or the OpenAPI 3.1 document - two of the assets the header's check (c) explicitly promises. The comment at 981-982 gives the correct arithmetic and the code does not implement it: 'The floor is 5 because busbar has never shipped fewer platform archives than that plus its two metadata assets'.
positive_control: The same file DOES floor a set correctly at line 1556 in check (j) - `[ -n "$assets" ] || { echo "::error::(j) could not parse any asset filenames out of the tap formula..."; exit 1; }` - so a floor assertion is the house pattern; the (c) floor is simply off by the two metadata assets.

quote: # FULL HISTORY, for the `audit-ledger` step at the end of this job: every record in
category: stale prose / dead cost on every push and PR
summary: Two of CI's heaviest jobs unconditionally take `fetch-depth: 0` plus an extra remote ref fetch to serve an `audit-ledger` gate and a `gates::audit_ledger` test module that no longer exist anywhere in the tree.
failure_scenario: `structure-lint` (ci.yml:249-251) and `check` (ci.yml:815-817) both set `fetch-depth: 0` - a full-history unshallow of the whole repository - and `check` additionally runs ci.yml:823 `run: git fetch origin '+refs/backup/audit-pins/*:refs/audit-pins/*' || true`. Both are justified in prose by the audit register: ci.yml:455 'THE AUDIT REGISTER. `audit-ledger` judges the instrument that judges everything else', ci.yml:804 '`cargo test -p xtask` below runs `gates::audit_ledger::tests::...`'. None of it exists: `qa/audit-ledger.json`, `scripts/audit-ledger.py` and `xtask/src/gates/audit_ledger.rs` are all absent, there is no `pub mod audit_ledger;` in xtask/src/gates/mod.rs, and no `run:` step in any workflow invokes the gate. Every push and every PR therefore pays a full-history clone on the two longest jobs for a gate that was deleted. The comment at ci.yml:455-469 also terminates mid-sentence ('...name a commit that is not an') and runs straight into the next comment block's heading at line 470, which is what a partial deletion looks like. Three more workflows carry the same dead fetch: gate-mutants.yml:164 and :256, manual-keep-proof.yml:507.
positive_control: `grep -rn audit-ledger .github/` returns six lines in ci.yml, all inside `#` comments and none a `run:` step. The identical grep for a gate that IS wired - `grep -rn inventory-coverage .github/` - returns ci.yml:614 `run: cargo xtask gate inventory-coverage --selftest` and ci.yml:616 `run: cargo xtask gate inventory-coverage`, proving the grep distinguishes a comment from an invocation. `grep -n '^pub mod' xtask/src/gates/mod.rs` lists 48 modules including `pub mod inventory_coverage;` at line 36 and no `audit_ledger`.

quote: echo "::error::`cargo test --no-run --message-format=json` produced no artifact this step could list,"
category: unescaped backtick executes a command inside an error message
summary: The backticks in this double-quoted shell string are command substitution, not markdown - so the diagnostic for a blind test census actually RUNS `cargo test --no-run --message-format=json` and splices its JSON output into the error annotation.
failure_scenario: The test-binary census finds zero binaries (the exact case this branch exists to report). Line 1047's `if [ "${binaries:-0}" -lt 1 ]` fires. Line 1049 then invokes `cargo test --no-run --message-format=json` - without `--workspace` or `--locked` - which on this workspace takes minutes and emits thousands of JSON lines, all of which are substituted into the `::error::` annotation. The operator sees a wall of compiler-artifact JSON instead of 'the test-binary census found 0 binaries after the workspace run.', on the one failure that means the instrument is blind. `echo`'s own exit status is 0, so errexit does not fire and the step still reaches the intended `exit 1` at 1051 - the damage is the lost diagnostic and the extra build.
positive_control: This is the ONLY unescaped backtick pair inside a double-quoted shell string in all 29 workflow files. `grep -n 'echo "[^"]*`' *.yml` returns 6 matches; the other 5 (ci.yml:146, 152, 161, 2660, 2668) all use `\``, and so does every one of the ~30 further matches in docker.yml, release.yml, plugin-consumer-verify.yml, manual-keep-proof.yml and verify-deploy.yml. The escaping convention is universal and this line is the single exception.

category: dead code under errexit / a diagnostic that can never print
summary: The release gate's `run:` block has no `shell:` key, so GitHub runs it as `bash -e {0}`; `set -uo pipefail` does not clear errexit, so when `cargo test` fails the pipeline at line 588 aborts the step and lines 589-609 - including the `::error::cargo test --workspace FAILED in the release gate` message - never execute.
failure_scenario: `cargo test --workspace --locked --verbose 2>&1 | tee "$RUNNER_TEMP/release-test.log"` (line 588) fails on the commit being staged. With errexit on and pipefail set, the step terminates immediately. `rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}` (589) never runs, the `if [ "$rc" -ne 0 ]` branch (594-596) is unreachable dead code, and the annotation at 595 that names the exit code has never once been printed. The release is still refused (the step is red), so the outcome is safe - the cost is that the gate's stated design does not operate and the operator gets a bare step failure instead of the named diagnostic.
